Uniform Title: *Sakalāgamasārasaṅgraha* Manuscript: IFP Transcript T0351 Description:
Transcription of IFP Transcript T0351. For details, consult the catalog record of the transcript in the IFP section of the Muktabodha Digital Library.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski.
Publication year: Pre-1900. Publication country: India.
Having entered a pure place, one should not look upon dogs, outcasts, those of the lowest castes, donkeys, dogs, women in their courses, dog-cookers, bones, or the food of pigs.
One should not injure the gums or the flesh of the teeth. As long as the teeth remain free from impurity, that indeed constitutes the cleansing of the teeth.
This is prescribed as the cleansing of the teeth, as well as the scraping of the tongue.
Śvaddhā (or *utthā*), *arkakhadira*, *kara*,
and *nālikera*;
likewise, grass, leaves, *palāśa* wood, flour, and the ashes of a woman and a man.
Nor should one praise one's fingers; otherwise, there will be a loss [of merit].
The mantras, sages, gods, and ancestors will turn their faces away from him if he performs it on a Sunday.
Thus, on the sixth lunar day of the dark fortnight, as well as on the ninth and eleventh, if there is contact with wood and teeth, it burns one's lineage up to the seventh generation.
On the eighth [day]... on the fifteenth, in three births.

One should avoid oil, meat, sexual intercourse, and the use of a tooth-stick on the full moon day, the new moon day, and at the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign. One who desires to eat should perform the cleansing of the teeth using purifying leaves.
In the absence of tooth-sticks, or when they are likewise prohibited—
(4B)— the purification of the mouth shall be accomplished by means of mouthfuls of water (*gaṇḍūṣa*).
Elsewhere:
In the case of urine, feces, food, or likewise the eating of [forbidden] things,
[it will be purified] by means of a mouthful of water.
Having rinsed the mouth with mouthfuls of water, one becomes pure on the left side.
Out of delusion, one may go to hell by [using it] on the right side;
in the *Cintyaviśva*,
it is stated that for one desiring liberation, the cleaning of the teeth with a twig must always be performed specifically.
The auspicious ritual bath in water should be performed.
The procedure for bathing is described in the Kāmika:
O Goddess of the Gods, five types of ablutions have been established for the sake of purification:
the Vāruṇa bath, the Āgneya bath, and so forth.
The Varuṇa bath is with water; the Āgneya bath is with ashes;
the Divya bath is with rain accompanied by sunshine; the Vāyavya bath is with dust.
p. 3) It is said that "new" refers to what are proclaimed as the five types of baths.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"In a river, a pond, a lake, or even a well—thus they are fourfold."
Even when rivers and such exist nearby, he would cross by swimming.
O Gajānana, it is true that one may perform a bath in a well without incurring fault, and likewise in tanks and other such bodies of water.
(The Procedure for Bathing) (5ā) A pond is ten times more meritorious than a well; a river is ten times more meritorious than a pond;
and a river flowing to the ocean is ten times more meritorious than that.
Thereafter, it is said that bathing while facing east yields a hundredfold merit;
one should perform the bath in a river while standing facing the current.
Even there, one should bring water—whether pure or impure—that flows near a temple of Śiva to the southern bank; this shall yield fruit.
One should know that [water] as Śivagaṅgā because it has been sprinkled from the water of Śiva’s abode.
In the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"One should never defile a sacred bathing place situated within a temple."
One should never, under any circumstances, perform a bath there while being extremely impure.
In the *Kāmika*:
"Alternatively, in one's own home, with either hot or cold water from nine, eight, or five jars consecrated with the *śiva-mantra*... (p. 4).
Then, seated upon a seat on a ground surface smeared with cow dung, one should perform the ritual bath.
Elsewhere it is stated:

"Having entered the water below the navel and washed the hips with clay and water, one should wipe the body with a clean cloth; this is remembered as the *mārjana* (cleansing) of the followers of Kapila."
For women, children, kings, those who are not ill, and travelers,
bathing with warm water or even a neck-bath (kaṇṭhasnāna) is prescribed.
One should not bathe in water without first removing five lumps [of earth];
[otherwise], the earth would become a hundredfold more effective.
Silver is a hundred times more meritorious than copper, and gold is a hundred times more meritorious than silver;
furthermore, bathing in the Kuṇḍoda and Nipāta [tirthas] is equal to performing a ritual bath.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Bathing at night is not recommended, yet it is recommended during eclipses;
for rivers always flow with blood at night."
Therefore, one should never perform bathing or drinking [of water];
nor should one show fire or gold in the vicinity of water.
The most excellent preceptor should also cause three breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*) to be performed;
O God, there shall be purification by water, for bathing at night is not prescribed.
Therefore, one should collect [the materials] during the day itself for the sake of the gods and for oneself with auspicious things.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Having sipped water, performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), holding *darbha* grass in his hand, and being of serene mind..."
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should recite the Saṃhitā preceded by the Praṇava.

Today, on such-and-such a day of the week, in such-and-such a month, on such-and-such a lunar date and weekday, O Lord, on this best of rivers, I shall perform my bath for the sake of worshipping you; be gracious to me.
Having gathered pure clay with the mantra *hūṃ phaṭ*, the practitioner [should do so] according to the *Kālottara*:
"From mountains, riverbanks, sacred fields, or pure locations."
From the Brahma-tree, [the water] situated at the base of the Kra-... flows from the well of the Dastras, well-guarded.
Taking clay the size of a palm tree, with its heart intact,
one should collect it on a pure spot of ground for a period of four months.
One should collect [the earth] during the rainy season, especially under the asterism of Rikṣa.
Having first performed the ritual bath for removing impurities, the wise practitioner should take up the clay while reciting the Astra-mantra once, and then perform the formal ritual bath.
As it has been said:

"That which draws out the filth from the limbs and minor members by means of powders ground with the moon (camphor) is called the 'impurity-bath' (malasnāna). Now hear about the 'mantra-bath' (mantrasnāna)."
The nose, the ears, and the eyes are purified by water.
One should cleanse the mouth with a tooth-stick, the hair with *āmalaka* and other such substances,
and the rest of the body with water and pure clay.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Water that is constantly frequented by fish, frogs, snakes, and other aquatic species is therefore specifically prescribed."
To pacify those defects, one should prepare a Śiva-tīrtha. The wise practitioner, having taken up earth with the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
should establish it with the Hṛdaya-mantra and sprinkle it with the Vāmadeva-mantra.
The eastern, southern, and northern [sides] shall each be three parts of a man's height.
One should cause each [deity] to enter with the Īśāna mantra;
one should then place the Brahma and Śiva-limbs (śivāṅga) in order, starting from the east.
One should cast that portion consecrated with the Astra-mantra into the ten directions;
one should cast that portion consecrated with the Śiva-mantra into the middle of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
By means of the mantra containing the syllable *phaṭ* and through the employment of the iron-arrow weapon (*nārācāstra*),
there shall be the eradication of those subtle defects that exist within the water.
Having consecrated the limbs of one's own body with a portion [of the water] over which the *brahman* has been recited,
one should then perform the ritual sipping (*upaspṛśya*) and bathe in the center of the *śivatīrtha*.
In the *Cintyaviśva*,
it is said: "One should sprinkle [the disciple] with the hands in the form of the moon and sun, using the *kumbha-mudrā*,
repeatedly with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and with the Brahma-mantras."
One should consecrate [the disciple] in sequence, visualizing the earth as nectar-water;
then, at the conclusion of the water-play, one should consecrate him with the face-mudrās.
In the Siddhānta:
"One should bind both ears with the two thumbs, the two eyes with the two index fingers, the mouth with the middle fingers, and the pair of nostrils firmly."
One should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times along with the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva.
In the Suprabheda it is said:
"Having covered the eye with water, one should not show [the face] with any part of the body."
And then one should show the face of the object, whether it be of Agni or otherwise.
That which is recited at the mouth and at the fire becomes a hundredfold;
by means of the "limb of wealth" (the heart), it becomes a thousandfold when submerged; and it is said to be ten millionfold [when submerged] in the navel.
In the *Smṛti*:
"O God, the gods drink from the head; the ancestors drink from the mouth;
all the Gandharvas [drink] from the middle; and all living beings [drink] from below."
Therefore, having bathed, one should not wipe oneself with the hand used for bathing; for as many as there are hairs on the body—three and a half crores in total—[so many sins are removed].
All sacred fords flow [within him]; one should not wipe away [the water] from them.
Having gone out while engaged in meditation, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in the proper sequence.
One should collect the water from Śiva’s sacred pool using the *vikāra* mantra;
then, one should wipe away the water clinging to the limbs with a dry cloth.
If it is damp, one should shake it seven times and not wipe it;
having covered it with a clean cloth, one should discard the damp cloth.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī* (7B): "A wise person should not perform a ritual while wearing only a single garment, nor while naked, nor while wearing only a loincloth (*kaupīna*),
during bathing, worship of the deity, sacrifice, or eating."
In the *Smṛti*:
"One who wears soiled garments is naked;
one whose garment is burnt is considered naked; and one who wears a cloth of human waste is traditionally known as naked."
p.
9) One should perform the ritual without sloth while still wearing a moist garment;
otherwise, that action becomes futile, and one must purify oneself by bathing again.
In the *Vīratantra*: "When one has sneezed, when lightning has struck, after vomiting, after the act of shaving, after sexual intercourse,
and after a bad dream or contact with a wicked person— bathing is prescribed in these six cases."
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"I shall now declare the purification of clothing, for by its purity one becomes pure;
one whose self is devoid of the purification of clothing becomes impure even if [otherwise] pure."
For the purpose of performing rites for the gods, purification of garments is required every day;
for other types of clothing, however, purification is to be performed whenever dirt appears.
In the Smṛti:
"Having folded the cloth fourfold and wrung it out of the water,
and having placed it on the left forearm, one becomes pure by sipping water twice."
Whenever he has bathed, he should perform the twilight devotions (sandhyopāsana),
because at the time of bathing, all [deities] always attend upon him.
Therefore, one should offer libations to the gods, sages, perfected beings, and ancestors.
Otherwise, they will turn away from him and depart upward in despair;
yet if they do offer them, all their desires will be satisfied.
The wise one should sprinkle [the vessel] three times with the Astra-mantra;
he should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) three times with the Astra-mantra and mutter it ten times.
And thus one should satisfy [the deities] at the twilight; or else, as it is said from the heart [mantra]:
"This is declared to be the water-bath; now hear about the ash-bath."
As the ocean Kṣīroda was being churned by the gods and the asuras, as stated in the Ārṇava [Purāṇa],
the five cows were born, the mothers of all the worlds.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and likewise Sumanā—
these five auspicious cows arrived at Śivapura by the will of Śiva.
[He saw] one that was tawny, black-and-white, smoky-colored, and likewise red,
for the benefit of all the worlds and for the gratification of the gods.
The mothers of the cows stood upon the ground for the purpose of bathing Śiva;
[they provided] cow dung, yellow pigment, urine, milk, curd, and ghee.
The six limbs [of the Veda] are pure and bestow all accomplishments.
Through cows, sacrifices are performed; in cows, the gods are established.
From cows, the Vedas were produced, together with their six limbs, words, and phonetic sequences.
(8B) At the base of the horns of cows, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are eternally established.
At the tip of my horn are all the sacred fords, both stationary and moving;
there I dwell as a calf, surrounded by all living beings.
O child, the brother [Vāsuki] is especially situated there on the forehead;
the two Nāgas, Kambala and Aśvatara, are stationed at the nostrils.
The two Aśvin gods are in the ears; the Moon and Sun are in the eyes;
the Marut gods are in the teeth; and Varuṇa resides in the tongue.
Sarasvatī resides in the *skāra*, Yama and Yakṣa in the two cheeks,
the Sandhyās in the two lips, and Indra is situated in the neck.
In the middle of the hooves are the Gandharvas, and at the tips of the hooves are the Pannagas;
at the rear tips of the hooves, the hosts of Apsarases are stationed.
The Rudras reside in the ten channels at the junctions;
the Pitṛs are situated on the surface of the hips, and Umā should be located in the chest.
Śrī resides eternally in the drinking water of cows, resting upon the tips of their tender grass;
the primordial [Ganges] herself is present in cow urine as the river Jāhnavī.
And likewise, all the sages are stationed upon the tips of his body hairs;
within his belly is the earth, complete with its mountains, forests, and groves.
The four oceans are indeed full breasts for the embodied one;
the glorious Bilva tree, beloved of Śiva, has arisen from cow dung.
There dwells Śrī, the lotus-handed; therefore it is called the Śrīvṛkṣa (the auspicious tree).
Furthermore, the seeds of blue and white lotuses are produced from cow dung.
All [virtues] have been declared to be eternally established in cows;
thus, having observed the cows, one should take cow-dung for the purpose of sacred ash.
In the Svāyambhuva [Kalpa],
O Goddess of gods: having risen at dawn, observing silence and the vow,
one should go to a cow-pen and pay obeisance to the herd of cows.
One should cause to be given yellow orpiment, ghee, milk, and cooked rice;
and having caused betel-leaf to be given, one should recite the Gosāvitrī mantra one hundred times.
We know the one with the sharp horns; we meditate upon the one whose feet are divine; may Gāya inspire us.
Likewise, the [flag] of a Brāhmaṇa is white, that of a Kṣatriya is red,
that of a Vaiśya is yellow, and that of a Śūdra is said to be black.
On the full moon day, the new moon day, the eighth lunar day, and during both types of eclipses, one should collect cow dung in the respective order; otherwise, one should not collect it.
One who is barren, aged, diseased, or possessed of ill-omened marks; likewise one who is devoid of earlobes, and one who is bereft of what is called a "child" [or lacks a child].
Impure food, that which is meditated upon, that which is not meditated upon, the secondary substitute, the near substitute, and the non-substitute.
O you of noble vows, listen now to their characteristics and their sequence:
the tawny cow with its proper marks, the red, the white, and the one other than white.
And one should hold their cow-dung,
along with lotus leaves or even palāśa leaves, in both hands while in the air.
Or, having taken cow dung in a vessel, one should hold it with the *sabda-mantra*;
the balls [of clay] should be formed with the *vāma-mantra* and dried with the *aghora-mantra*.
In the body, [the rite] is performed with Tatpuruṣa alone, while in the case of the Īśāna [face], it is in summary;
now listen, O Nandikeśvara, to the secondary alternative (anukalpa) as well.
Having taken dried [substance] from the forest and powdered it, one should likewise burn it;
the resulting ash, placed between a cloth and formed into a ball bound with cow urine, [should be used].
The preparation of the ashes should be performed according to the previously stated procedure;
setting aside the previously stated procedure, there is the practice of the ashes alone.
Ash prepared by another is considered non-ritualistic; however, that which is prepared by oneself is ritualistically valid. One should especially place it in nine new vessels.
(10ā) One should recite the Vyomavyāpin mantra once, together with the five Brahmans and the Śiva-aṅgas.
According to the Cintyaviśva:
"With camphor, uśīra, hībera, and ketakī, as well as with saffron..."
One should especially cast it into that [vessel] with the mantra of Damaneśāna.
The *ketakī*, *mallikā*, *nāgakeśara*, *campaka*, and *pāṭala* flowers, as well as the *padma*, *palāśa*, *tulasī*, *apāmārga*, and the tips of *kuśa* grass.
Having placed the *jāti* seed there, one should take hold of it along with the excellent vessels;
the wise person should then cast it into a receptacle of ash within an earthenware bowl.
The abode of the ashes shall be Śakti, and those ashes are indeed Śiva;
one should wear that thread, which has Brahmā as its presiding deity, with the Kavaca mantra alone.
O Mataṅga, having first performed the water-bath, one should thereafter perform the ash-bath;
if one is unable to perform the water-bath, one should perform the ash-bath instead.
In the Somaśambhu [Tantra]: "The head is to be smeared with the Īśāna [mantra], the face with the Tatpuruṣa,
the heart with the Aghora, and the navel is proclaimed to be with the Vāma."
The wise one, having immediately sprinkled all the limbs with the mantra, [should proceed].
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Now, therefore, by that which is perfected through ritual and consecrated by the *saṃhitā* mantra..."
One should perform a bath with ashes that have been purified by the *nivṛtti* and other kalās.
From the head down to the feet, using the arrow-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
this should be known as the "impurity bath" (*malasnāna*), which does not require clay for the "pure bath" (*śuddhasnāna*).
In the *Cintyaviśva*,
the practitioner of mantra should separate [the breath] at thirty-two junction-points, or sixteen,
or eight junctions, within the five locations.
On the head, on the forehead, on the two ears, as well as on the two eyes,
on the tip of the nose, and then on the two shoulders.
In the upper arms, at the wrists, in the heart,
in both sides, in the navel, in the two private parts, and in the pair of thighs, the bones, and the knees.
The two shanks and the two feet constitute the thirty-two supreme locations;
they are indeed dear to the eight forms and likewise to the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas).
One should assign the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and the Vasus to the head and other parts:
in the cause [body], on the head, the forehead, the two ears, and also on the two shoulders.
In the ears and the shoulders, in the forearms and the wrists, in the heart, at the sides of the navel,
and likewise on the back— at each of these locations, as well as in the shanks— reside their respective presiding deities.

One who has taken the vow of Śiva should indeed wear the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) on sixteen locations. Ash worn on the head burns away sins committed over the cheeks; that [ash] on the neck [burns] the sin of eating forbidden food; that on the two arms [burns] the sin committed against one's child; and that on the chest [burns] what is cherished by the mind.

(p. 16) One should say that [the wound] is caused by the penis at the navel, likewise caused by the anus at the back, and caused by the feet at the knees and sides; and anything else is called "other."
It is recorded in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Śiva, Sadāśiva, Maheśa, Brahmā, and Pañcaka—
these, O child, are the sixteen presiding deities of the Vidyeśvaras.
I shall now declare the eight locations as well as the deities of the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra): Brahmā himself resides in the place of the head, and Skanda indeed in the forehead.
Vināyaka is pleased at the throat, and Viṣṇu indeed at the two arms;
Īśvara is pleased at the heart, and Vasundhara at the navel;
and the Pitṛs are pleased at the back—thus eight tripuṇḍras are proclaimed.
Alternatively, [one may worship] the head, the arms, the heart, and the navel.
There are five locations on the forehead, and the deity consists of five forms;
one should perform all sacrificial rites by means of the *tripuṇḍra* alone.
The letter *a* is said to be the ring finger, the letter *u* the middle finger, and the letter *m* the index finger;
with these three, one forms the *tripuṇḍra*.
In the Dviśatikālottara (p.
17): Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the presiding deities of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
creation, maintenance, and dissolution are the very nature of the triple mark.
The ancestors are pleased on the back, and Vasundhara is likewise in the navel.
In the *Suprabheda*: "A width of six finger-breadths is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas;
the *tripuṇḍra* of Kṣatriyas has a width of four finger-breadths."
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) three finger-breadths wide grants all desires for Vaiśyas;
for Śūdras and especially for women, it should be one finger-breadth wide.
For women belonging to various lineages, the corresponding deity is prescribed for each.
When ignited, a width of seven finger-breadths is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas;
five finger-breadths for Kṣatriyas; and four finger-breadths for Vaiśyas.
For Śūdras it should be three finger-breadths, and for women it should be one finger-breadth.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"A half-line [tilaka] destroys longevity, while a long line causes the loss of austerity;
therefore, a wise person should wear the triple-line (*tripuṇḍra*) with a measurement equal to the distance between the two eyes."
Whatever mark has been drawn on the forehead with ash,
one should likewise draw that same mark on the two arms, the head, and between the breasts.
For the remaining [deities], it is specifically taught that the *tripuṇḍra* should be one finger-breadth (*ekāṅgula*) in width.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"From head to foot, the twice-born indeed performs the ash-bath;
[the body] above the earth is the self, [anointed] with blood and with ash."
For the Vaiśya, a vertical line is prescribed; for the Śūdra alone, the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra).
In the *Sūkṣma-tantra*,

it is stated that for Brahmins and the other castes, the quantity of ash is one *niṣka* and two *niṣkas* respectively for the two purposes [of purification and adoration], according to the descending order of castes.
The ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) is indeed prescribed for the four classes beginning with the Brahmins;
however, for all those of the outcaste classes (*antyajātī*), it shall be performed without mantras.
In the Dviśatikālottara:
"The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is for gods and brahmins;
the half-moon (ardhacandra) is for kings and vaiśyas; but for śūdras and those outside the [four] castes, it is the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka)."
The *liṅga* form, the lamp, the *puṇḍraka*,
the circular *uddhūlana*— these six constitute the teaching of Śiva.
p. 19) Regarding the cause:
by means of the single method of applying two or three *puṇḍra*s [of ashes] upon the practitioner’s son who has entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*), all protection is established.
In the *Dviśatikālottara*:
"One who wears a single-line *tripuṇḍra* with its lines facing downwards shall,
after passing through a hundred births as a dog, take refuge in the possession of a *caṇḍāla*."
Whoever applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with two hands using upward-facing [ashes],
is glorified in the world of Rudra for thousands of years.
One should always wear the Tripuṇḍra mark with ashes mixed with water;
having uplifted twenty-one generations of one's lineage, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
As many atoms of ash as fall upon the ground,
for that many thousands of eons shall that perpetrator go to hell.
One should not look upon the face of a Brahmin who is devoid of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
if one converses with him, one should recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times.
Know, O Great Sage, that ash is the supreme Brahman, associated with truth and bliss;
by means of ash, all sins and defects are destroyed.
It is celebrated as *bhasma* because it terrifies the [obstacles];
it is *rakṣā* because it protects from fears; and likewise, it is *bhāsita* because of its radiant brilliance.

The syllable *bha* signifies the severance of existence (*bhava*), and likewise, the syllable *sma* signifies the connection with the recollection of existence; thus it is called *bhasma*. [This should be applied] at the three junctions of the day (*sandhyā*), at midnight, and at the beginning and end of sleep.
(13ā) Having performed [his duties], having drunk milk, and having attended to his natural calls and other necessities,
he should avoid a woman, a eunuch, a Śūdra, a cat, a crane, and a mouse.
Having touched such [impure things], one should not perform any other fire-related ablution (*āgneyasnāna*).
As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"From seeing an outcaste in the vicinity of the gods, the fire, the guru, or the *vidyā*..."
One should not perform the smearing with cow dung on a path where the ground is impure.
He who, having conquered his senses, performs daily that Agneya bath shall uplift twenty-one generations of his lineage and go to the supreme state.
Even by means of deceit, he who upholds the divine sovereignty and governance of these two [the king and the priest] attains a state that cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices.
In the Śivadharmottara: "Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords (tīrthas) and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices—
all that fruit one undoubtedly gains from bathing in ashes."
One who is joined with great sins, or joined with all sins, should practice the bath of ashes; he is liberated from all sins.
That [instruction] was declared to all the gods by Śiva himself when he had bathed.
From that time forward, Brahmā and the others, as well as the sages seeking Śiva,
have diligently performed the ash-bath on all festival days.
Therefore, one should perform this fire-related auspicious bath in such a manner.
O Agni, there is no doubt that one does not become Rudra by means of the physical body alone;
rather, after performing a hundred ritual baths with water, one must perform a hundred thousand ritual baths with mantras.
By the mere act of smearing oneself with ashes, one becomes Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt.
With a body smeared with ashes from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, [one attains liberation].
The body becomes the *liṅga* through constant vibration; that body is called the *liṅga*.
In the Vāsiṣṭhalaiṅgika:
"One should perform a bath with ashes or apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) at the three junctions of the day;
having one's self purified of all sins, one rejoices together with Śiva."
Those who follow the Śrauta and Smārta injunctions yet abandon the wearing of ashes—
the ritual acts performed by them always yield contrary results.
O Brahmin, if anger arises in those who see the ashes on [one's] forehead,
a wise person should infer that their own birth is of mixed origin.
Those men who, upon seeing one who wears ashes, revile him with their speech—
their birth from a Śūdra should be inferred by the wise.
Those men who, out of anger, strike one who wears the sacred ash, shall be reborn as Caṇḍālas; this should be understood by the wise for many births to come.
(14ā) O Sage, for those who always lack faith in what is heard [in the Vedas],
it is certain that for them there are no purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the impregnation ceremony (*garbhādhāna*).
O Brahmin, those whose hearts always harbor hatred toward their ashes— their lineage shall become defiled.
Those who become truly delighted upon seeing one who wears the sacred ash are undoubtedly worthy of worship by gods, asuras, and humans alike.
In the Vāsiṣṭha:
"O Sage, he who knows me as the supreme ash-form and [the fire] arisen from the Agnihotra and other rites..."
By means of this mantra, he bestows the fair [state];
through supreme knowledge alone, he attains liberation.
O Brahmin, there is nothing equal to ashes even in the three worlds;
formerly, for the sake of protection, for the sake of auspiciousness, and for the sake of purification, [I used it].
The ash seen by the Sage was given to the Goddess by the Beloved;
the Vedic ash worn upon the surface of the forehead generates divine vision.
Since she spreads that crescent moon upon her head, the white mark upon her neck,
the deer upon her body, and the trident upon her two arms, [she is a woman].
Blessed are those who possess that; O faultless one, I shall speak of this stainless [nature] of yours.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "One should apply the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with white ashes during the three junctions of the day;
being liberated from all sins, one rejoices together with Śiva."
Truth, charity, recitation of mantras, and the worship of lamps—
all this is in vain for one who does not wear the Tripuṇḍra.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"One whose self is purified by the ash-bath, who has conquered anger and subdued the senses,
having approached my presence, does not return again."
In the Śaiva-saṃhitā: "Whoever, having performed thousands of actions, bathes with ashes—
that entire [karmic residue] the ashes burn away, just as fire consumes a forest by its heat."

In the Skanda Purāṇa: "One who desires prosperity and one who desires nourishment should always apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with a paste of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, jasmine, and saffron."
(24) For all castes and stages of life, and for all living beings,
the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is proclaimed as the means for the pacification of all bonds.
Just as Rudra is celebrated in all the Vedas as being superior to the universe.
Likewise, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is also extolled in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa] and in all the Purāṇas.
In the description of the deities associated with the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) within the *Sāpatyasaṃhitā*:
"The fourteen great sages, beginning with Svāyambhuva..."
With all their limbs golden like glowing coals, they wear white sacred threads.
With their bodies adorned with the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) and decorated with various rudrākṣa beads,
they offered a garland of Śambhu’s lotus feet to their heads and paid homage.
And the highly fortunate Sāvitrī, whose form resembles the jasmine flower and the moon,
is radiant, adorned with rudrākṣa beads, and wears a crown of matted locks.
With a rosary in one hand and a water-pot in her lotus-like hand,
her limbs smeared with ashes and marked with the triple-line forehead-tilaka, she shone with the Āṣāḍha staff.
He served Maheśvara with the resonance of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
his arms were like the great sun, possessing a luster equal to seven golden [mountains].
Endowed with the resonance of the Veda and adorned with the three auspicious marks,
he shone with matted locks and a crest, and was encircled by rosaries of rudrākṣa beads.
The highly auspicious *praṇava* is the designator of the Supreme Being;
[he is one] adorned with ornaments of *rudrākṣa* beads and having his forehead marked with the triple-line (*tripuṇḍra*).
He worshipped Mahādeva, the abode of the hearts of yogis,
adorned with triple-lined sectarian marks (tripuṇḍra) and rudrākṣa beads.
And then Viṣṇu, whose body hairs were scorched by the ashes, shone;
thus [it was seen] by all the sages, including those who recite the Vedas, the Gāyatrī, the Praṇava, and Viṣṇu.
One who wears ash, rudrākṣas, and so forth, as prescribed by the Śiva-scriptures, is liberated; how much more so others? Indeed, since ash requires purification, it possesses no inherent purity.
Because white clay does not require any further preparation (*saṃskāra*).
Because of its inherent purity:

"He on whose forehead a white sectarian mark (puṇḍra) made with clay is seen above, even if he be an outcaste (caṇḍāla), he is a pure soul and is certainly worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt."
Such also is the statement of the Smṛti.

For this very reason, some say that only white clay should be worn. To this we reply: because the ash-bath is declared to be a purifier superior to bathing in water, and because ashes are to be thrown into food that has been defiled by flies or hair at the time of eating.

Furthermore, because it has been so stated, ash is eternally pure. For that [ash], the purificatory rites such as drying and so forth are performed with mantras, just as the purificatory rites such as initiation (*upanayana*) are for the soul (*ātman*) which is pure by birth; these are intended for the attainment of excellence in qualities and for the removal of defects.
Furthermore, if clay were primary by virtue of its independence from human effort (*saṃskāra*), it would follow that even a Śūdra is primary compared to a Brāhmaṇa.
Moreover, an option (*vikalpa*) arises only when there is a conflict between two things of equal force; however, in a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, the Śruti alone prevails.
By the principle that "the stronger prevails," since the wearing of that [ash] is primary according to the Śruti,
even the performance of the Smārta practice of wearing clay and so forth is indeed fruitless;
thus Garga said:
"A Brahmin who, disregarding Vedic ritual, performs only Smārta and Itihāsa rites, is not joined with merit.
Furthermore, it is not merely fruitlessness; rather, there is the fault that such [neglect] destroys the Vedic ritual of the Brahmin.
Likewise, ash is both a subordinate quality and otherwise;

it is eternally pure. Its consecration consists of drying and other rites performed with mantras. For, having abandoned that which is dominated by impurity (*ṣma-pradhāna*), one goes to a lower state.
And so it is said in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"A learned Brāhmaṇa should not transgress the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) even in his mind;
since it is enjoined by the Śruti, one who abandons it becomes fallen."
Therefore, because it is held that "it is called *smṛti*," it is well established that the wearing of the *vibhūti* [ash] prescribed by the *śruti* alone is primary, and nothing else.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"One should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), which bestows the fruit of liberation for all living beings," so said the unborn Lord in the *Smṛtisaṅgraha*.

Fie upon Time devoid of ashes! Fie upon the village that is the abode of the inauspicious Śivā! Fie upon a birth spent in the worship of Nīśā! Fie upon a village that is hostile to the nature of Śiva!
In a *śrāddha*, a sacrifice, a recitation (*japa*), an oblation (*homa*), a ritual for the ancestors (*vaiśvadeva*), or the worship of the gods—
whatever is performed by one who does not wear the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) shall all become fruitless.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Saṃhitā]:
"One who bears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) upon his forehead, adorned with the emblem of the trident—even if he be of low birth—he is to be honored by the gods, let alone by human beings. (p. 28)
In the Liṅga Purāṇa: "One should devoutly wear a trident at the root of the right arm,
carry a bull upon the left shoulder, and [apply] the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead."
Constantly serving Rudra, one shall attain the form of Rudra.
In the northwest—
to him whose body is smeared with ashes, he who joyfully gives wealth,
all his sins perish; of this there is no doubt.
O Sage, for those who first smear themselves with ashes, even that which is normally unfit to be eaten becomes fit to be eaten; there is no doubt about this.
Even the killing of a thousand cows and tens of thousands of Brahmins—
by means of even a small amount of this sacred ash, one becomes the destroyer of all sins.
When the Soma has entered the forest trees, one whose body is smeared with ashes,
upon seeing the temple of Īśvara, casts off the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Whether he be immoral or endowed with virtue, or whoever he may be, lacking auspicious marks yet joined to the prosperity of the teaching— he is to be honored like a prince.
What is the use of saying much? The wearing of ashes is the means to liberation.
In the *Makuṭa*:
"O Sage, I shall explain specifically the form of the deity [constituted by] the ashes."
Three-eyed, three-headed, fierce, with what [is] in his hand, and having qualities as his face.
Three-legged, with three eyes, his body smeared with ashes and carrying a water-pot;
he is formidable with the grandeur of his Tandava dance, adorned with red flowers.
Having meditated upon the Lord, the Sovereign of Protective Mantras, a person shall obtain power;
facing north, remaining silent, and having meditated upon Śiva as the Guru.
As long as not even a particle of ash the size of an atom has fallen upon the ground,
for that duration one should apply the Tripuṇḍra by smearing it with the collected ashes.
One should perform the ritual at the three junctions of the day, or even according to one's capacity for bathing and intelligence;
women should also wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), provided it is devoid of water.
For those such as forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas) and maidens, and likewise for men who have not received initiation,
[the rite] is performed with water before midday and without water thereafter.
What need is there for much speaking here, O Lord of Gods? Like the glance of the Lord, all sins whatsoever shall perish without effort.

The ash-bath is purifying, constantly making one pure, destroying disease, leading to excellent liberation, equal to the sacred ford of the Gaṅgā, removing all poisons, destroying anger, and bringing perfect peace.

This enumeration of the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Yakṣas, and Śrutigaṇas brings satisfaction and nourishment; it is a means of subjugation in the world for men, a source of happiness for all people through the grace of the Lord of Pārvatī.

The ash-bath is the foremost for pacifying manifold sins, superior to the water-bath in effecting both external and internal purification; it utterly destroys the fear of worldly existence by its mere sight,
is preeminent in removing all diseases and impurities, and brings about the manifestation of the fire of the Vedas.
It was lifted up by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śatakratu, and others, who bowed their heads in reverence.
It is prosperity, the bringer of prosperity, the supreme purifier that destroys the flood of sins;
it is the destroyer of all calamities, the bestower of the highest wealth of good fortune,
and the protector against ghosts, spirits, piśācas, rākṣasas, and the hosts of apasmāra.
May this manifestation of power, which directly brings about liberation and is laden with fruit, be always worn [upon the body].

O men, those who have performed the prescribed bathing with water and ashes, the salutations at the three junctions of the day (*sandhyā*), and the worship of the Sun, and who have carried out the fivefold purification (*pañcaśuddhi*)—
if such people behold you here, they shall be victorious according to the sacred injunctions.
O Śiva, you grant them liberation free from obstacles.
The sacred ash applied to the surface of the forehead produces the mark of the moon;

when placed upon the head, it spreads that crescent; white ash on the neck forms the spot; on the body it creates a woman; and since the trident is formed by the two arms— [it is the very form of Śiva].
Blessed are those who uphold this stainless [teaching]; I shall speak of it, O faultless one, to you.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"When the rain of sunbeams has fallen [upon the earth], the Lord, facing east with arms raised,
should perform the *māhendra* bath for seven steps."
Thereafter, the wise man, facing the sun, should offer salutations;
when this is done, he is liberated from great sins—of this there is no doubt.
One situated in the center of a cow's horn should perform a bath with the dust raised by its hoof-strikes,
using the *pāvana* human mantra or else that [cow's] armor-mantra.
O God, sprinkling with water using the mantras beginning with *sadyojāta* constitutes the *mantra-snāna*; this applies to both the *vāruṇa* and *āgneya* types of bathing as well.
In the *Kālottara*:
"Having bathed in this manner according to the prescribed rule, the destruction of all sins occurs.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: [p. 32]
Having tied his topknot and washed his head, feet, and hands with water,
he should sit in a clean place facing either the east or the north.
With hands placed between the knees, remaining silent, and with a mind focused on nothing else, one should not look at dogs or other such creatures while using clear and cool water.
One should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with water that is free from foam and bubbles, purified by a cloth, and drawn up [from a vessel],
but not with water that is defiled by worms, deficient, or frequented by those of other castes.
Having taken up water sufficient to submerge a masha-bean with the hollow of the left hand,
one should gaze at it and drink it using the Brahma-tirtha located at the base of the thumb.
O Ajita, that which is indicated by a Brahmin should be at the heart; for a king, it should be at the throat;
for Vaiśyas, it should be at the palate; and for Śūdras, it should be at the lips.
And for the castes beginning with the Brahmins, the *ussāga* (exhalation) should occur in sequence.
As stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"With the syllables *hāṃ*, *hīṃ*, and *hūṃ*, preceded by the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), and followed by *svadhā*, [one should perform the rites] beginning with the *ātmatattva*."
By those who have attained purification through the principles ending with the power of the message of Māyā.
However, having washed one's hands repeatedly at intervals,
one should cleanse the two lips in the prescribed manner with the base of the thumb for the goddesses.
As stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
Four-armed and four-faced, seated upon a square lotus,
this is indeed remembered as the Ātmatattva, possessing the luster of molten gold.
He holds a garland and a water-pot in his left hands and a rosary in his right;
resembling a dark blue sapphire, he is dark blue and endowed with eight arms and eight facets.

He holds in his right and left hands the discus, arrows, lotus, the gesture of consciousness (*cinmudrā*), conch, bow, water-pot, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the gesture of union (*yoga*).
One should know that the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), which is called "Gentle" (saumya), has one face;
it resembles pure crystal, is circular, and contains all objects within it.
This is indeed remembered as the Śiva-tattva, having five faces and four arms;
in the right [hands] a lotus and a rosary, and in the left a trident and a water-pot.
In the *Tantrasāra*: "One should touch the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, heart, arms, and head with the tips of the thumb and ring finger, using the right and left hands respectively."
The thumb is called *parā*; the portion [of the earth] measured by the ring finger is *anāmikā*.
By means of that [earth], which is essentially clay, the gods are satisfied; through it, O Trita, they become free from disease.
The actions of the performer of that rite become augmented by the presence of the *bhāva*;
the Goddess of Speech resides at the tip of the tongue, and the *praṇava* is situated within the cavity of the lips.
In the two nostrils reside the breath, the eyes, the moon, and the sun;
in the two ears, all the directions; Brahmā is in the navel, and Rudra is in the heart.
For the sake of purification, Viṣṇu is situated on the head and the two Aśvins in the armpits;
having meditated upon the *puṇḍra* according to the previously mentioned rule, one should then perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and perform the placement (*nyāsa*).
Regarding the cause:
one should purify the palms and the backs of the hands with the *astra-mantra*.
One should purify the right hand once and the left hand twice with the *astra-mantra*.
Having performed the visualization with "Oṃ hāṃ [Name] Śaktaye Vauṣaṭ," one should assign the two seats and the two forms. Then, having placed [the mantras] on the thumbs of both palms,
one should subsequently assign the five Brahmans from the thumb to the little finger.
Having sequentially deposited [the mantras] beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta upon the two palms, the wise one should then deposit the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) upon the thumbs.
If one places the eye upon the palm of the hand with the middle fingers,
having assigned the temple (prāsāda) to the fingers, one should then assign the limbs.

Having performed the placement [of mantras] from the heart to the ends of the hands and from the little finger to the other fingers, one should enclose the center with the fingers using the *kavaca* [mantra],
as stated in the *Kālottara*:
"Having placed [the mantras] with the fingers, one should enclose the middle with the *kavaca*."
Then, one should place the temple upon all the fingers of the hands.
The ritual placement on the hands has been fully explained; now hear the ritual placement on the limbs.
Having taken [the substance] with the right thumb and ring finger and having placed it upon the seat and the image,
one should then duly install the five Brahmans within the body.
O Ajitā,
one should place the five *piṇḍas* in sequence, beginning with Īśāna, upon the head, the mouth, the region of the heart, the secret region, and finally the two feet.
One should place Īśa on the crown of the head with the tip of the thumb while forming a fist;
and Tatpuruṣa on the mouth by joining the index finger and the thumb.
One should likewise place the Aghora mantra at the heart by joining the middle finger with the thumb;
and one should place the Vāma mantra at the private parts by joining the thumb with the ring finger.
Joining the little finger with the thumb and placing the feet in the *savyojāta* posture,
one should place the body of the Vidyā upon the heart using the tips of the thumb and ring finger.
One should place the eye [mantra] at a distance of three middle fingers from the eyes;
having placed the temple [mantra] in the heart, one should subsequently place the limbs and other parts.
One should assign the deity to the heart and other limbs, the armor (kavaca) between the breasts,
and then assign it with the two index fingers as a covering for the throat.
One should place one's own mantra on the palms with both ring fingers. (p.
36) According to Somaśambhu:
"One should cast [the mantra] in all directions, preceded by three *tāla* claps."

Having displayed snapping of the fingers at the front of Śiva for the sake of protection as a warder-off of obstacles, and having shown the enclosure with the armor-mantra (tanutra) outside that, accompanied by a moat, one should then [recite] from the letter *ka* to the end of the feet while displaying the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*).

The *hṛdaya* is the protection for the heart, the binding of a cloth; the *padāhika* is for the feet. The *śiras* is the protection for the head, the wrapping around the head. The *cūlikā* is the protection for the crown of the head, and the *kaṅkaṭa* is the armor that protects the limbs.
But when he stands upon the ground with a terrifying weapon grasped in his hand.
Because they are not to be touched by the low-born, they are called Tākṣya and Arkashravasa;
Brahmāṇī is said to be short, while the six-faced one has long limbs.
The *anusvāra* should be the eye, situated above all [the letters];
the weapon-mantra (*astra*) should be accompanied by the *visarga* and devoid of the *anusvāra*.
O twice-born one, in the case of the *kāraṇas*, one should perform salutation in due order to Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna, and Brahmāṇī. O son of Kṛṣṇa, this is the salutation.
The heart, the head, the crest-lock,
the armor, the eyes, and the weapon— these are proclaimed as the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in their proper sequence.
*Namas*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ* are, in their respective order, the six suffixes;
these are indeed joined with the seed-syllables of the heart-mantra and the others, up to the weapon-mantra.
In the *Sārddhatrīśatikā*:
"The short [vowel] burns away sins; the long [vowel] bestows liberation;
and the prolated [vowel], adorned with a bindu on its head, causes [the elements] to expand."
In the *Mantrāvartika*:
"Vaṣaṭ" is for subjugation (*vaśya*); "phaṭ" for eradication (*uccāṭa*); "hu" for hatred (*dveṣa*) and also for killing (*māraṇa*);
"vauṣaṭ" for paralyzing (*stambha*); and "namaḥ" for summoning (*ākarṣa*).
"SVĀHĀ is power (śakti) and SVADHĀ is nourishment (puṣṭi)—these are the sprouts of mantra.
Having performed the act of supreme unification (paramīkaraṇa), one should employ the great mudrās."
The wise one should touch with both hands [the body] from the letter *ka* at the feet to the end;
for those [deities], the Mahāmudrā is the mudrā used in the rite of purifying the limbs.
In the Pauṣkara:
"If there is no distinct purpose for those whose essential nature is undivided,
then that [act] is indeed the immortalization of the attribute together with the substratum."
In the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī*:

"Having performed the ritual of total identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and being established through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the practitioner of mantra should mentally recite the *Śivasaṃhitā* three times. (p. 38)
Having sipped water again as before and performed the binding of the ears, [it is said] in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Prāṇa is the vital air residing in the body; its *āyāma* is its restraint."
Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka) are known as the three types of breath control.
The wise one, concentrated in mind, should exhale the upward-moving breath for thirty-two mātrās; then, as before, he should fill [the body] with the left [nostril].
One should properly fill the abdomen with external air like a leather bag;
first, one should fill it for sixteen mātrās, and likewise perform the kumbhaka.
One should properly fill [the vessel] with a *kumbha* measuring four or eight [units];
then, until the sun [sets], one should meditate upon oneself as being filled with nectar.
One should exhale through the right nostril and fill the abdomen through the left;
one should then perform the retention (kumbhaka)—this is the definition of prāṇāyāma. Through exhalation, the lotus faces downward; through inhalation, it becomes adorned with flowers.
Through the retention of breath (kumbhaka), the proximity of Śiva is attained; this is remembered as the fruit of prāṇāyāma.
Iḍā should be known as the digit of the moon, and Piṅgalā as the solar ray;
one should fill the wind through both nostril-circles by means of these two.
Alternatively, having assigned ten measures (mātrās) to each syllable of the Praṇava,
perform the filling [of the breath] and so forth in sequence, conjoined with the Saṃhitā mantra.
One neither releases nor inhales the air situated within or without;
one should remain like a completely filled jar—this is the immovable *kumbhaka*.
Having purified the water by means of inspection and other rites, the knower of mantras, using the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*,
draws the sacred site (*tīrtha*) onto his forehead with the *śakti-mantra*.

One should perform the rite of *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the transformation into nectar) to ward off obstacles. As stated in the *Suprabheda*: "Having formed the *veṇībandha* mudrā with the hands, the two thumbs should be placed together."
The index and middle fingers are joined, and the little fingers are joined together.
(22ā) Thus, the four pairs are the showerers of divine nectar;
Eḍā and Surabhimudrā are said to be for the purpose of purifying the substances.
In the *Mohaśruttara*:
"The best [time for] the lunar mansion is when it is not yet visible; the middling is when the stars have disappeared;
the maiden [should perform] the morning twilight worship when the sun has half-risen and is reddish."
Likewise, at midday, it should be known as consisting of three ghaṭikās;
[the time] when half the solar disc has set is excellent, while when the sun has fully set, it is middling.
The evening twilight, when the youngest constellation is visible, is considered to be threefold;
one should perform the twilight worship by standing with palms joined in reverence during the morning and sitting during the evening.
Seated or standing in the midst, the practitioner should recite while seated;
for one established in the twilight rite (saṃdhyā), there are two special daily observances.
For one who has been initiated into nirvāṇa here, the three junctions (sandhyās) have been proclaimed;
at the fourth junction as well, the supreme teacher [should act] as before.

For a householder, [the practice] at night is never [permitted], except during the sun's southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). However, for those who have renounced [worldly life], it is always recommended for everyone without distinction.
One should meditate upon Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, Raktā, Śuklā, and Sitetara, at dawn, midday, evening, and twilight, respectively, in their proper order.
One should meditate on all the witnesses of every rite as wearing black antelope skins,
their bodies entered by the coils of the circle of their radiance.
(22B) Now, the four supreme junctions (*sandhyā*) for the wise are described:
thin like a lotus fiber, red, white, and blackish-white;
or that which is perceived at midnight, having the nature of the Fourth (*turya*).
These [energies] reside, in sequence, in the heart, the bindu, the brahmarandhra, and the supreme state.
Three [periods] are joined with the breath and so forth, while the fourth consists of qualities (*guṇavartitā*).
At the end of the sun and moon are the two twilights for those practitioners of prāṇayoga.
That which is intent upon the awakening of Śiva is called the supreme *sandhyā*;
for the wise, the state of constant absorption in Śiva is declared to be *sandhi*.
Then, having made the sacred water (tīrtha) consist of Śiva through mantras that are Śiva-natured,
and having first formed the *kumbha-mudrā*, one should then meditate once upon the *saṃhitā*— which is very smooth, uniform, and flowing with nectar.
Then he would be as one who has bathed in all the sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist upon the earth.
The practitioner of mantra should join the water from the left hand with all the fingers;
sprinkling it sequentially upon the head is declared to be *mārjana*.
In the *Kāmika*:

"Having brought that water for worship, which is white in nature and consists of consciousness, held within the hollow of the right hand, one should draw it in through the left [nostril] and retain it in the *kumbhaka*."

Then, taking water that has the luster of collyrium with the fist of the Piṅgalārcī [mudrā], one should pour it upon the vajra-stone; that becomes the *aghamarṣaṇa*. Then, having sipped water twice and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one whose mind is composed—

Whenever one has sipped water for purification (ācamana), the practitioner of mantra should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the hands and body for the sake of attaining the goal of the mantra.
In the *Sūkṣma*—
One should take water in the left hand and circumambulate it while reciting the Astra-mantra;
then, in the subtle [state], one should meditate upon the peaceful Sadāśiva residing in the center of the solar disc.
With the auspicious mantra ending in "svāhā," accompanied by kuśa grass, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice.
Having offered water for the *arghya* to Śiva, one should recite the Gāyatrī [mantra] three times,
[visualizing] the Supreme Goddess, who possesses the luster of molten gold and who establishes the observance (*samaya*).

Having meditated upon Gāyatrī as four-armed and three-eyed, arisen from that [Brahmā], bearing in her hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a rosary, and a water-pot— one should then begin the recitation of Gāyatrī according to the prescribed method.
Recited seven times, it purifies him; recited ten times, it causes him to reach heaven.
If that goddess is recited twenty times, she leads one to the abode of Īśvara;
by reciting it one hundred and eight times, she delivers one from the ocean of births.

For the purpose of illuminating the mantras, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) of the Saṃhitā in due order. As stated in the Kāmika: "The mantra accompanied by kuśa grass, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds should be offered as a libation of water."
(23B) For the deities of those mantras, [the ending] is *svāhā*, but for the sages (*munis*), it ends with *namaḥ*.
For humans, the word is "vaṣaṭ"; for spirits, it ends with "vauṣaṭ";
and for ancestors and others, it should end with "svadhā," performed appropriately while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītin).
The libation offered at the tips of the fingers is dear to the gods. A wise man should satisfy the gods with *kuśa* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains;
the sages with *kuśa* grass and barley; and the ancestors with sesame seeds.
In the *Kālottara*:
"One should satisfy the gods and the sages with water alone.
This is also stated in the *Smṛti*:
Having lifted up water in a quantity equal to the tip of a cow's horn, one should pour it into the midst of the water;
however, for the ancestors, one should always perform the rite according to the rules on the bank of the water.
In the Kāmika:
"The divine (daivika) sacred site (tīrtha) is at the tip of the hand; the rishi-related (ārṣaka) is at the joints of the fingers;
the sacred site at the base of the little finger is proclaimed as that of Prajāpati (prājāpatya)."
The paternal [portion] is at the base of the index finger, and the portion for Brahmā is at the base of the hand;
having understood this specifically, perform the libation for the gods (one should always offer libations to the gods and others).
The libation (tarpaṇa) is pleasing to the gods and the water for the feet (pādya) is dear to the sages (ṛṣis). For other classes of deities, the libation becomes their very life.
[This applies] to the guardians of the quarters and intermediate directions, the Siddhas, the Mothers, the planets, and the Rākṣasas.
The libation (tarpaṇa) should be offered according to the rules, beginning with the ancestors.
Thereafter, one should offer libations to Gaṇeśa and the others according to the prescribed rite:
"Oṃ, those living beings in my family who have been consumed by fire and those who have not been consumed by fire..."
"May those [beings] who have been satisfied on the ground with water attain the supreme goal.
At the time of twilight, during the collapse of the illustrious Lord of Beasts (Śiva), one should recite the *Śivaikādaśika*.
In the *Kāmika*: p. 44)
Having dispelled those obstacles that obstruct the path while seated in his aerial chariot consisting of weapons,
he should proceed either to a temple or to his own excellent residence.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"A hundred and fifty cubits on all sides from the base of the *liṅga* constitute the sacred field (*śivakṣetra*) of Śiva;
dwelling within that very area is the cause for [attaining] the world of Śiva."
That which is known as the human measure of the field is said to be one thousand [cubits] when self-manifested, and half of that in the case of a seer (ārṣa).
All things, both stationary and moving, when propitiated,
attain a divine state beyond doubt through the power of the Supreme Lord;
therefore, one should perform the rites for the attainment of liberation in the vicinity of a sacred field of Śiva.
Kāraṇa: Garuḍa:
"O Blessed One, it has been stated that there should be a deity representing one's own self in the northeast direction;
tell me what kind of house for that deity is auspicious, and describe its characteristics."
Īśvara says:
Regarding houses with four wings, another arrangement is prescribed there:
the Śrīgṛha (Treasure Chamber) is said to be in the east, and the Mahānasa (Kitchen) should be in the southeast.
(24B) The bed should be in the south; the armory in the southwest;
the dining area should be in the west; and the storehouse for grain in the northwest.
In the north is the arrangement of substances, and in the northeast is the temple of the deities.
Mataṅga:
One should construct [the temple] with one hall, two halls, three halls,
or even four halls, according to one's wealth.
O tiger among sages, one should duly arrange the placement of the playful Bhaṇḍas within the southeast sector according to the prescribed ritual.
O gentle one, for all four-footed creatures, the eastern direction is praised;
thereafter, I shall fully explain the purification of the surface of the earth.
A ground that is endowed with fragrance and sweetness, adorned with white and red flowers,
and exceedingly fragrant with dust, is auspicious and accomplishes all goals.

May those who find satisfaction in their own limbs— limbs that are like hair, bones, insects, herons, and crows— abandon this place which is filled with snakes, ant-hills, discarded skins, ashes, charcoal, and husks.
On ground three cubits in extent, free from all defects,
one should level the earth according to the scriptures using a cloth and a water-level.
Having constructed a sacrificial pavilion made either of baked bricks, or likewise of pure wood,
or even of clay, one should establish it.
In the *Sarvajñānottara* (p.
46): (25a) Having made the length double that [of the door], the width shall be one part;
the door shall be in the third part, measuring one and a half cubits.
In the *Kiraṇa*: "One may make the western, southern, or eastern door;
thus, in the daily worship, the temple is praised as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
The construction of that [temple], which may be of one or two storeys, is described here:
having divided the site into five parts, the *vedikā* (altar-platform) is placed in the central portion.

For rites performed with oblations (iṣṭi), a clay image is best; those made of stone or plaster are not so. It should measure sixteen finger-breadths in height and be provided with corner pillars and other such features.
O Aṃśumatī,
he [beheld] that beautiful fan made of *sagusta* grass, strewn with flowers blazing with brilliance,
rich with the fragrance of incense smoke, and anointed with sandalwood and other perfumes.
Let us enter the place of worship, which is enriched by lamps with steady flames, filled with the rays of mirrors,
and provided with water from conch shells.
Having washed his feet, the wise man should discard that remaining water; then, taking water again, he should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having entered the interior of the pavilion, one should perform the worship of the Sun:
"O Aṃśumatī, the Sun is indeed with parts (sakala), yet Śiva is himself without parts (niṣkala)."
Having first propitiated the deity residing within the body, the wise person should subsequently worship the external deity.
One should worship the solar deity either with an image or with a disc;
or, having drawn a lotus on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) according to the method previously described.
Having performed the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs with the heart-mantra and others,
one should contemplate oneself in the form of the sun and [prepare] the vessel for the arghya offering.
Having thoroughly purified it with the weapon-mantra ending in "namaḥ" and using the Khaṣolka mantra,
one should fill [the vessel] with a red-colored drop drawn from the forehead.
Having worshipped that [deity] with the limbs of the Sun, performed the protective veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*),
and sprinkled the ritual materials with those waters, one facing east should worship the Sun.
In the subtle [state],
there is a staff-bearer; in the right [hand] is a fair-complexioned, stout man with a beard,
holding an ink-pot and a pen in his two hands.
He is the witness of the deeds of living beings and he records those very deeds;
he is richly adorned with a beautiful red-colored form and is endowed with the sun in his hand.
On the left side is Piṅgala, and [on the right] is the doorkeeper Daṇḍin;
[the deity] is seated upon a red lotus throne, possessing tusks, and holding a noose, a goad, and a fruit.
And [he saw] the elephant-faced Lord of the Gaṇas, holding [various objects] with his four hands,
enriched by the splendor of a crown of matted locks, and his body white with ashes.
Adorned with a meditation band over the region of the navel and the sacred thread,
and having formed the mudrā known as Kṛtayoga, one should meditate upon the supreme, peaceful Guru.
White, saffron-colored, and red, resembling the beautiful form of a lion,
[these are placed] in order within the corners starting from the southeast and ending at the northeast.
One should worship the supreme bliss, which is stainless, substantial, and worthy of honor;
in its center is a red lotus, adorned with petals in the eight directions.
And one should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Diptā, upon the filaments, starting from the east and ending in the northeast; and in the northeast, Sarvatomukhā.
The nine Śaktis are to be meditated upon as having the form of blazing lamp-flames;
they are red, adorned with ornaments on all their limbs, and hold a lotus and a chowrie in their two hands.
Facing the sun, adorned with all ornaments,
one should meditate thus, worship, and display the Visphurās.
The solar [form] resembles saffron in hue, adorned with all ornaments,
two-eyed, with a beautiful face, and anointed with jewel-garlands and unguents.
Endowed with four arms, with two lotus-like hands in the gestures of boon-granting (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), adorned with a halo of light,
wearing a sacred thread (*upavīta*), and accompanied by Uṣā and Pratyūṣā.
Queen Uṣā is on the right side, and Pratyuṣā is on the left flank.
She has two arms and two eyes, possesses a face like a lotus,
is adorned with all ornaments, and is endowed with all auspicious marks.
One should meditate upon the god whose body is that of the sun— lotus-handed, possessing excellent limbs, endowed with a ruddy hue, exceedingly serene, and with brilliantly radiant members.
If one desires worldly enjoyment or liberation,
[one should meditate on the deity] seated upon a white lotus, possessing the luster of a pomegranate flower,
with throbbing, great red radiance, situated in the center of a circular mandala.
One should meditate upon the Sun-god as having a single face and two eyes, clad in red garments, seated upon a swan that is white with crimson markings, and holding two lotuses in his hands.
Having performed the invocation and other rites with the appropriate mudrās,
one should display the *praṇāmabimba-mudrā* for the sake of [the deity's] pleasure.

Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa and the unification, one should perform the rites for the Kaṣolkins; one should worship the feet, the water for sipping, and the head, each with a mere handful of offerings.
Having worshipped Bhāskara with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the root mantra,
one should devotedly show him the mudrā called Padma-bimba.

One should worship the Heart mantra in the southeast (Agni), the Head in the northeast (Īśāna), the Tuft in the southwest (Nairṛta), the Armor in the northwest (Vāyu), and the Weapon mantra in the directions from the east to the south.
One should meditate upon the limbs of the Sun as being gentle, red in color, granting boons with hands joined in the *abhaya* and *varada* gestures, adorned with ornaments, and free from poison.
One should visualize the *Tīrtha* weapon as having terrifying fangs, exceedingly fierce, blazing with the brilliance of fire, and threatening the hosts of obstructing spirits (*vighna*).
The *dhenumudrā* is for the heart and other [limbs], and for the cow-dung and the two genitals;
the *kiraṇa* is for the weapon (*astra*), the *trāsanā* is for the [deities], and the *namaskriyā* is for the houses.
Soma, resembling the bulb of a white water-lily and endowed with the luster of gold.
One should meditate on Jupiter as having the luster of yellow orpiment, Venus as resembling cow’s milk, Mars as red, Saturn as resembling the rājavṛtta flower,
Rāhu as black with palms joined in reverence, and Ketu as resembling a smoky serpent.
All of them were divine, assuming forms at will, and adorned with celestial ornaments.
With their left hands resting on their thighs and their right hands granting fearlessness,
they gaze upon the gentle Śītapadmākara, who has joined his palms in reverence toward Rāhu and Ketu.
Seeing those with half-bodies and half-heads, with red eyebrows and red eyes,
as well as Karālā and Rāhu with his distorted face.
One should place the eight planets at the tips of the petals in the directions starting from the east;
having thus worshipped the planets in due order preceded by meditation.
Incense, lamps, and food offerings should be presented to the one who wears away all things;
having recited the root mantra according to their capacity, they should remain composed.
Having prepared the vessel for the *arghya* offering, one should present it with devotion to the Sun;
having performed prostrations and worship, and having offered the *arghya*, one should turn one's face away.
Having withdrawn the well-compacted [body] with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, saying "O [Mother], forgive me," he should dissolve it by means of the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā].
One should place Śiva-Sūrya in the center of the heart-lotus;
he is fierce, red, and terrifying, with two hands displaying the lotus and the gesture of fearlessness.
(28ā) With this [mantra], one should offer the remains of the sun's garland to Caṇḍeśa.
Thus ends the procedure for the ritual bath and the worship of the Sun, in the *Sakalāgamasārasaṅgraha*.
Hariḥ Om! May there be auspiciousness! Salutations to the Gurus!
This is the book of Vedanāyaka Paṇḍita.
Written by the scholar Nāgagiripaṇḍita.
Now follows the procedure for the worship of Śiva.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the worship of Śiva,
which removes all sins and brings happiness to all the worlds."
It yields the fruit of all forms of giving and bestows the fruit of all sacrifices;
it destroys the taint of killing a Brahmin and other such sins, and grants the merit of the horse-sacrifice.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a merit equal to the worship of Śiva— one that bestows victory, brings prosperity, increases the kingdom, and destroys enemies.
In the Śivadharmottara:
"There is no merit anywhere greater than the worship of the Liṅga.
Having understood this, Sadāśiva should be worshipped with diligent effort.
Smṛti: (28B) It is prescribed as a general rule that the worship of the deity is to be performed immediately after the midday bath. Thus says Yoga:
Yājñavalkya says:
(p. 53) Having wrung out the bathing garment, having sipped water, being self-restrained and pure, one should perform the worship of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, without envy.
Thus, these are the pairs of deities:
Gaṇapati or Skanda, Sūrya or Sarasvatī, her Lord or Śrī, her Lord or Gaurī, her Lord—or whichever other [deity] is desired by you; choose from among these according to your preference.
They worship them all together:
Manu says—
Āditya, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Gaṇanātha, and Maheśvara.
A Brahmin devoted to the five great sacrifices should honor these five.
Thus [it is said].
Some [worship] Gaṇapati, Āditya, Śakti, and Acyuta.
"And do they gradually attain Śiva?

Thus it is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* that there is even a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for failing to perform this: "He who, out of delusion, does not worship the Lord, having failed to perform the worship of the deity..."
(29ā) "He who eats [forbidden food] goes to the hells, or is born as a worm, or is born from a corpse. Therefore,

it is established that for the sake of avoiding transgression and for the attainment of one's desired goals, everyone should perform the propitiation of at least one among these [deities] according to their preference.
p. 54) Therefore, how is it that Śiva alone is to be worshipped?
On this point, the following investigation proceeds:
Is the status of being worthy of worship and the fruit of worship the same for all the gods, or rather...
"There is a distinction.

This being so, among the gods, Mahādeva possesses the status of being most worthy of worship (*pūjyatama*), while others possess merely the status of being worthy of worship; this [distinction] follows from the force of the compound with the word "great" (*mahat*).
It is understood [from Pāṇini 2.1.61]: "The words *sat*, *mahat*, *parama*, *uttama*, and *utkṛṣṭa* form a compound with those being honored (*pūjyamāna*)," as in *mahārāja*.
Thus, a compound of the word *mahat* with that which is worthy of honor is appropriate;
for [the Lord] is the substratum of infinite auspicious qualities such as unsurpassed knowledge, bliss, supreme sovereignty, and so forth.

Furthermore, the state of being free from all defects is ascertained through the fact that Mahādeva is denoted by the word "Śiva. For who else— other than Mahādeva, the Lord of Umā— could possibly possess such [purity]?

Is there the denotation by the word "Īśvara" without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*)? For the word "Śiva" indeed illuminates the supreme human goal, which is the collective totality of the nature of pure, auspicious qualities free from limiting adjuncts.
This is well-known in the world and in the Vedas; for instance:
"May your actions be auspicious! May your paths be auspicious! (p. 55) *śivakarmāstu*. *śivāste panthānassantu*.
"May there be auspiciousness for all the worlds.
Now, Śiva alone is understood to be superior to other deities;
as it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:

It is said that Mahādeva is the progenitor of the gods, beginning with Brahmā; the Supreme Lord is the father of Heaven and Earth, of Indra and Agni, of Viṣṇu, Dhātṛ, Yama, Varuṇa, and the Moon. Thus it is stated.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, the words of the Lord (*Īśvara*) addressed to Brahmā:
"O Creator, the son born before Kūrma has emerged for a specific purpose."
From my own right limb [arose] the Supreme Person from the left limb.
From the heart of that god, the Lord Śambhu, this Ādirudra was born; he is his supreme, yet other, body.
And in the Śivadharmottara:
"Brahmā arose from the right limb, Hari was born from the left limb;
Rudra emerged from the heart."

Now, my son, how can there be equality in the performance of worship and other rites between Mahādeva— who stands as the father of the world-protectors (sthānīya) such as Brahmā and others— and those very protectors?
Furthermore, according to the rule that "the root *yaj* means 'to worship a deity' (*yajadevapūjāyām*)," one should sacrifice to those who are deities.
"Even among those beginning with Brahmā, Mahādeva is the one to be worshipped.
Thus it is said in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Brahmā always worships the Liṅga with Vedic syllables and mantras."
One should constantly worship Viṣṇu and Śiva with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Brahmā worships a stone linga as Śiva for daily adoration;
by the very act of worshipping it, he attained supreme Brahmanhood.
The linga made of sapphire is always worshipped by Viṣṇu;
through that, he attained the state of Viṣṇu, [observing] that one eternal vow.
Śakra, the king of the gods, also daily worships this auspicious linga made of jewels with devotion; by that, he attained the status of Śakra.
Dhanada always worships a beautiful linga made of gold;
by that, the god Dhanada attained his status as the giver of wealth.

The high-souled Viśvedevas worship a beautiful linga made of silver according to the prescribed rites; by that, one attains the state of the Viśvedevas. Vāyu worships with devotion an auspicious linga made of bell-metal.
By mere worship alone, the supreme state of Vāyu was attained.
The Vasus worship a linga made of bell-metal according to the prescribed rites;
by that means, those high-souled ones attained the status of Vasus, which brings forth excellent joy.
The two Aśvins, worshipping the earthly *liṅga* according to the prescribed rite,
both attained divine bodies as a result of that.
Varuṇa always worships a stainless crystal linga;
by that means, he indeed attained the status of Varuṇa, endowed with the power of wisdom.
The sage, being purified, worships the auspicious linga composed of food;
by that act, he attains the state of fire, endowed with the form of splendor.
The gods and the Sun-god always worship Tābuliṅga with devotion three times a day; by that, he attained the supreme state of Sūrya.
Soma always worships a linga made of pearls;
by that [act], Soma himself attained his eternally radiant state as the Moon.
At Jayanta, the best of serpents worship a linga made of coral;
by that merit, the Nāgas, enriched with great enjoyments, attain the supreme state.
The best of the Asuras worships the Kṛṣṇa-liṅga according to the prescribed rule;
and because of that, those high-souled Rākṣasas possess such great prowess.
The Piśācas worship a liṅga made of cucumber;
by that, endowed with the power of supernatural success (ṛddhi), they attain the supreme state.
The best of Guhyakas worship a liṅga made of the three metals;
endowed with enjoyment and power by that means, they proceed to the supreme state.
The Mothers always worship a linga made largely of iron;
having attained motherhood, they all proceed to the supreme state.
Thus, the gods, along with the gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas,
always worship Īśāna, the leader of the deities.

Therefore, Mahādeva Śiva alone possesses a majesty that exceeds even the inner hosts [of his attendants], and he alone is the bestower of the fruit culminating in liberation; thus, O you who desire the purpose of immeasurable flowers, one should worship Śiva alone— who is the form of the unsurpassed human goal— and not anyone other than Śiva.
"Bestowing a mass of results other than auspiciousness"—this is the condensed meaning.
And so it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Just as a salutation to Rudra bestows the fruit of all actions..."
One would not obtain that fruit by paying homage to other deities;
therefore, having abandoned other gods who are not the Supreme Lord, one should take refuge in the god Maheśvara. O you of diverse forms, if you desire the imperishable supreme state, do so.
Without knowing the Śiva-principle, the entire circle of mantras, vidyās, and so forth, should be understood as being like a lump of clay; by such [ignorance], one becomes fallen.
Therefore, having abandoned all the gods headed by Brahmā,
