one should worship Virūpākṣa, who dwells within the sun.

One should place a leaf or even a single flower upon the *liṅga*; whether without mantra or with a good mantra, one shall deliver ten million members of one’s lineage. As stated in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*: [p. 59]
In the dialogue between Keśava and Āditya,
the words of Keśava are as follows:
"The God of gods is Mahādeva, the blue-throated Lord of Umā."
For he alone is to be honored by all three, as he is the cause of everything.
If anyone else were to worship [him] other than the Three-eyed One, he would not be considered "well-eyed" (sulocana); rather, one is intended as "well-eyed" by virtue of his two eyes.
Thus, it is established that the worship of Śiva alone is superior to the worship of all other deities, being the primary means that bestows the greatest fruit. Specifically:
Mahādeva alone is to be worshipped by the Brāhmaṇas.
As it has been said:
"Even there, for the Brāhmaṇa, the specific deity is Śiva;
the Brāhmaṇa is the Lord Rudra, while the Kṣatriya is said to be Viṣṇu."

Statements from the Skanda Purāṇa, such as these, should be considered. Therefore, Śiva alone is the singular mass of Brāhmaṇas; he is to be worshipped by Brāhmaṇas in the form of the Liṅga and other icons.
The worship of Śiva is the primary duty for all, and it is stated to be especially so for Brāhmaṇas.

(60) That worship is appropriately performed toward a specific form, such as a *liṅga* and so forth. Therefore, the worship of this Mahādeva—the sovereign of all deities—is indeed the most excellent. And that [worship] is likewise [performed] toward a specific *liṅga*.
Thus it is said in the Mahābhārata, in the Droṇaparvan: "O God of gods, whose nature is inconceivable, the invincible and imperishable Viṣṇu—
knowing him to be the source of all forms, one worships that Lord through his symbols."

For those who worship Sadāśiva—who is difficult to attain, difficult to reach, and worthy of being propitiated—their birth is indeed fruitful; those best of men have accomplished their life's purpose.
In the Bṛhatkālottara:
"Whatever holy places and sacred shrines exist upon the earth dwell at the base of the Liṅga; therefore, one should worship the Liṅga."
In the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*, the words of Śrī Keśava:
"What indeed might not be attained here for one who worships the Śiva-liṅga?
Sons, grandsons, kingdoms, heavens, and liberation—of this there is no doubt."

O Lord of Pārvatī, whether one has attained sovereignty over the three worlds or the prosperity of that sovereignty, or even the acquisition of a thousand cows— if this liṅga of yours is worshipped here even once; [then all is gained].
Whence could there be fear of birth for them in this saṃsāra, which is a vessel of suffering?
There is no merit greater than the worship of the *liṅga* in the three worlds.

Therefore, even the state of being a *liṅga* has been rightly honored by the Great Lord. But he who, having abandoned the worship of the *liṅga*, worships other deities, is like a fool who, having discarded a jewel, seeks out glass.
In the Śivadharmottara:
"The deity in the form of the Liṅga is Mahādeva himself, established directly for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds; therefore, one should worship the Liṅga."
He who, out of delusion, does not worship the Liṅga, the Lord of the three worlds,
quickly becomes a recipient of heaven, liberation, and kingdoms.

If these statements concerning the greatness of the worship of Śiva were written in their entirety, then all the trees growing in the fourteen worlds would be like palm trees without trunks; enough with such prolixity, for this is a compendium.
p. 62) 2 || Now, the procedure for the daily worship (nityārcana).
I shall describe the daily worship, which is meritorious, bestowing auspiciousness, and destroying sins;
it removes the defects of great transgressions and grants the fruit of all sacrifices.
In the *Makuṭa*:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have been initiated are those who enter [the mandala].
One may perform a sacrifice for one's own sake, but one must not perform one for the sake of another. (33B)
O Aṃśumatī,
one should especially perform the worship of the glories arising from the four castes;
one should not perform any other rite until Śiva has been propitiated.
As it is said in the *Śivadharmottara*: "Viṣṇu and Brahmā as well, with palms joined in reverence,
first propitiated the Liṅga and only thereafter performed their respective duties."
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform sacrifice until death.
It is remembered as being threefold: pure (*śuddha*), solitary (*kevala*), and mixed (*saṃmiśra*), performed for the sake of the Self.
That which is honored by those who have conquered their senses is "pure"; one should honor that which is pure and solitary.
One should worship either the mixture of the Ācāryas alone as pure,
or the pure [deity] without Śakti, or the solitary one joined with Śakti.
That which begins with Saura and ends with Caṇḍa is proclaimed as "mixed" (miśra).
In the Kāraṇa [Tantra], it is said: "The Ekaliṅga and likewise the Mokṣa—these two forms are of the nature of disease."
Likewise, one should fashion the three genders, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
(34ā) Among those, the four-linga [form] destroys longevity, prosperity, and fame;
the five-linga [form] is most excellent and destroys the five great sins.
If the sixth [day] should cause death, the seventh destroys one's dwelling;
the eighth, however, brings about a great disease or the increase of enemies.
Likewise, the excellent *navaliṅga* is glorified in the world of Śiva.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Emerald is said to bestow nourishment, while ruby is for those seeking wealth."
Vaidūrya brings longevity and prosperity; crystal increases one's progeny.
Stambhana (paralysis) is accomplished by puṇyarāga; subjugation of a kingdom by coral; karṣaṇa (attraction) by that which is called vajra; and the maṇikya grants all supernatural powers.
Sapphire (indranīla), however, yields the fruit of all gems for the sake of liberation.
One should fashion a linga made of gems measuring from one finger-breadth up to a span (vitasti).
The pedestal for the jewel-liṅga should be made according to its own proportions, with a circumference equal to its length and joined with a rounded top.
Because of their respective origins, [the materials for] the pedestals are gold; in its absence, silver, copper, and even base metal are proclaimed [as alternatives].
The pedestal for a movable liṅga may be either square or circular;
its width should be twice, or else double or triple, the length of the liṅga.
Its width should be known to be equal to that; perform the remainder as previously described.
One-third of the length of the *liṅga* should be placed in the middle of the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
The linga that brings about all-encompassing knowledge is three-partite and devoid of a cord;
this is declared to be the jewel-linga (ratnalinga), and the metal-made linga (lohajalinga) is now described.
A liṅga fashioned from gold bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
one made of copper is said to grant sons, while one of silver brings about prosperity.
Bell-metal is said to bestow happiness, brass destroys disease,
iron destroys enemies, and the three metals together bring about death.
And likewise, the one most skilled in ritual procedures should fashion [an image] from tin or lead;
the one most skilled in ritual procedures should fashion it according to the path prescribed for those made of precious gems.

In the subtle [state], one should always worship with supreme devotion toward the stone, as if it were the Liṅga itself, that which has arisen from the great river and originated from the Siddhakṣetra and other such sites. (35a) p. 65)
White, red, yellow, and black are honored by the Brahmins and other castes;
however, that which is black by its very nature bestows success upon all classes.
Free from pride;
the Bāṇaliṅga is said to be a manifestation of that which is free from pride.
Self-manifested, it is always worthy of worship, the most excellent among all liṅgas.
The crystal is indeed threefold, known as *śuci*, *indu*, and *sūryakānta*, which respectively possess the defects of whiteness, redness, and the brilliance of lightning;
another [type] shines intensely like moonlight at night, while the *pīṭha* (seat) shines in the sunlight.
Indeed, its own power resides within the nine internal channels; it is like a drop of water, transparent, endowed with the luster of the full moon, and even like gold.
A crystal that is free from all defects grants all desires;
however, one that is lusterless, faceless, rough, multicolored, or rattling is inauspicious.
The pair of lips has lines of terror from the falling particles of frost;
it is joined with a central pillar containing an embryo and is accompanied by a wound like sugar.
One should discard a crystal that is tainted by being overlaid with another species;
for Bāṇa, Śiva, and Śakti call that which possesses such arrows the Bāṇaliṅga.
Through his worship of that [Liṅga] which was offered to Śiva, a son named Bāṇa was born to him.
There may be ten million [deities] on Triśṛṅgagiri, a crore on Liṅgaśaila,
and Nirmadā at Kālīgarta; there is one [deity] at Bāṇaliṅga, and a crore at Āmareśa on Mahendra.
In Kanyātīrtha, Araṇya, and among the Nepālakas.
If, by means of an incomparable scale, that which is held is brought to great equilibrium,
or if water is poured [until it reaches] that very point, they know that to be the Bāṇaliṅga;
its head is high, and its base is slender (kṛśa).
Or rather, if a five-year-old girl were to touch it while it is being worshipped, then indeed his face would never be devoid of prosperity.
Now hear of the origin and characteristics of the Bāṇaliṅgas,
as well as those of Narmadā, Daivika, Artha, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā.
O Six-faced One, there are Bāṇaliṅgas of the rivers of merit;
Bāṇa should be known as Sadāśiva, and Bāṇa is the Asura Andhaka.
"Bāṇa" should be understood as water; therefore, it is called "bāṇa" here.
In the *Tantrasāra*:
"The best [form] is bubble-shaped, and the middling has the appearance of a *caṇḍāla*."
(36ā) "The inferior [mark] is shoulders like those of a bull"—these are the characteristics of the [male] gender-mark (*liṅga*).
Having the appearance of a ripe bimba fruit, with a luster like that of buffalo-eyes and resembling the eyes of a tawny cow— such are the characteristics of a Bāṇaliṅga.

The head should be thick and the feet raised, while the face should be elevated. The width of the pedestal should be equal to the circumference of the *liṅga*, and its height should be four times that [width]. Then, for the sake of the forgotten meaning, from the end of the *gomukha* to the end of the *gomukha*, there should be the measurement of the neck's circumference.

If the *liṅga* is larger [than the pedestal], it results in death; one should make the *śakti* larger than *Dhanañjaya* (the *liṅga*). One should make the *liṅga* equal to the pedestal (*pīṭha*), for that bestows both enjoyment and liberation.

A dark spot (kalaṅka) portends consumption; a crow’s foot (kākapāda) indicates injury to the head; a line (rekhā) signifies being struck by a disease of the feet; and a dot (bindu) brings about the destruction of joy.
If the Bāṇa-liṅga is harsh, there will be the destruction of sons and wife;
if the Bāṇa is fixed upon the head, there will be disease and even death.
In the Raurava [tantra]: "The head should be thick, the root thin, and the mouth elevated;
those [lines] worshipped by Indra and the others, when severed here, result in their being severed."
These six faces and limbs, especially when applied, are called the "Indra-marks" (*indraliṅga*); they indeed bestow the fruit of universal sovereignty.
The unassailable [liṅga] made of snow and nectar, which by its touch makes one free from duality;
this fiery liṅga, resembling a spear (śakti) and marked with the emblem of a churning-staff (mathana), should be installed. By doing so, one becomes the sovereign of splendor.
The southern [channel] consists of the form of a staff, or else it has the shape of a tongue.
Just as attachment is completely washed away in a moment, so too [is it purified];
the seat of Varuṇa is circular in shape, a part of the pedestal, and exceedingly radiant.
When one stands in the midst of water, the waters undergo states of increase, stability, and difficulty;
that which is black or smoky belongs to Vāyu, who is adorned with smoke as his banner.
Placed upon the head of that [enemy], or indeed deposited with his clothes,
it is intended for the expulsion of an enemy when placed in a windless spot where there is no movement;
it has the shape of a mace, is heavy in the middle, and possesses the characteristics of Kubera’s [seed].
Whether by day or by night, it increases the growth of the crops.
A bull, triangular in shape, marked with tridents, fierce, and possessing the luster of snow, jasmine, or the moon— whether consisting of the four castes or otherwise— arises before him.
The Vaiṣṇava [form] is marked with the conch and discus, adorned with the mace, lotus, and other [emblems], bearing the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem; it has the form of a boar or a lion.
That which is marked by the presence of Vainateya and the goddess Śrī is called Vaiṣṇava; it bestows the fruit of all sovereign powers.
The color of the lotus-leaf, or a lotus-mark, or a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu),
or the color of a staff and rosary— this is the manifestation of Brahmā that grants knowledge. A tawny-colored linga should be worshipped by sages who desire liberation.
One should never accept or worship a linga that is small or tawny.
One should avoid a linga that has sharp edges, a curved top, or is triangular;
likewise, one that is excessively thick, excessively thin, or possessed of seven white spots.
One seeking liberation should avoid such a planet; it is beneficial for one who is joined [to it] when it is worshipped. When situated in a planet, its color is like that of a bee.
When the Bāṇaliṅga is in the hand, then it becomes a *ṇagraka*.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Whether three, five, or seven times, the balance [of weight] is not achieved."
At that time, the arrow was declared to be made of reed-grass, while the remainder was produced from stone.
Or one should throw it again into a river; when it is recovered, then it is declared to be a "Bāṇa" arrow; otherwise, it brings suffering.
Regarding impurity due to childbirth (*aṃśumatī*): during the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), the fetching of water for one's own sake is prescribed.
Worship should be performed even during a period of birth-impurity or death-impurity, or when one is angry.
The ritual should be performed with the Śiva-mantra; by mere bathing, one becomes pure.
Therein, no impurity remains, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should enter [the inner sanctum], especially during periods of ritual impurity;
thus should one perform the worship of the Liṅga, free from the pursuit of optional rites for specific desires.

Alternatively, during a period of impurity (sūtaka) or upon the death of a person, the wise man should not perform the worship of the Liṅga himself; rather, he should perform mental worship, for everything is a mental construction.
Having worshipped that linga, one should not perform worship of other gurus or those of one's own caste;
however, one may offer three handfuls of flowers upon the tooth.
How should a woman in her menses perform the worship of the guru and the deity? She must perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) for three days prior.
On the fourth day, having bathed and consumed the products of the cow, she should perform the sacrifice;
however, if the linga has been taken by thieves, she should then perform the sacrifice mentally.
And one should observe a fast for forty days,
subsisting only on coconut water, milk, fruits, and the like.
The wise person, devoted to the meditation on Śiva, should protect himself;
therefore, with every effort, that *liṅga* must indeed be grasped.
If it has been obtained, the wise man, taking it up with particular joy,
should perform the purification of the *liṅga* in due order and worship it as before.
If that specific *liṅga* is not obtained, he should instead collect a new *liṅga*.
Having taken the *liṅga* of one's own guru, one should worship it according to the ancient tradition.
If the previous sign is seen, then one should worship both;
as stated in the Kālottara:
"The earthen [liṅga] should be made of two kinds: uncooked and cooked."
One should know that merit arising from what is cooked is ten times greater than that which arises from what is uncooked.
A vessel made of baked clay is known to be meritorious; one made of wood is ten times more meritorious than that.
A wooden vessel is [meritorious], and one made of stone is known to be ten times more meritorious than that.

Therefore, the fruit is a hundredfold greater in iron than in [ordinary] metal; in a jewel, it is infinite compared to that of iron; and in a linga made of precious gems, the fruit shall be a hundred thousandfold greater than that of a jewel.
A Bāṇaliṅga that has been consecrated with recollection is said to be ten million times more meritorious than one made of jewels;
a Rasaliṅga is remembered as having a fruit ten million times greater than that of a Bāṇaliṅga.
O Siddhas, the powers such as Raṇimā and the rest are well-established within the *saliṅga*;
through the worship of the *rasaliṅga*, there shall indeed be liberation along with the wealth of Śiva.
Therefore, one should worship that *liṅga* of the *samaya* with great effort;
indeed, when the *rasaliṅga* is worshipped, there shall be the destruction of all sins.
By seeing [the Liṅga], one destroys evil; by bowing, one destroys misfortunes;
and by worshipping the Saliṅga, one attains all desires.
Therefore, O Śikhidhvaja, the *rasaliṅga* should be worshipped with great effort; likewise,
rice from the *kāraṇa* tree, sesame, food, clay, and cow dung [should be used].
Fresh butter, a rudrākṣa bead, sacred ash, sandalwood paste, and a kūrca brush.
Flower garlands, water, and ground flour are said to be the twelve *kṣaṇikās*.
O Aṃsumatī, I shall now describe the fruit of these *kṣaṇikās* for those who have attained the path and desire liberation.
One who desires prosperity [should give] rice, and food to one who bestows food.
Cow dung from a riverbank destroys diseases, O King;
fresh butter gladdens the mind, and the rudrākṣa increases wisdom.
Incense is for those desiring objects of enjoyment; the *kūrca* is said to be for those seeking liberation. The flower increases longevity; the resin (*gulu*) grants the attainment of desired goals.
The ground powder (*piṣṭa*) is declared to bestow nourishment; the fruit shall be for those seeking momentary results.
And when the Guru has bestowed the *liṅga* upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), the self-manifested (*svayamātman*), or within himself;
In the *Niśvāsakārikā*, it is stated that in the momentary (*kṣaṇika*) maṇḍala, worship for one's own sake is performed with water:
"At one time, at two times, at three times, or at midnight."
Then, having taken it up, the practitioner should worship Śambhu constantly.
O Pārvatī, for one who lacks initiation, the use of rudrākṣa beads, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and all acts such as recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and sacrifice are entirely fruitless.
In the *Kāmika*: "At whatever time is possible, and by whatever means available;
when the lapse of the proper time has occurred, one should not perform an expiation."
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"The Śiva-liṅga is of great merit and is saluted by all the gods;
even he who merely touches it with his two hands is not defiled by sins, which are destroyed."
Even a heap of evil karma as vast as Mount Meru or Mandara,
upon encountering the Lord who is the Physician, perishes like a malignant disease.
Just as this ocean of terrible saṃsāra flows like a river,
so too do those who liberate one from beginningless saṃsāra exist within it.
Even one joined with existence and non-existence shall go to the supreme goal;
for in the Cause, all actions are honored, and knowledge is known within the Self.
Because it arises from filling [the body], it is recited as "pūjyam" (to be honored).
In the Kālottara:
"If a practitioner of mantra performs the worship of Śiva without wearing rudrākṣa beads,
all of that is declared to be fruitless, like an oblation poured into ashes."
Therefore, a wise person should wear the rudrākṣa with every effort.
In the Vātula [Tantra], Īśvara says:
"In ancient times, there was a demon named Tripura who was invincible in every way."
By him all the gods were slain—the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Agni.
When all of them had spoken thus regarding the burning of Tripura,
he contemplated the Great Scripture, which is the most enchanting among all scriptures.
It was divine, composed of all the gods, blazing and of terrible form;
it was created for the sake of slaying Tripura and as a means of protection for the gods.
Meditating upon the Aghora-weapon for the destruction of all obstacles,
my eyes have been opened for a thousand divine years.

On this earth, he who wears Rudrākṣas is honored like Rudra himself; [my beads] are not seen from my eyes on the earth. (Page missing; no. 75; p. 76) (41a) He who wears Rudrākṣas is honored like Rudra himself.
The merit in seeing it is a hundred thousandfold, while in touching it, it becomes ten millionfold.
A person who adorns his own body with Rudrākṣa bracelets and other ornaments obtains a hundred times ten million crores of merit through wearing them.
Having gathered all the requisites for worship,
the practitioner should sit upon a comfortable seat situated in the south-eastern direction from the deity.
Regarding the cause:
having turned toward the north and being seated upon a beautiful throne,
one should place the two knees together and join the tips of the feet like a casket.
The tip of the nose is slightly visible there, and the body is indeed elongated;
this is known as the beautiful posture (rucirāsana), which the wise declare worthy of all worship.
On *Aṃśumatī* wood, a square or rectangular seat bestows good fortune;
on *Dāru* wood, it provides a dwelling; on a cloth seat, there is the destruction of disease; and on a woolen blanket, the liberation from suffering.
Success in knowledge is attained on a black antelope skin, and the glory of liberation on a tiger skin.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"In whichever direction the opening may be, one should designate that as the west."
That which is directly facing the linga is considered to be the eastern door.
In that regard, the Tatpuruṣa face should be upward and facing forward.
As it is stated in the *Sūkṣma*:
"The western door is thus [the entrance], while the food offering is at the eastern face."
In the *Makuṭa*: "Since that which is declared as the heart of Aghora contains all the sense-faculties,
one should therefore perform all acts such as worship within Aghora."
Then, having sipped water according to the rule, with his lotus-like hand holding the offering for the Praṇava,
he should recite the syllable Oṃ seven times and perform the rite known as *samānī*.
Having sprinkled the door with water consecrated by mantras, one should worship the gatekeepers;
the door should be known as facing inward, while the gatekeepers face outward.
One should meditate on Gaṇeśa, who has a protruding belly and a dark body, holding an axe and a rosary in his two upper hands,
a sweetmeat ball and a tusk in his two lower hands, and [a goad and a noose] in his two left hands.
I praise him who holds [it].
One should meditate upon Sarasvatī, who is white in complexion, clad in white garments, holding a rosary and a book in her right and left hands respectively, and is exceedingly gracious.
Holding a *śrīphala* fruit and a lotus with her left and right hands,
she is the Great Śrī being bathed by these two golden jars containing all-fulfilling wealth.
Nandikeśvara is red in color, has three eyes, and wears matted hair; with his two hands, right and left, he holds a rosary and a trident.
Seated upon the makara-throne, she is white in form, holding a blue lotus in her right hand and a full water-pot in her left.
(78) [One should meditate on] Mahākāla, who is black, three-eyed, with a gaping mouth, and holding a skull-cup and a trident in his two right and left hands.
One should visualize Yamunā as dark-complexioned, standing upon a tortoise, holding a club in her two right hands and a blue lotus in her left hand.
In the *Somaśambhu*:
"By the descent of divine vision,
[the teacher] casts flowers into the sky toward those who do not turn away from the divine and who are protected by flaming iron arrows."
With three strikes from the right hand, the mantra-practitioner should dispel the various obstacles— whether numerous, desirable, or of three kinds— from within the midst of the sacrifice.
One should step slightly over the threshold and take refuge in the left side;
having entered with the right foot, one should place the weapon-mantra upon the door-post.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The weapon is formidable with fangs, most fierce, with a radiance equal to fire;
it has four faces and four arms, and its splendor is like a blazing fire."
Facing Śiva, [he is] endowed with the Śakti, the trident, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons;
he is joined with a crown of matted locks, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Seated upon a swan, pot-bellied, fair-complexioned, with a beard and four faces,
he holds a staff, a rosary, and a water-pot in his right and left hands respectively.
Having taken the *laḍḍukas* purified by the weapons [of the senses] such as gazing and so forth,
and having obtained permission, one should follow the path of Manu at night or during the day, avoiding the Gaṅgā and other [forbidden waters].
With water purified by a cloth and consecrated by reciting the *pavitrāṅga* mantras,
one should fill those vessels for the garments while reciting the heart-mantra of the *Gāyatrī*.
(42B) A collection of all substances, such as incense, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and so forth; according to the *Suprabheda*:
"Pāṭala, utpala, padma, and karavīra flowers [should be used] at all times."
Smooth and fragrant substances should be employed in the bathing water.
A water-channel should be constructed of gold, silver, copper, or even clay; it may be circular or square.

And one should fill the water-vat (jaladroṇī) with three *droṇas* according to the prescribed rule. As stated in the *Kāmika*: "The food offering (*naivedya*) consists of one *droṇa* of rice, and the water is one *droṇa* or half a *droṇa*."
Four palas of incense are recommended, and the cloth should be the measure of one cubit.
One should consecrate clarified butter, honey, oil, and ghee;
likewise, one should worship the presiding deity of the water-vat upon the back [of the image] and Vighneśvara as well.
On the two sides are Nandi and Kāla, and in the center is the presiding deity of the Gaṅgā.
In the *Śivadharmottara*: "Bathing in a copper vessel from an earthen jar yields a hundredfold greater merit."
The merit of [offering] a hundred thousand silver coins would be greater than that of ten million gold pieces.
The fruit obtained by one who has mastered the Vedas through the gift of a silver vessel is a hundredfold greater when a clay vessel is given to Śiva.
He who, out of devotion, offers a golden vessel to Śiva—
for him, it is especially impossible to describe the infinite merit [that results].
Facing north, with a disciplined mind and his two hands placed upon the mantra,
he should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites for the purpose of bringing [the deity] into presence for worship.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The external elements residing in the six paths are purified by initiation;
however, the elements situated within the body must be purified day after day."
Having visualized [the power] within the hollow of the body from the pair of big toes of the feet,
one should then contemplate the pervasive Śakti both inside and outside that hollow.
When the syllable *hūṃ* is situated in the center of the aperture, blazing like a fire—
having performed the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one should settle the mind upon the mantra.
At the end of the exhalation (recaka), with the syllable *phaṭ*, having pierced the knots at the heart, throat, breasts, palate, between the eyebrows,
and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and having turned [the breath] back;
One should place the syllable *hūṃ*, star-like in form, which is the life-force (*jīva*) enclosed within the heart,
the consciousness of the heart through inhalation (*pūraka*), upon Śiva.
Having meditated upon the completely purified *bindu* and having performed *kumbhaka*,
the wise one should unite it with Śiva by means of *recaka* through a single upward thrust.
Having taken [the deity] from the body with the withdrawal mudrā and the mūrtimantra,
for the purpose of enjoying the karma to be experienced, [he should place it] in the moving or the tranquil state as appropriate.
By means of the process of dissolution into the seed, one should purify the principles (*tattvas*)— from the seed up to the end— by dissolving them in reverse order into their own causes within Śiva.
In the [tanmātra] of smell, there is earth; in taste, water; in form, fire; in touch, air;
and in sound, ether. Again, these subtle elements (tanmātras) belong to the tamasic aspect.
The organs of action belong to the rājasa aspect, while the mind, along with the intellect and the sense organs, belong to the sāttvika aspect.
In the intellect (*buddhi*), that [ego] dissolves; in the qualities (*guṇas*), the multitude of qualities goes to dissolution in the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
Its attachment (*rāga*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) pass into *kalā*; likewise do the male principle (*puṃstva*), time (*kāla*), necessity (*niyati*), and *kalā*.
Māyā, the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśa*), the Sadāśiva, and Śiva with His Power—these are the Bindus among them.
Having thus performed this purification, one should purify the five elements;
beginning with earth, water, and fire, each pair should be purified in relation to the other.
And it is explained how space is to be purified by means of opposition:
the earthly mandala is yellow, solid, and marked with a vajra.
With the seed-syllable *hvāṃ* belonging to herself, she consists of the stage of the cessation of that [impurity];
she has the appearance of molten gold and is adorned with four arms.
The manifestation of the vajra, the gesture of fearlessness, the rosary, and the lotus is proclaimed;
when joined with its own mantra, it is sattvic and has Brahmā as its presiding deity.
Having contemplated [the body] as a square from the feet up to the crown of the head,
one should purify it by means of five upward thrusts, becoming like the wind.
The seed-syllable, which is half-moon-shaped, liquid, gentle, white, and marked with a lotus,
has attained the nature of consecration through this very seed-syllable.
Resembling pure crystal, with one face and four arms, she is established upon a lotus; she holds a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, and is adorned with jewels. (44a)
Conjoined with the Vāma-mantra, characterized by passion (rājasa), and having Viṣṇu as its deity,
one should purify the element of fire, which belongs to the water [category], by means of four udghātas.
One should visualize the fire-mandala as triangular, red, and marked with a svastika;
by means of this seed-syllable "Hrām," one should contemplate it as having the form of the Vidyā.
With tawny eyebrows, beard, and round eyes, adorned with a crest-moon,
having the appearance of molten gold, and resembling a blazing fire of knowledge.
Joined with the Aghora mantra, which is of the nature of tamas and has Rudra as its presiding deity,
one should purify the fire— which has become water— by means of three breath-impulses (udghātas).
The six-spoked maṇḍala is marked by six wind-bindus;
it is black, born from the seed-syllable *mit*, and consists of the Śāntikalā.

Śānti has four faces, four arms, and a dark complexion; she possesses great strength, holds a banner, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, wears a serpent as her sacred thread, and is clothed in the earth.
Having meditated upon Maheśvara as the presiding deity (adhideva) conjoined with the Tatpuruṣa [mūrti],
one should purify him, who has become the ocean, by means of a pair of *udghātas*.
It is an entity consisting of the sky and the bindu, adorned with the power of the bindu;
it has the form of space, is perfectly circular, and is as pure as clear crystal.
With the syllable *hauṃ* ending in *phaṭ*, she consists of the *śāntyatīta* kalā;
she resembles pure crystal, has five faces and four arms.
(44B) Having meditated upon her holding a lotus, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a rosary, a lotus, the *śāntyatītā* mudrā, and the gesture of granting boons (*varapradā*),
one should contemplate her as completely purified through the yoga of emission (*udghāta*).
One should purify the body with the fire located at the right big toe;
thereafter, one should drench everything with the root mantra, which rains down nectar.
The lotus of the Dharma-knowledge is called the Foundation and is infinite;
having drawn the Self into that, perform the nourishment thereof.
Having bathed [the deity] with divine nectar, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa;
as stated in the Suprabheda:
"Joined with the Praṇava, [the deity] is seated upon a white lotus."
Having formed the body of Śiva, one should meditate upon it as consisting of the thirty-eight kalās.
In the Kāmika:
"Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the lord of all vidyās, and to Śaśinī"—
thus [one should worship] above on the head.
Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Īśvara, the lord of all beings, to Aṅgadā; thus on the eastern head. Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Brahmādhipati, the lord of Brahman, to Brahmādhiṣṭhā.
Thus on the right head: *Oṃ hoṃ, may Śiva be mine; obeisance to Marīcī*. On the left head: *Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva and Jvālinī*. On the rear head: *Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva and Jvālinī*.
Thus is the pentad of the *kalās* of Īśāna. (p.
84) *Oṃ hoṃ*, we know Tatpuruṣa; obeisance to Śānti at the eastern face.
*Oṃ hoṃ*, we meditate upon Mahādeva; obeisance to Vidyā at the southern face.
(45a) Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Rudra for the sake of *pratiṣṭhā* at the northern face;
oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to *nivṛtti* for the sake of *pracodayāt* at the western face.
Thus are these four kalās preceded by that [syllable].
Oṃ hūṃ (hraṃ) aghorebhyaḥ stamāyai namaḥ, at the heart;
oṃ hūṃ aghorebhyaḥ mohāyai namaḥ, at the throat;
oṃ hūṃ aghora rakṣāyai namaḥ, on the right shoulder.
Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the most terrible ones and to Niṣṭhā on the left shoulder; Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to universal death on the navel;
Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to all and to Māyā on the belly.
Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to you, O Rudrabhayā; obeisance to the back. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the forms, O Jarā; obeisance to the chest.
Thus ends the eightfold group of Bahurūpa-kalās.
Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to Rajā—on the private parts.
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Jyeṣṭhā; salutation to Rakṣā—on the two testicles. Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Rudra; salutation to Ratī—on the right thigh.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kāla and obeisance to Pālinī on the left thigh;
Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Kalakumārī on the right knee;
Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Vikaraṇa and obeisance to Saṃyaminī on the left knee.
(45B) Oṃ hīṃ, homage to Balakriyā; on the right calf. Oṃ hīṃ, homage to Vikaraṇa, homage to Buddhi; on the left calf. Oṃ hīṃ, homage to Jalakārī; on the right buttock.
Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Pramathana; salutation to Dhātrī on the left hip. Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana; salutation to Brāhmaṇī on the waist.
Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Manomohinī on the right side.
Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Unmanā; obeisance to Manonmanī—thus on the left side.
These are the thirteen kalās of Vāmadeva.
Oṃ hāṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; obeisance to Siddhi—thus on the right foot.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta; obeisance to Madhyā on the left foot.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhavadyuti on the abdomen.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Abhavalakṣmī on the left shoulder.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Medhā, the primordial existence; on the nose.
Oṃ hāṃ, accept me, salutation to Kānti; on the head.
Oṃ hāṃ, be present, salutation to Svadhā; on the right arm.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Udbhava; salutation to Dhṛti on the left arm.
Thus ends the eightfold division of Sadyojāta.
Thus the thirty-eight-fold group of eight divisions is complete.
There are thirty-eight powers (*kalā*) and thirty-eight lords of the thunderbolt (*indra*);
thus, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) endowed with these powers even at the [specific] times.
The kalās of Īśāna are five; those of Puruṣa are four;
the kalās of Aghora are eight; and Vāmadeva has thirteen.

The eight *sadyakalās* are to be known; one should place them in the sequence beginning with *makuda*. This is declared to be the placement of the *kalās*; now the placement of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*) is described.
O Ajitā,
having placed the letter *a* on the crown of the head and the letter *ā* on the forehead;
likewise, *i* and *ī* on the two eyes, and *u* and *ū* on the two ears.
The vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ* are on the two cheeks; *ḷ* and *ḹ* are on the two nostrils;
likewise, the vowel *ī* is on the upper lip, and *e* and *ai* are on the lower lip.

One should place the syllable *o* on the two rows of teeth and the syllable *au* likewise; then *vi* is to be placed on the tongue, and subsequently *sthālu* is to be applied according to the sequence.
One should assign the *ka*-group to the right hand and the *ca*-group to the other;
having assigned the *ṭa*-group to the belly, one assigns the two *ta*-groups to the two sides;
the *ya*-group to the right foot and the *śa*-group to the left foot.
Having placed the letter *ha* in the heart, one should then perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the root mantra.
Having thus performed the placement of the syllables of the mantra upon the body consisting of the Vidyā,
one should contemplate within oneself the form of Śiva exactly as it is;
always perform this placement of the Śiva-mantra upon yourself.
In the *Skandakālottara* (p.
87): "Having cast off the ordinary state of being, one should contemplate, 'I am Śiva.
One who is not Rudra should not recollect Rudra; one who is not Rudra should not worship Rudra."
One who is not Rudra should not recite the Rudra-mantra, and one who is not Rudra cannot attain Rudra.
As stated in the Kālottara:
"In the center of the pedestal of the heart-lotus, one who is not [united] with [the deity] should not perform worship."
In the *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"The heart of all embodied beings resembles the flower of the plantain tree;
situated in its center is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp."
It is twelve finger-breadths wide, pure, unblemished, and white;
its stalk is eight finger-breadths long, arising from the navel-center.
The eight lotus petals are to be known as the eight qualities beginning with *aṇimā*; the pericarp and filaments are knowledge, and the stalk is supreme dispassion.
One should meditate upon that lotus as having the Śivadharma as its root,
seated upon the lion-throne of mantra, with its body armored by mantra.
Having fully perfected the mantra-worship, one should sacrifice there to Maheśvara; as stated in the Kāmika:
"One should worship with mental offerings such as perfumes and other articles."
In the *Suprabheda*:
"The wise one should likewise arrange all the seats and the prohibitions within the heart-lotus, exactly as stated and according to the rule. (p. 88)
In the naturally perfected navel-pit (nābhikuṇḍa), which is endowed with the purification of the limbs,
one should place there the fire of knowledge (jñānānala), possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns. Thus ends the placement of the fire of knowledge.
(From here onwards, a leaf marked as 47 is written in the middle; however, upon examining the sequence of the preceding and following sections, it appears to be 51?
(51B) — one should envelop [the deity] with that very armor (*kavaca*).
In the middle [direction] are Supratiṣṭha and Suśānta, as well as Pūrva.
To the south is Tejas, and to the north is Ratnodaka;
Amṛtapātra is in the west, and Avyakta is in the northeast corner.
In the southeast there should be the Vyakta vessel; in the southwest, the Sūrya vessel;
and in the northwest, the Saṃyukta vessel—thus is the worship of the vessels prescribed.
One should take cow urine from a tawny cow and cow dung from a black one;
however, for the cow dung, it should be from a tawny cow that is free from disease and other ailments.
One should take the cow dung situated in the calf-sign or that which has fallen in an auspicious place;
having discarded the upper half, one should accept it while avoiding the western portion.
One should collect the milk from a white cow, the curd from a smoke-colored one,
and the ghee from a red one, according to the sequence of the five products of the cow.
Alternatively, the supreme instructor should collect a single-colored [substance];
in the center, milk and *trikuṭu* (the three pungents), and in the east, curd measuring half a *prastha*.
On the southern side, there should be ghee together with one *kuḍuva*;
on the northern side, one *prastha* each of cow urine, cow dung, and what is held by the herd of cows (cow's milk).

Then, in the western [direction], there should be a five-footed [pedestal] joined with water; it should have the syllable *ṣya* at its head. After that, one should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and thereafter with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
(51a Thus it should be: one should bathe [the deity] with water purified by mantras, and thereafter perform the anointing of the limbs and so forth.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before Śiva, one should arrange the Vedic cords separately with rice grains and *kuśa* grass, or according to the availability of materials."
Having sat down facing north, he is thus described;
he should spread darbha grass on the outside with the tips pointing east and the tips pointing north.
In the center is the Śiva-tattva, while Sadāśiva is in the eastern cell;
the Vidyā-tattva is in the south, and likewise the Puruṣa-tattva is in the north.

The principle of time (kālatattva) is in the west, while that of fire (pāvaka) is in the east; the principle of water (ap) is in the southern compartment, and the principle of wind (marut) is in the northern compartment, in due order.
In the northeast corner of the main chamber, the worship of the chamber is prescribed;
an excellent vessel is one made of gold, and a middling one is a vessel of bell-metal.
An inferior vessel made of clay is so designated;
one should avoid one that is cracked, broken, chipped, or blackish in appearance.
Having taken up a new vessel, one should wash it with scented water;
one should sprinkle it with *puru* [mantra] and fill it with two *kuḍuba* measures of *kuśa* water in the northeast direction.
One should not fashion a nose with twelve, five, or even three [parts].
At a height of one palm-span, there should be a tuft of *kūrca* grass and water infused with *kuśa* grass.
According to the *Vātula*: it should be prepared with *āmalaka* fruit ground together with *kapittha* fruit, in the quantity of a single *kapittha* fruit.
And the night [should be measured] by the size of a plantain fruit.
The best of preceptors should place the flour of śāla wood in the southeast;
likewise, he should place āmalī in the southwest and rajanī in the northwest.
In the absence of curd, milk [should be used]; in the absence of milk, curd [is acceptable].
In the absence of cow dung, cow urine [is used]; and in the absence of that, cow dung [is used].
Among the five products of the cow, whichever may be available should be used; in its absence, ghee may be used.
Cow dung is considered superior or middling according to whether it resembles a hen’s egg.
Alternatively, one should fill it with water to the depth of the eye;
it should be purified with a cloth and placed according to the prescribed ritual.
One should consecrate the flour, in sequence, with the collection of their respective qualities by means of the mantras beginning with Īśa;
the water for grinding, however, with the Heart mantra, and the winnowing basket with the Head mantra.
One should consecrate the night with the *varma* mantra either repeatedly or once;
likewise, one should consecrate the *kuśa*-water six times with the *gāyatrī* and the five *brahma* mantras.
Having thrown cow dung into cow urine, one should cause the cow urine to boil with ghee;
having combined the ghee with curd, one should then pour it into curd and milk.
(52B) Then, one should sprinkle *kuśa* water there with the Heart-mantra and the Root-mantra;
one should also recite the Brahma-mantras, the Śiva-aṅgas, and the Gāyatrī once.
Having performed the purification of the vessel with astringent water (kaṣāya), one should display the dhenumudrā;
having worshipped it thoroughly with perfumes and flowers, one should then offer incense and a lamp.
Having placed them together in one spot, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with Śiva alone;
ghee indeed has Rudra as its deity, and curd has Soma as its deity.
Milk has Śukra as its presiding deity; cow dung has Agni as its deity;
cow urine has Naṭa as its deity; and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) have the Adhidevatas as their deities.
Cow’s urine should be known as bestowing prosperity; cow dung destroys disease;
curd leads to the increase of sons and the destruction of enemies beyond measure.
They know that ghee is the fruit of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for one who is worthy of worship;
he who performs the rite of pañcagavya upon the linga for even a single day [attains great merit].
Having shaken off all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
having fasted for a day and night and bathed, he stands before Śiva.
Facing east, one should slowly drink [the water] with a single mantra beginning with the syllable Oṃ;
by this, one is liberated from all sins, including the killing of a Brahmin.
During the subtle solstices and equinoxes, during lunar and solar eclipses,
on other auspicious days, and even during daily and occasional rites.
(53a) For the rite of atonement and on one's birth-star, one should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
This is declared to be the *pañcagavya*; here it is called the *pañcāmṛta*.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"In front of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), there should be a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) as before;
one should arrange the vessels and the mantras in the compartments as before."
In the center, milk; in the east, curd; in the south, ghee;
having added honey in the north, sugar should be placed in the west.
One should specifically place the plantain, breadfruit, and mango trees, as well as the scented water,
starting from the southeast and extending to the northeast.
In the absence of sugar-candy, however, the essence of sugarcane may be used; in the absence of the middle part, ghee should be used.
Then, having performed the sprinkling with pure water upon the subtle [deity] who has been brought forth,
[one should worship] in the lotus-abode—

O Prajāpati, at the time of offering incense, lamps, food oblations, and the fire sacrifice (homa), the word "svāhā" should be employed at the end; however, during the consecration (abhiṣeka), it should end with "namaḥ."
The jackfruit, the coconut, two citrons,
as well as the orange, the liguca, and the mango— this is the water of these fruits.
On the horn of a bull, in a sacred field, by the ocean, on an elephant’s tusk,
on a mountain, on a riverbank, on an anthill, or in a hole inhabited by crabs.
The decoction water is said to be prepared from the barks of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *madhūka*, *plakṣa*, *pāṭalī*,
and *jambū*.
One should rub the linga and its pedestal with the powder of ground *śirīṣa* flowers,
perform an ablution with pure water, and place a flower upon the top.
In the center of the *Cintyaviśva* [mandala], one should cause incense and a lamp to be offered;
having bathed [the deity] with the five products of the cow and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one should consecrate [him] with water alone.
In the *Aṃśumatī*: "Milk, curd, ghee, honey, and likewise coconut water.
In the *Suprabheda*:
Having bathed [the image] with scented water in a quantity equal to the tip of a cow's horn,
one should perform the consecration with sugarcane juice, pure water, and fragrant water.
But for one's own sake, one should especially have [images] such as the *prastha* and others made;
[this destroys] whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of *kalpas*.
Just as fire consumes fuel, that [merit] burns away everything through a bath of ghee.
As stated in the Śivadharmottara: "He who gives a cow to one who has mastered the Vedas and is a consumer of sacrificial offerings [attains great merit]."
The fruit of that [act] is obtained by bathing with milk those [images] endowed with garments, gold, and other [ornaments].
That man who bathes the Liṅga with curd even once with devotion,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having reached the world of Savitṛ with water from flowers, that of Kubera with golden water,
and that of Mahendra with water from jewels, he rejoices.
Having bathed Śiva once with pure water over which the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times, out of devotion, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Ten offenses are destroyed by water, a hundred by milk;
a thousand are forgiven by curd, and by honey, ten thousand shall be removed.
With ghee, one attains a hundred thousand-fold merit; with the essence of sugarcane juice, three hundred thousand-fold;
with coconut water, ten million-fold; and through fragrance, it is infinite.
One should rub [the image] with bilva leaves and likewise purify the pedestal. [The substances for purification are:
oil, ground āmalaka, turmeric, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) of cow products, milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugarcane juice, and the fruit of the adhyakṣura.

O Śivā, they say that the spring season originating from the jambīra and other fruits, as well as the coconut, should be placed in order within the fragrant and auspicious water-pot (gandhaśrīkumbha) for the arghya offering during the consecration.
In the Kāmika [Tantra]:

"Whether for daily rites, occasional rites, or rites for specific desires, bathing Maheśvara at the conclusion of the ritual ablution with a thousandfold stream certainly bestows prosperity and good fortune."
Let them fashion a well-rounded vessel out of gold, silver, or copper;
the best is twelve finger-breadths in size, and the middling is seven finger-breadths.
It is proclaimed that it should be five finger-breadths in width at the bottom,
and it is likewise proclaimed that it should be three finger-breadths in width at the top.
(54B) Thus, the width of the bowl and the height of its wall are described.
A height of one *aṅgula* is proclaimed to be the best.
Half of that, or half of that again, is called the smallest [size]. A hollow space in the ladle (sruca) is said to be three barley-corns thick.
In this manner, the vessel should be fashioned with eight petals and a pericarp;
in the center of the pericarp, there should be one [lotus] with apertures for the Vasus in the directions starting from the east.
Outside that, in the middle of the petals, make the twelfth opening;
outside of that, in the middle of the circle, there should be a pair of great spokes.
In this manner, one should sequentially fill that vessel, renowned for its hollows, one hundred and eight times with conch-water while reciting the root mantra.
Then, having offered the mantra-flower, one should present the mantra-food.
Having consecrated [the deity] with a thousand [mantras], having offered the special arghya, one should wrap [the image] with a cloth.
Having wiped [the image] with armor or a cloth, one should install Śiva upon the pedestal.
Having abandoned the seat, the enclosure, and the worship of the gatekeepers,
one should worship the images without Caṇḍa and the retinues.
Without the daily bath, one should perform a bath on every festival day on the metal [image].
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The pedestal should be two cubits long, or even one cubit."
It should be twelve finger-breadths in height, or else one cubit high and firm.
Adorned with various colors and decorated with a lotus in its center,
it is situated in the northwestern direction of the *Cintyaviśva* seat, facing south.
One should first worship Gaṇeśa, and afterwards one should fully worship Lakṣmī.
In the northeastern direction, one should worship the entire group of gurus as previously described,
as well as Sadāśiva, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Ambikā.
One should worship Guha and Kṛṣṇa as the Sustainer, while remembering the seven preceptors;
[then] the God, pure as a jasmine flower or the moon, the fifth [form], possessing a great body.
Sadāśiva has ten arms, a gracious face, and five faces;
[another form] has eight arms, four faces, the luster of crystal, and three eyes.
He who wears a serpent as a sacred thread should be known as the eternal Lord;
he has five faces, fifteen eyes, and ten arms that inspire awe.
Rudra, resembling a jasmine flower or the moon, stands upon a bull;
he wears the sacred thread and is adorned with bright white garments glowing with the color of gold.
Adorned with all ornaments, with full thighs and hips,
enriched with the scent and flowers of the three-eyed one, and decorated with locks of hair.
The goddess holds a lotus and a blue water-lily, granting boons with one hand while holding [the gesture of] fearlessness with the other;
he has six faces, twelve ears, and is encircled by six crowns.
Reddish in appearance, with twelve eyes, and endowed with twelve hands;
he holds a trident, a sword with a hilt, a discus, and a noose in his right [hands].
He holds a goad, a banner, a shield, a bow, and a vajra;
he is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and is adorned with red garlands and unguents.
One should meditate upon the god Hari, who holds the conch and the discus, who is dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments,
accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, and adorned with all ornaments.
The god with four faces and four arms, holding a water-pot and a sacred thread,
accompanied by Sāvitrī and adorned with all ornaments.
One should worship the gurus, who set all knowledge in motion, as if they were Śiva himself;
then, having received permission, the practitioner of mantra should perform sacrifice according to the teachings of the Śiva scriptures.
Therefore, [one should meditate on her] seated upon the tortoise-stone, her body white as the ocean of milk,
with the form of a seed-sprout upon her crown, bestowing boons and granting fearlessness.
One should worship Śiva, whose mind is blissful, as he is mounted upon the Brahma-stone— the embodiment of the support, the power of action (Kriyā-śakti), who holds a noose and a goad.
The earth is its bulbous root, with the final digit (kalā) as its single stalk;
it has the contemplative heart as its neck, and the agitated Māyā as its great lotus endowed with many petals.
Having pervaded the region situated in their midst with your dark form,
you appeared like various tigers facing one another, each looking at the back of the other.
The throne and sandals of Śiva, appearing in the forms of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages, as well as dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty, respectively; (56a)
In that context, Dharma has the form of a bull, Jñāna has the nature of a lion,
Vairāgya is the departed spirit (or yellow), and Aiśvarya is the white elephant.
One should worship camphor, saffron, gold, and collyrium in the southeast,
southwest, northwest, and northeast, respectively.
Black and white in the eastern part, white and red in the south;
red and yellow in the west, and yellow and black in the northern direction.
These four are indeed known as the *gātraga* [mantras], while the others are the *śabanya*.
One should know that the *gātragas* are like crystal, three-eyed, and extracted from the head of a lion.
With their arms, heads, and necks rendered motionless, with their heads fixed upon their sandals, and with their forebodies,
feet, weapons, and heads [protruding], they took on the forms of men.
The opposites of adharma and the others are said to be located in the four directions starting from the east,
resembling rājāvarta gems, in the order beginning with Indra.
In the *Tantrasāra*:
"Above the pedestal (*pīṭha*), upon the girdle (*mekhalā*), one should always worship the red-hued [deity] Kṣubdha; then, in the southwest (*nairṛta*), one should worship Āyānta, and below, Candana."
Above that, one should worship the white color, then the sandalwood at the top,
Śuddhavidyā in the lower part, and finally Jñāna at the end.
Having worshipped a white eight-petalled lotus as the infinite lotus at that very moment, one should display the lotus mudrā above the row of lions.
Regarding the causes:
the radiant [center] is like a ruby, possessing a luster equal to a blue lotus stalk;
the thorn has the appearance of coral, and the petal indeed has the luster of silver.

Having worshipped the petals as the eight forms of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara), one should contemplate the filaments as having the luster of gold and being shaped like pearls at their tips. (p. 99)
Then one should worship the pericarp, which has the luster of molten gold, contains fifty seeds,
and is surrounded by sixty-four filaments.
In the *Tantrasāra*:
"All [the goddesses] are equal to ten million suns, adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon;
they have four arms and three eyes, and hold chowries in their hands."
Having thus visualized [the goddesses] in the filaments, from the east to the northeast, with their hands granting boons and fearlessness, and their lotus-hands joined to the hand of Śiva;

One should worship the eight Śaktis—Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and the others—in their proper sequence as the presiding deities of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas); one should offer salutations and display the Mudrā.
In the northeast is the Śakti white as cow's milk, and Manonmanī;
she resides in the center of the solar mandala at the tip of the petal of the circular lotus.
And upon the tip of the lotus's filaments, within a circular lunar mandala,
is Viṣṇu, four-armed, [wearing] a crown, and holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
Resembling a blue lotus and situated in the center of the lunar mandala,
one should indeed worship the solar mandala at the tip of the pericarp of the lotus.
Rudra, blue-throated and three-eyed, stands in the midst of the fire,
adorned with all ornaments and wearing a serpent as his sacred thread.
One should worship the Śakti-maṇḍala in the center of the pericarp of the lotus;
and [therein] the one seated upon the Śakti-maṇḍala, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
He has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, possesses three eyes, and is as pure as clear crystal;
he holds a sword, a trident, an arrow, and a rosary, while extending the gesture of fearlessness.
The god holds a water-pot and carries a choice lotus,
with a lion skin and elephant hide as his garments, arranged respectively from right to left.
Having meditated upon the seat that pervades the principles from Earth up to Śuddhavidyā, O God of gods, one should worship it immediately thereafter.
In the *Candrajñāna*:
"The infinite earth is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and likewise water is the lion-throne;
fire is declared to be this yoga, and wind is likewise the lotus."
The sky is indeed stainless; now hear the procedure for the five seats:
the lion-seat is quadrangular, and the command of Ananta is triangular.
One should visualize a lotus of circular shape as a six-cornered pure seat,
and an eight-cornered seat as the yoga-seat.
Regarding those born of yoga:
first is the seat called Ananta, after that the Lion Seat (Siṃhāsana),
the third is the Yoga Seat (Yogāsana), and the fourth is the Lotus Seat (Padmāsana).
The fifth is declared to be Vimala; one should arrange them in sequence above.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"The invocation, the seat, the yoga, and for the bath, there should be the lion-throne."
In the act of worship, there is the great lotus, the stainless seat for the meal.
In the Vinoda [Tantra], one should indeed conceive of these as being called "Ananta.
Regarding the Cause (kāraṇa):
that which ends with the lotus of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) is known as the firm seat (sthirāsana).
Having clearly visualized the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), one should place the form within it.
One should install the embodied form (mūrti) ending with the Īśvara-tattva within the circumference of the liṅga.
As stated in the Vātula:
"One should also employ the installation of the thirty-eight kalās for one's own spiritual benefit."
Then, one should arrange the mātrikās beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'.
Having thus bowed, the practitioner of mantra should then fashion the body of knowledge (vidyādeha),
which is the stainless power of Śiva that is ever-united with him.
That very [form], through the differentiation of its manifestations and actions, is considered the body of Sadāśiva;
it is crooked at the end due to the destruction [of bonds] and the like, and is seated upon the lion-throne of mantra.
Resembling pure crystal, endowed with the thirty-two marks,
five parts long, four parts short, five parts subtle, and six parts elevated.
(58ā) It is praised when seven parts are red, three are deep, and two are broad:
the distance between the arms, the eyes, the knees, and likewise the nose.
The space between the breasts is praised as being five finger-breadths long;
likewise, the neck, the face, the back, and short shanks are praised.
The fingers and their joints, the hair, teeth, and nails; the armpits, the belly, and the chest; the nostrils, the shoulders, and the forehead—these are subtle.
The hands, feet, lower lip, tongue, eyes, skin, ears, voice,
disposition, and navel— these nine are praised as being deep.
The head and the forehead-ornament (lalāṭikā) are both praised as being broad;
he is seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), five-faced, with three eyes in each face.
And by means of the [Kriyā] powers, one should meditate on the wide-eyed Lord, endowed with the digit of the moon of knowledge,
whose face is like that of Dhavaleśāna, and whose Tatpuruṣa face is yellow.
Sadyojāta is proclaimed as having a black and terrible face, with a red upper face,
and a single very white western face.
Wearing a sacred thread, peaceful, adorned with matted locks and a crescent moon,
his limbs anointed with divine perfumes and decorated with celestial garlands.
His lotus-like hands, held in excellent gestures, carry a spear, a sword, a trident,
and a khaṭvāṅga staff on the right side, while on the left side they hold a hand-drum and a citron.
Visualizing [the deity] holding a snake, a rosary, and a blue lotus with five hands,
one should manifest the form as the unfolding of the mere potency of the seed-syllable.
By dissolving the form of the *liṅga* during meditation, one should abandon the state of being a *liṅga*;
having contemplated the supreme Śiva as partless and self-luminous.
Having led the mantra to the abode of Śiva by abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā,
[it is said] in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The letter A, the letter U, the letter Ma, and the Bindu as well— "
And the sound that suppresses the half-moon, as well as the very end of sound.
And she is endowed with power, all-pervasive, and of the nature of the void; she is Ananta, Anaśritā, Anantā, as well as Samanā and Unmanā.
From the end of Samānā up to the end of Unmanī, Paraśiva [resides];
thence, situated in the middle of the forehead, is that which shines with the brilliance of a throbbing star.
Having meditated upon Śaṅkara, who is pervaded by the limbs of Brahmā and exists in the form of a drop (bindu),
situated within the handful of flowers, one should cause him to enter the target-form (lakṣyamūrti).
Having invoked Śaṅkara with the *āvāhinī* [mudrā] at the heart, and having established him with the *sthāpinī*,
one should effect his close presence (*sannidhāna*) and then restrain him with the one called *niṣṭhūra*.
As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
One should establish [the deity] with the Ācāryasadyomantra; one should effect its presence with the Guṇyamantra; and one should perform the confinement with the Bahurūpa and Puruṣa mantras.
(59B) One should not, however, meditate on Īśāna as complete in all his limbs.
Regarding Somaśambhu, it is said here:
"Invocation (*āvāhana*) is defined here as the state of being present before one's eyes with reverence."
The wise have stated that "niveśana" (establishment) therein is performed with devotion.
O Jagannātha, even for one who has merely seen you, the acceptance that "I am yours" ensures that your presence is never obstructed, even though he remains a man of the world.
The complete exhaustion of proximity, extending as far as the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa),
is proclaimed to be the supreme power within the omnipresence of Śambhu.
Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa with the six mantras, and then having unified [the self] with the peaceful mantra of Kālakaṇṭhī, one should expel the obstacles with a fist.
Having performed the salutation with the *liṅgamudrā* while reciting the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*),
one should pour [the offering] into the fire-pit for Śiva, the seed of bliss, who consists of awakening and bliss.
That which is unmanifest among those who are unworthy is the "burning of the pit" (ava-kuṇḍana);
one should effect the equality of the limbs with the whole body, rendered immortal.
Therefore, one should bind the mudrā and not rotate the hand above;
for by this quality, which exists above, the glorious Lord of Beasts (Mṛgendreśa) rules over the entire universe.
Because it occupies the uppermost part of the body, the head is not a constituent limb of the body.
Whichever body belongs to each [deity], he enters into that by means of which [he does so];
thus, through the Tatpuruṣa [compound], he is the mouth of both the Tantras and his own self.

(59B) Since he is Śiva, who is non-terrible (*aghora*) because he is synonymous with the awakening of the heart, and because [the Lord] is metaphorically called "Rau" due to the severity of what is to be avoided; therefore, he is the one who brings about the transcendence of that [severity].
Because he is by nature the enemy of the left—the three aims of life (trivarga) and the Samaveda—he is the supreme, secret, left abode; thus he is Vāmaguhyaka.
By whose mere will forms come into being instantly, he is therefore designated as "Sadyojāta" (the Instantaneously Born).
Or rather, he bestows the form of Sadyojāta upon those yogins who possess that form, having fashioned it with such swiftness that even the form of the Destroyer (Antaka) is surpassed.
His heart is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), and his glory is eightfold sovereignty;
that state of Śiva-hood is not dependent on anything else, for it exists above Śiva.
The non-difference from the Supreme Lord is desired as the armor;
it is an unbearable majesty that removes obstacles to the weapons.

Omniscience, contentment, primordial awakening, sovereignty, eternal and undiminished power, and infinite power— these six, they say, are the limbs of the Great Lord, the permission of the All-pervading One.
Endowed with the thirty-eight kalās, Sadāśiva is manifest and possessed of parts (sakala); otherwise, Śiva is partless (niṣkala).
A person who is present nearby becomes [manifest] by calling them by their own name;
likewise, Śiva becomes present through the application of mantra,
just as fire residing within wood is revealed by friction and other means.
(60ā) Likewise, Śiva is manifested through devotion by the power of mantra.
O Lord, Sovereign of the entire world, [this continues] from the root to the tip until the conclusion of the worship.
Therefore, through a state of joy, be present within this linga.
At the time of invocation, that form melts like molten gold;
therefore, O radiant one, the wise practitioner should offer the arghya water at the moment of invocation.
Water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, dūrvā grass, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth.
(p. 106) Even before performing the rite of a warm welcome, one should perform the ritual according to the procedure.
In the *Somaśambhu*, it is said: "Namassvadhā, svadhā, and vauṣaṭ should be used in their respective order."
Having recited [the mantra] preceded by the heart-mantra, one should offer the water for the feet and the other articles.

Water for the feet (pādya) is offered at the pair of lotus-feet; water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) at the faces; and the respectful offering (arghya), along with flowers, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice grains, upon the head of the Lord. Water for the feet brings about the attainment of Śiva’s state, and the water for sipping shall be a source of joy.
But the worthiness of Śiva [arises] from his manifestation as Śiva, his equality [with others], and so forth, whereas that of the self [arises] from these same factors.
Having invoked [the deity] upon a firm seat, one should perform the mental bath;
one should touch that seat with the left hand while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Having taken fresh flowers, one should dismiss Tatpuruṣa;
at the conclusion of the consecration with mantra-water, one should cause the mantra-flower to be offered.
Then, having offered the mantra-flower, one should present the mantra-food;
likewise, one should offer the lamp for the fire and the oblation for the purpose of pacification.
Mantra is said to be the secret; from the word *madana*, it is called food (*anna*). Furthermore, that which illuminates the secret is called the food of mantra (*mantrānna*).
Likewise, O Aṃśumatī, having recollected the Śiva-mantra, one should then place fragrant flowers;
one should also apply the *golaka*, clarified butter, water, and the crown.
One should adorn [the image] with various jewels such as bracelets, armlets, and necklaces.
If these materials are unavailable, one should mentally resolve that they are to be given in the form of clarified butter.
In the Vātula:
"Having purified it with silk, fine cloth, or divine garments, or likewise with variegated cloth, or even with cotton cloth, one should collect [the materials]."
One should avoid old, torn, or burst cloth, as well as that which has been used for the month of Māgha;
one should wear white cloth in the forenoon and red cloth at midday.
One should wear yellow garments at the evening twilight in all respects; as stated in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"The garments should be very variegated and adorned with various ornaments."
And one should offer flowers that are pure, free of loose fibers, and fresh.
For as many thousands of years as there are threads in that garment, for so long one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Regarding the cause:
the sacred thread should be performed with the Kavaca mantra, while the garment is indeed [consecrated] with the Hṛdaya mantra;
it should be three-stranded, white or yellow, and made of silk thread or similar material.
Having offered the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) to Rudra, one becomes a knower of the Vedānta.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Saffron, agallochum, camphor, musk, sandalwood, and so forth..."
One should apply snow-water, oil, musk, and yakṣakardama.
One should perform an anointing of the Liṅga with divine and fragrant scents—
namely, gorocanā, saffron, sandalwood, camphor, black agallochum, and devadāru—
as well as musk and other such substances; by thus anointing Śambhu, one obtains the merit of ten million horse sacrifices.
The merit from anointing with fragrant unguents is twofold that of sandalwood;
it should be known that the merit of agallochum is eight times greater than that of sandalwood.
The fruit is especially desired to be double that of black agalloch;
from that, the merit of saffron is ordained to be a hundredfold greater.
One should offer incense made of *devadāru* wood to Śiva;
one attains the world of Śiva for one kalpa, without a doubt.
By offering incense made from the root of the Bilva tree to Umāmaheśvara,
one attains great sovereignty and, at the end of that life, shall go to the city of Śiva.
If a man, devoted to Mṛtyuñjaya, offers incense made of *āraśvadha* wood, he shall conquer death;
being victorious over death, he shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
(61 B) Hear now the fruit of the merit of one who, like a bearer of water, offers a crown adorned with every kind of jewel to Śiva.
Accompanied by tens of millions upon tens of millions of celestial mansions endowed with all objects of desire,
he dwells happily in the city of Śiva until the final dissolution of the world.
Whoever should indeed offer even a mere tuṭi upon the head of a golden liṅga,
he shall remain as Indra for as long as fourteen Indras occupy the throne of Indra.
p. 109) Thus, the fruit based on what is to be known should be understood according to one's wealth.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"On Sunday, [one should offer] a ruby; on Monday, a pearl."
One should give coral on a Saturday, and emerald on a Wednesday.
On a Saturday, there should be a Puṣyarāga; on a Friday, a diamond is prescribed;
and on a Saturday (Mandavāra), an Indranīla—indeed, all these [gems] should be used.
On all days of the week, the prescribed method for ornaments is considered appropriate;
one should likewise avoid flowers and garments that correspond to those specific days.
One part is for the portion of worship; one part is for the wrapping of cloth;
the cloth is to be adorned with ornaments; and one part is beautified with flowers.
One should place the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) on the left, the principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva) on the right,
and the knower of ritual procedures should conceive of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) in the middle.
In the Śivadharmottara:
"With flowers produced in the forest, or with leaves grown on mountains—
[flowers and leaves] that are not stale, without holes, sprinkled [with water], and free from living organisms."
One should worship Śiva with fresh flowers or even with dried ones;
[specifically] with jasmine, blue lotuses, red lotuses, jasmine, punnāga, and campaka.
With Aśoka, white Mandāra, Karṇikāra, and Bakula flowers;
and with Karavīra, Arka, Mandāra, Śamī, Tagara, and Kesara.
With *kuśa* grass, *apāmārga*, and flowers from the *kadamba* and *droṇa* trees,
as well as with white and golden *dhūrdhūra* and red *kāñcana*.
Palāśa and pāṭalī are praised when their blossoms have fallen;
so too are bilva, tulasī, dhurdhūra, kalhāra, and hemapuṣpaka.
One should repeatedly wash the head of the deity with [water infused with] tulasī;
this should be done for one year, and likewise for six months with bilva.
The lotus [is used] for twelve months; other flowers include the *kuṣṭha*, *vāraka*, *bilva*, *apāmārga*, mango, *damana*, *maruva*, and *arjuna*.
And there are the *nandyāvarta*, *śamyarka*, *tilaka*, *stana-mallikā*,
*saugandhika*, *āsana*, *sindhu-keśa*, *mālikā*, and *arjuna* trees.
Dūrvātalaśikhākola, gaurīsurabhikā, śamī,
muṇḍakāntaramadana, bhṛṅgāra, and paribhadraka.
(62B) Jambū and kuśāgra—these are the recommended collections of leaves.
In the absence of the previously mentioned flowers, one should worship Śiva with these leaves.
But if even leaves are not available, one should worship with fruits as well—
such as citrons, jambīras, and the auspicious plantains and pomegranates.
One should worship Śiva with fruits that provide immediate satisfaction;
likewise, with *tulasī* leaves, *bilva* leaves, golden flowers, and pearls.
One should worship the liṅga at the three junctions of the day, washing it again and again;
on Sunday, one should offer bilva, and on Monday, tulasī.
On Tuesday, there should be wood-apple (*kapittha*); likewise, on Wednesday, citron (*mātulaṅga*).
On Thursday, there should be *dāntava*; and on Friday, *jambūpatra*.
On Saturday, *viṣṇukrānti* is used; on a weekday, the leaf is said to be used here.
Or with whatever flowers, whether grown in water or on land, [one worships] Śiva.
Having worshipped with devotion using flowers sprinkled [with water], one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
likewise, he who, having personally gathered flowers, worships Śiva properly.
Śiva constantly accepts all of those with devotion:
flowers from the finest gardens as the highest, and those produced in the forest as the middle.
The lowest sale and even a supplicant shall be fruitless;
among a thousand *arka* flowers, the *karavīra* is superior.
Among all varieties of flowers, the *karavīra* is preeminent;
within it resides the Lord, in the form of the pedestal of the *liṅga*.
That flower and the golden flower (hemapuṣpa), when used for worship for years, do not become *nirmālya* (worn-out offerings) therein; such is the certainty of the scripture.
By worshipping Nīlakaṇṭha with even a single Karavīra flower that has been scented with perfume, one shall uplift ten million members of one's lineage.
A single bilva leaf is superior to a thousand karavīra flowers;
the wise know that the three bilva leaves represent the powers of will, knowledge, and action.
By the sight, touch, or even the salutation of the bilva leaf, the sin committed during a day and night is destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
O Nārada, by worshipping the Lord of Girijā even with dry or stale bilva leaves, one is liberated from all sins.
One who worships the Liṅga even once with unbroken Bilva leaves is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva.

One should avoid insects and the like, as well as defects; one should specifically avoid spider-silk. [One should also avoid] the leaf called *kunda*, the parrot-wing leaf, the *bilva* leaf, the *nirguṇṭhī* leaf, and the *kapittha* leaf.
These five, along with a bilva leaf,
are for the worship of Śiva with the Vyomavyāpin mantra.
A single lotus flower is superior to a thousand bilva leaves;
a bakula flower is superior to a thousand lotus flowers.
The wise know that among a thousand *bakapuṣpa* flowers, one *dhūdhūraka* is superior;
and among a thousand *dhūdhūraka* flowers, the glorious blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) is the best.
Among all species of flowers, the blue lotus is the most excellent;
after the blue lotus, the large-flowered variety is distinguished as superior.
The *droṇa* flower is superior to thousands of large flowers;
the *apāmārga* is superior to thousands of *droṇa* flowers.
A single *kuśa* flower is superior to a thousand *apāmārga* flowers;
a beautiful blue lotus is better than a thousand *kuśa* flowers.
Among all species of flowers, the blue lotus is the most excellent;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a flower equal to the blue lotus.
A single act of devotion excels thousands of blue lotuses;
for those [lotuses] may be white, red, or blue, and they correspond to the *sāttvika* and other [qualities].
