One should specify yellow-colored flowers as being of the mixed (miśraka) type;
one should avoid all others that are dark (tāmasa), with the exception of the blue lotus (nīlotpala).
One should offer the *nandyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, and white *arkapuṣpa* at sunrise; and the *karavīra* flower and *droṇa* are beneficial when [the sun] is at midday. (64a)
Mallikā and kṛṣṇadurdhūra are beneficial in the evening; campaka is beneficial at midday; and kadamba, kanaka, ājāti, and dvikarṇī are beneficial at midnight.
The *droṇa*, the white lotus (*śvetapadma*), the jasmine (*jātī*), the *cambha*, the *karṇikā*, the *nandyāvarta*, the *śriyāvarta*, the *mandāra*, and the hundred-petaled rose (*śatapatrikā*).
One should designate flowers such as the white arka, mālatī, bilva, punnāga, and kurava as sāttvika.
One should designate the red lotus, the white lotus, the *durdhūra*, the two types of *bṛhatī*,
the *palāśa*, the *pāṭala*, and so forth as being of the *rājasa* nature.
In the *Kālottara*:
"The *kara*, *vakula*, *kāśa*, *śirīṣa*, and likewise *ketakī*,
*lāṅgalī*, *ḍāḍimī*, *jāpa*, *śrīparṇī*, and *vibhītaka*."
One should avoid the bandhūka, kunda, and yūtha flowers, as well as cotton, the nimba thorn, the kiṃśuka, the madantī, and water lilies.
One should avoid [leaves] that are unripe, over-ripe, or still in bud;
as well as those pierced by hair or insects, and those covered by spiderwebs or threads.
One should avoid flowers that have fallen on their own, those gathered by others, those from a single-day-old plant, and those that are damaged.
One should also avoid flowers from a plant lacking leaves.
One should not worship Viṣṇu with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), nor Vināyaka with *tulasī*; one should not worship Maheśāna with *dūrvā* grass, nor Maheśvara with *ketakī*.
One should avoid flowers that are scentless or have a pungent odor.
As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"During festivals and the like, during processions, and during the acts of serving food..."
In the ornament of poetry, everything should always be avoided or accepted as appropriate.
In the Kālottara:
"One should worship the goddess Umā with black flowers, mahiṣākṣī flowers, and śiṃśumāraka flowers."
One should not offer flowers grown in a divine garden to a planetary deity;
rather, one should properly worship the Liṅga with fragrant flowers.
Or by means of well-constructed garlands, one shall obtain infinite fruit;
a person should wrap the *liṅga* with garlands and worship it.
Śiva rejoices with the Goddess and his son when he is worshipped according to the rule;
O Goddess, the altar becomes the *liṅga*, for the *liṅga* is Maheśvara himself in person.
By worshipping those two, both the Goddess and the God are worshipped.
One who constructs a flower-pavilion over Śiva with ease [attains great merit].
It was adorned from the pedestals upward with hanging flower garlands and other ornaments,
and with most wonderful great vehicles beautified by divine flowers.
Surrounded by all [his followers], the illustrious one shall go happily to the city of Śiva. Worship performed with leaf-cuttings destroys the Rākṣasas.
Worship with flower offerings shall bring about all accomplishments;
having first worshipped the limbs of dissolution (layāṅga), one should then worship the limbs of Śiva and Brahmā.
In the *Somaśambhu*:
"Having taken up divine knowledge through prostration, one should worship the limbs of enjoyment.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
Worship is the means for the self to attain the sixfold qualities of Śiva and to enjoy them;
it is the reintegration of the limbs of the self and the union of the self with Śiva.
One should worship Īśāna on the eastern petal, Nara on the eastern petal,
Aghora on the southern petal, and likewise Vāmadeva on the northern petal.

The mantra ending in *ajā* is on the western petal; the heart-mantra is on the fire-petal (southeast); the head-mantra is on the northeast petal; the crown-mantra is on the southwest petal; and the armor-mantra is on the northwest petal.
The Eye is in the center, and the King of Weapons (the Astra-mantra) along with the ornaments are in the four directions.
In Vijaya:
the five Brahmans and the six limbs of the Lord are situated all around.
One should draw [the essence] from the faces and those respective limbs, like transferring light from one lamp to another.

(116) [He meditates on] Īśāna, who has the luster of crystal, the cause of the world, three-eyed, with the moon upon his crest, gentle, serene, and holding a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands.
[He saw] a man resembling gold, wearing yellow garments and a sacred thread,
holding a citron and a rosary, and bearing the moon upon his crest.
Then [he should visualize him] with three eyes, gentle, adorned with a crown and the gaze of Indra,
with tawny beard and hair, and a face formidable with fangs.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, decorated with snakes and scorpions,
he holds a khaṭvāṅga, a rosary, a shield, and a noose.
In his four left hands [he holds] a quadrangular [shield], and in his four right hands a trident,
an axe, a sword, and a staff for crushing enemies.
Thus, the non-terrible (Aghora) face has the luster of a fresh cloud and grants all desires;
the left (Vāma) face has an intensely red hue and is adorned with a garland, garments, and a sacred thread.
With a prominent nose and a red turban, holding a sword and a shield in his hands,
he is richly adorned with white garlands, perfumes, and ornaments, wearing a white turban and white garments.
He is endowed with the gentle moon upon his crest, has the form of a youth, and possesses three eyes;
he is Sadyojāta, with one white face, bestowing boons, holding a lotus, and appearing formidable.
Having thus meditated [on the deity] from the beginning of the *ī* vowel to the end of the *na*, one should always worship [the following]:
the cow, the lotus, the trident, the crocodile, and that which is called the garland.
One should display the five mudrās precisely in the sequence beginning with Īśāna;
then, one should worship Netra in the northern portion of Īśāna.
The eye of the All-pervasive Lord is the vessel of ruddy light, consisting of vision and action;
its threefold form, resting upon the triad [of powers], is the maṇḍala beginning with the forest-dweller (Vanya).
With the face and limbs as described for the heart-mantra and so forth, joined with the hand-held implements and the rest;
or else, according to the teaching of Yogaśiva, having one face and holding a trident in the hand.
In the four directions, the [seats] of the mouth, hands, feet, and anus are placed in sequence.
In the *Kālottara*:
"The heart is like the moon, and the head has the luster of gold."
Her crest is rich with the color of vermilion, and her armor shines like a bumblebee.
He has eyes resembling lightning, and his weapon possesses a radiance equal to fire;
he sits in the lotus posture and wears a crown of matted hair adorned with the crescent moon.
[They are] three-eyed and four-armed, adorned with all ornaments, facing Śiva, and endowed with hands holding a spear, a trident, and the gesture of fearlessness.

"The invocation and the seat for him are said to be the twelfth [service]."
The water for washing the feet should consist of five *mātrās*, and likewise, the water for sipping should consist of three *mātrās*.
The arghya offering should consist of one measure; scent is said to be six measures;
incense should be twelve measures, while [the lamp] is fifteen.
The lamp is indeed six measures, while the *nīrājana* is sixteen;
afterwards, one should cause it to be offered with ashes, which is said to be seven measures.
The fan should be three *mātrās* in size, and the chowrie should be ten;
the umbrella should be five *mātrās*, while the mirror should be one *mātrā* of a sage (*munimātra*).
Then one should present the food offering (naivedya) consisting of twenty-four items;
the water for honor (arghya) is for the pleasure of the Deity, and the fragrance (gandha) is for the pleasure of Brahmā.
One should know that flowers bestow nourishment; a lamp is dear to Vaiśvānara (Agni). A lamp is to be known as dear to Arka (the Sun), while an incense burner (ārātrika) bestows victory.
Protection is also for the sake of one's own defense, especially for that of the king;
the mirror bestows knowledge, and the parasol brings strength to the king.
The chowrie (cāmara) brings the destruction of enemies and brings delight through song and instrumental music;
the letter *ha* signifies abundance from bathing, while water (*pānīya*) is the protector of life.

One should know that betel-leaf bestows prosperity, while the burnt offering destroys disease. If it lacks fragrance, there will be a loss of wealth; if it lacks flowers, there will be a great commotion.
If incense is omitted, disease is certain; if the lamp is omitted, loss of intelligence occurs;
if the food offering is omitted, famine ensues; but if the fire is omitted, there is turmoil.
If [the rite] is devoid of mantra, there is death; if devoid of ritual action, it bestows disease;
if devoid of worship, there is deficiency, as well as the destruction of sons, wife, and land.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship Śiva according to the prescribed rules.

[The offerings are: scent, roots, fruits, tubers, flowers, and so forth; the earthly [offering], that which comes from water, from trees, and from curd; the desired fiery [offering] consisting of jewels; and so on.

Then, [he performs] the five types of offerings (*pañcopacāra*) consisting of lamps and so forth, ornaments and so forth, incense fanned by the wind, as well as incense, fly-whisks, cloths, songs, and excellent offerings, along with the light.
Having offered the *arghya*, flowers, and other offerings, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
As stated in the *Kālottara* (p.
137): "One should diligently contemplate one's own body (*svadeha*) as being situated between the two moons."
Therefore, your body consists of nectar and cannot be slain even by the gods.
Self-protection has been fully described; now the protection of the mantra is being declared.
One should then place the mantra within the womb of Śakti, O Śivā, as a neuter [entity].
Those who reside in Śiva, possessing tranquil splendor, become powerless in the presence of this Puruṣa;
therefore, mantras that have entered into Śakti bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
She should be known as non-different from Śiva, like the rays of the sun at all times;
she is the Mother of Mantras, the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), the Primordial One, and indeed Kuṇḍalinī.
Constantly situated in the region of the heart, resembling the sun, moon, and fire,
she is to be known as one, though threefold, through the divisions of Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and the others.
Hidden within the Suṣumnā and known only through the mouth of the Guru,
it extends from the navel to the end of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta), pervaded by the circulating vital breath (prāṇa).

For yogins, that direction toward the state of Śaṅkara, which extends from the trident, the path, the water, and so forth, up to the dvādaśānta, is distinguished by the process of going and returning.
"By relying upon the nature of the other (parabhāva), one attains supreme bliss.
Having thus understood Śakti and the rest, one becomes capable of protecting the mantra.
Relying upon the power of *śakti*, one should begin the silent recitation (*upāṃśujapa*).
Power is declared to be twofold, consisting of the Sun and the Moon within the cave of the heart.
Within the heart, at the end of the three folds, it moves along the path of the bird;
for those desiring liberation, the mantra should be recited during the day when the breath is rising with the sun.
At the rising of the moon and during the night, one who desires power should perform recitation (*japa*).
When the breath flows through the mouth of the *suṣumnā*, this recitation grants all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
In the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*: "One hundred and eight is proclaimed as the best;
half of that is praised as the middling; half of that again is considered the lowest."
(77a) Having opened his eyes for a thousand autumns for the sake of destroying the enemy with the Aghora weapon,
they likewise became the eyes of Ākulaṇḍa.
Then, from those three, tears fell.
By the command of Śiva, who acts for the welfare of the entire world, the rudrākṣas came forth from the branches;
these rudrākṣa trees were born from the twelve suns and are distinguished by their various brownish tints.
Sixteen [lines] born from the moon-eye are white in color; ten born from the fire-eye are black;
O Brahman, [the line] from the Brahma-eye is white and endowed with a tawny hue.
But a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya are of a fortunate nature.
They say that the black variety is of Śūdra origin,
while the one produced from the rudrākṣa tree is of noble birth (jātya).
That which has a single face is Śaṅkara himself in person.
The rudrākṣa seed destroys [sin]; it destroys the self. O Lord of Gods, the two-faced seed is the destroyer of many cow-slaughters; it is a divine, unattainable bead.

May that four-faced one, who bears three faces— each said to be of the nature of Agni— which in an instant destroys the host of mental afflictions, and which is worthy of being praised by the four-faced [Brahmā], grant us prosperity.
It destroys the sin of killing a human being in an instant.
Indeed, Kālāgnirudra has five faces that consume all things and destroy great sins;
for Skanda has six faces, with which he [holds] a hand.
One should maintain it with skill in order to abandon impurity.
The seven-faced one, whose lord is Ananta (the serpent king),
instantly effects purification from theft;
for the golden image of Vaināyaka has eight faces.
A falsehood is heavy, bringing ruin such as illicit sexual intercourse with women.
The nine-faced god Bhairava himself bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, possessing power equal to Śiva;
he holds that which is to be maintained with his left hand.
It destroys ten million times ten thousand killings.
(140) Hari himself [is] that seed-syllable of the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa),
which [subdues] piśācas, bhūtas, grahas, and rākṣasas, as well as vetālas, serpents, pratīyas, and lions.
He swiftly slays those [beings] such as tigers;
one should wear the eleven-faced and ten-headed Ekādaśarudra on the crest-lock according to the rule, O faultless one.
That which was spoken by the twenty mouths is equal to ten thousand human horse-sacrifices, a vājapeya sacrifice, and a thousand times a thousand gifts of cows.
That is known as the Bhāskarīya; when it is committed to memory, it satisfies the Sun and is equal to the merit of a horse-sacrifice and a gem-stone sacrifice combined.
An elephant, a horse, a female donkey, a jackal, a mouse, a bird, a eunuch, a blind man, a woman, a deer, a serpent,
an eye, a parrot, a snake, and a buffalo—
It removes the dangers of tigers and other such threats;
indeed, this which has three faces and six teeth is known as Kārttikeya— by its recollection, everything, including incomparable enjoyments and objects of pleasure, is accomplished.
This *pādukā* will be accomplished;
even through the killing of one's mother, father, brother, or wife for the sake of attaining desired objects, this essence of practice will succeed.
(78a) Even the most sinful man is purified by giving even a single coin; there is nothing superior to this.
With "Dhatke," he becomes pure;
for even while acting, he is not stained by the impurities arising from that sacrifice, since the tail is joined with the tail and the mouth with the mouth by those who are alike.
With pearls and corals interspersed,
and gold set with gems, one who offers this becomes a faultless mortal who attains the fruit of a sacrifice.
He who, firm in his vow, wears a thousand Rudrākṣas,
all the gods bow down to him just as they do to Rudra himself.
If a rosary of one hundred and eight rudrākṣas is worn,
one undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every single moment.
He who always wears a rosary of Rudrākṣa beads on his neck, in his hand, or on his palm—whether it be one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five—is Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt.
O Six-faced One, a rosary of eleven Rudrākṣas that lacks the central Meru bead grants immediate liberation to one who recites mantras at the base of the thumb.
He beheld that supreme, auspicious bestower of liberation, possessing great majesty,
with one face, or three faces, or four, or five.
It should also be made with six faces; therefore, one should avoid those that are mixed.
The face of the rudrākṣa is Brahmā, and its stalk is said to be Viṣṇu.
(78B) It is taught that Īśvara resides in the line; thus these are the presiding deities. One should fashion a face upon the face, and join the root with the root.
One should tie the *dhātrī* fruit, or the one called *sāvitrī*, or the knot known as *brahma*;
above that knot, however, there should be one called *meru*, which must not be bypassed.
One should wash it with the Sadyojāta mantra, rub it with the Vāmadeva mantra,
fumigate it with the Bahurūpa mantra, and smear it with the Puruṣa mantra.
One should consecrate each [of the other four] one hundred times with the fifth mantra alone;
likewise, one should consecrate Meru with the fifth and with the Aghora mantra.
Having worshipped Meru with the five [mantras] in due order, just like Śiva,
the wise one should take up a flower with the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger.
Having covered the torn cloth while recollecting the root mantra,
one should recite the mantra over a flower held in the left hand with the right hand.
Among the [types of recitation], that which is mental is the highest of the high;
the whispered (upāṃśu) is declared to be the middle, and the spoken (bhāṣya) is indeed the lowest.
Therefore, having set aside the recitation aloud, one should mutter [the mantra] mentally or in a whisper.
As stated in the Bhīmasaṃhitā:
"In the case of a whispered sacrifice, it is declared that the ritual of the oblation is performed verbally."
"One should mutter the mantra mentally"—thus has the mantra been described.
In the *Kālottara*: "One should grasp the thumb and ring finger and perform mental recitation;
one obtains merit a hundred million times greater—of this there is no doubt."
One should perform the whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa) using the thumb and middle finger;
thus, from a hundred such recitations, the fruit of one hundred thousand is produced for him.
One should perform the recitation and the verbal utterance using the thumb and the index finger;
the joining of syllable to syllable should be like a flowing river—neither hurried nor slow.
One shall obtain a thousandfold fruit; one’s speech does not become false.
One should recite according to the path of emanation and rub the rosary.
For the sake of liberation, one should gradually diminish [the practice] along the upward path year by year;
the mantra-practitioner must not overstep Meru, for by overstepping it, he becomes a partaker of fault.

One thousand recitations of the Bahurūpa mantra should be performed; by that, one is purified. However, if it has fallen on the ground through negligence, one hundred recitations must be performed as an expiation.
Likewise, when [the teacher] has fallen or in other such cases, penance is not desired;
similarly, one should not show the mantra or the rosary even to the guru.
(79B) But during the time of recitation, O Six-faced One, the rosary must be kept secret;
for if the rosary comes within the sight of others, the recitation becomes fruitless.
The rosary should be consecrated under a lunar mansion, while the central bead (nāyaka) should be for the child;
it should be provided with knots representing the Śaktis, and the threads should have Brahmā and the other deities as their presiding divinities.
The twenty-fifth [day] is for the purpose of liberation; the twenty-seventh is for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*);
the twenty-eighth is for the purpose of desire (*kāmya*); and the fifteenth is for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
Brahmā himself resides at the wrist; Śatakratu is known to be in the thumb;
Īśvara is to be known in the index finger; and Śiva is in the middle finger.
The Ananga [deity] is on the ring finger, while Bhāskara is on the little finger;
he resides upon the petals of the Yakṣas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, and all the gods.
Having thus resolved, one should first [perform the preliminary rites] and afterwards recite the five-syllable mantra;
the thumb and the index finger are the means for removing both worldly and otherworldly suffering.
One should indeed recite with the thumb and the middle finger for all subjugation rites;
with the thumb and the ring finger, there shall be rites such as summoning and the like.
Through the joining of the little finger and the thumb, one effects hatred, eradication, and killing;
the wise person should always recite the mantra in this manner using the thumb and the ring finger.
Without the eight-fold thread, one should avoid all recitation;
therefore, with every effort, one should commence the recitation using rudrākṣa beads.
Having circumambulated Mount Meru, one should perform the recitation with a concentrated mind for the rites of subjugation and attraction,
as well as for pacification and enrichment.
By reciting with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, one attains success immediately;
moreover, in the west there is attraction, and in the north there shall be pacification.
One should know that the rite for nourishment belongs to Indra; that for causing enmity belongs to Agni;
for those desiring heaven, it belongs to Yama; and they know that the rite for delusion belongs to Nirṛti.
One should perform rites for pacification (śāntika) in the west; in the northwest, there shall be eradication (uccāṭana).
In the north, there is attraction (karṣaṇa), while in the northeast, death is certain.
O Hero, red color brings prosperity, yellow indeed results in immobilization (stambhana),
crystal-like leads to liberation, and black is for malevolent sorcery (abhicāra).
A single recitation with finger-counting (aṅgulijapa) becomes tenfold by means of lines;
one should know that it is eightfold when performed with a desired [object], and it becomes tenfold in the presence of a lamp.
In a conch-shell [vessel], it is a hundredfold; in a ruby, a thousandfold;
with jewels, ten thousandfold; and crystal is said to be a hundred thousandfold.
A lotus weighing ten billion *koṭis* of gold,
joined with ten billion knots of *kuśa* grass, and an infinite number of *rudrākṣa* beads.

One should know that in one's own home the fruit is single; in a cow-pen, the fruit is tenfold. One should know that by a riverbank the fruit is a hundredfold, and at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), the fruit of recitation (*japa*) is a thousandfold.
On the shore of the ocean there would be ten million, and at a temple of Śiva, one hundred million;
in places of accomplishment (siddhisthāna), it would be infinite—this is the place, O fair-faced one.
Through recitation, one may exhaust all evil with effort throughout a succession of future births;
through recitation, one conquers disease and even untimely death.
Through recitation, one attains accomplishment and liberation.
Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, [one should perform] the five [protections] without delay;
as stated in the *Cintyaviśva* (p.
146): "The heart-mantra and others are consecrated, the armor-mantra encircles it, and it is protected by the sword."
Accompanied by kuśa grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, it is performed with the mudrā known as Bhavaka.
O you who guard the secrets of secrets and so forth, accept this recitation performed by us;
may accomplishment be mine through your grace while you remain present.
O Mahādeva, whatever action there may be, whether always virtuous or non-virtuous,
Śaṅkara destroys it for one who stands in the state of Śiva.
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire world;
Śiva bestows [or restrains] everywhere—He who is Śiva, I am indeed He.
Having caused [the disciple] to recite this verse with his right hand toward Śambhu,
he should present it into the hand of the one who grants boons (Vara) with water for the arghya offering while reciting the root mantra.
In the *Kāmika*:
"Having performed the recitation (*japa*) of the Brahmāṅgā mantra, one should offer a tenth part [of that number] as a dedication;
having offered the water of honor (*arghya*), flowers, and so forth, and having praised her with various hymns."
(81a) To the southeast of the deity, one should then worship the yoga-throne:
"Homage again and again to the feet of the venerable Guru, together with his Śaktis."
Salutations again and again to those who always cause the awakening of the self that is ever-ripened.
In the *Kāmika*: "To the west of the Lord, one should then worship the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*)."
I am the possessor of all knowledge, the Lord who bestows universal wisdom.

Having brought [the deity] residing at the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) by means of mental, vocal, and physical restraints, and having offered three handfuls of flowers to the God of gods with the utterance "Namaḥ," [one should proceed].
One should satisfy the Lord with hymns of praise along with supreme devotion:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods; salutations to you, O mine of compassion."
Salutations to you, O Lord of Pārvatī; salutations to you, O lover of your devotees;
salutations to you, O imperishable one who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon all living beings.
Salutations to you, the God of gods; salutations to you whose crest is the moon. Salutations to you, supreme bliss; salutations to you who are clothed in an animal hide.
Salutations to you whose limbs are smeared with ashes; salutations to you, the enemy of Tripura.
Salutations to you, O Blessed Śambhu; salutations to you, whose ornaments are serpents.
"Salutations to you, O Mahādeva; protect me from the phenomenal world, O Lord.
Then, having offered three handfuls of flowers to the God, one should satisfy the Lord with hymns accompanied by supreme devotion.
The excellent, the most venerable, the giver of boons, the most sublime, the remover of suffering.
I perpetually bow to the god Sadāśiva, who bears the crescent moon;
he who is earth, water, fire, wind, ether, the self, the moon, and the sun.
The intellect, the mind, the ego,
and even the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti) all follow his will, which scatters forth both existence and non-existence.
To that supreme deity, the highest, the Supreme Self,
who is greater than the great, and the master of the great illusion and other powers;
Having paid homage to the immeasurable Self, who is more subtle than the subtlest,
salutations to You, O Viśvarūpa, the initiator of primordial time.
Omniscient One, homage be to you; O Creator of all, homage be to you! As stated in the *Kāmika*:
"The fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) should be performed as prescribed immediately after the consecration (*abhiṣeka*)."
Without him, O Teacher, one has no authority in initiation and other such rites.
Indeed, by means of the oblation alone, practitioners are liberated from the bondage of birth.
As stated in the *Kālottara*:
"Then, having obtained the charcoal from the fire-offering of the Lord of Gods, one should proceed from there."
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The rites of the fire and the rites of the vessel [for offerings] may be performed either in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
However, for the daily oblation (*nityahoma*), it should be one cubit in measure to the southeast of the Vedāśrama."
One should likewise construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) together with its girdles (mekhalā), according to its width and height,
either to the northeast or to the east of the yoga-pīṭha.
(82a) The sacrificial pit for the iṣṭi rite should be very firm; from the point of striking, it should be one finger-breadth wide on the outside.
Its height should start at four finger-breadths and decrease by two finger-breadths [downward] starting from three finger-breadths.
Above that is the girdle (mekhalā), and above that is the womb (yoni), which is one red finger-breadth in length and one auspicious finger-breadth in width;
the rim (nemi) is half a finger-breadth in height.
Make the entire lip like a thumb; make it like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
Likewise, one should make the navel in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the shape of a lotus.
The measurement of two parts is for the [lotus] petals, while one part is for the pericarp (karṇikā);
thus the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) have been declared, and now the altar-ground (sthaṇḍila) is described.
The ground should be pure, strewn with dry sand, one cubit in width,
three finger-breadths in height, level, and free from depressions or elevations.
In the Bhīmarudrasaṃhitā:
"If sand is unavailable for the fire-ritual (agnikārya), one may use dust or even clay;
having smeared it with cow-dung, it should be made into a square."
Placing the navel of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in front, one should sit facing north;
then follow the inspection of the pit, its sprinkling with water, and its striking with kusha grass.
In the Kālottara [Tantra] it is taught:
"One should perform the sprinkling with the Astra-mantra and the Varma-mantra;
or one may perform that extraction (udghāra), filling, and leveling with the Khaḍga-mantra."
One should perform the protection with the armor-mantra, the pulverizing with the arrow-atom,
as well as the sweeping, the smearing, the fashioning of the digit-form, and the visualization.
One should perform the donning of the three threads and the worship of the armor with the heart-mantra;
three lines should be drawn facing east, and one line facing north.
One should perform the vajrīkaraṇa with the Astra-mantra using three *kuśa* blades in the form of a vajra;
the crossroads (*catuṣpatha*) should be prepared with the Hṛdaya-mantra using two *kuśa* blades from the directions of Soma (North), Indra (East), and Īśa (Northeast).
For the sake of the axle-base, one should place the kuśa grasses with the armor-mantra (kavaca) during the oblation in the sacrificial pits;
having arranged the seat (viṣṭara) in the center, one should contemplate the divine lion-throne.
Having specially established Vāgīśvarī in the center of that,
the wise man should duly invoke the Goddess, the Mother of the Universe, upon the lion-throne.
Having meditated upon a dark-complexioned woman in her menses, adorned with garlands and ornaments, and endowed with the essence of living beings.
[She has] a serene face and three eyes resembling lotus petals;
Vāgīśvara, however, is red-hued, three-eyed, and four-armed.
There, for a moment, he beheld the God, endowed with the boon of fearlessness, holding a noose and a trident, resembling an *atasī* flower in color.
In the same way, one should worship the god Vāgīśvara after having placed him within the heart.
As stated in the Kālottara:
"She is Gaurī as Vāgīśī, and Maheśvara is Vāgīśa."
Having understood this, one should worship the Mother of the Universe with diligent effort.
In the *Kāmika*:

"The fire, brought from its constant locus and placed upon a pure vessel, having discarded the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters, is purified by the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and the rest. (p. 151, verse 83a)
Having unified the three fires— the gross, the lunar, and the elemental—
the preceptor should install the consciousness of fire by means of the seed-syllable of fire.
The fire, consecrated with the *saṃhitā-mantras*, rendered nectarine by the *dhenumudrā*,
protected by the *heti-mantra*, and enveloped by the *kavaca-mantra*.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Having worshipped [it] and circumambulated it three times above the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) in a clockwise direction,
one should meditate on it as the seed-syllable of Śiva within the womb-globe of Vāgīśī."
The practitioner, with his knees on the ground and his soul centered in the heart, should visualize the mantra being cast forward by the god Vāgīśvara and project it directly ahead.
Then, one should perform the gathering at the navel region of the seed-syllable situated within,
as well as the bathing, clothing, purification, and sipping of water (ācamana) with the heart-mantra.
Having performed the worship of the fire of the womb, one should bind a darbha-grass bracelet upon the sprout-like hand of the Goddess for its protection, using the *śara* mantra.
Having worshipped the fire with the Sadyojāta mantra for the sake of conception,
one should offer three oblations of sesame seeds with the Hṛdaya mantra.
For the sake of obtaining a male child, one should worship with the left [hand] in the third month;
one should offer three oblations accompanied by drops of water from the head.
(83B) During the *sīmantonnayana* rite in the sixth month, having worshipped with a golden image,
one should offer three oblations into the flame, or indeed into the crest-lock itself.
One should perform the fashioning of garments and limbs, the rite for opening the mouth, and the birth-rite; and in the tenth month, his armor [should be provided] as before.
Having kindled the fire with darbha grass and other materials, one should perform a bath that removes the impurities of the womb;
then, having meditated upon the binding of the Goddess with gold, one should worship Her with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra).
Having spread kusha grass with its tips pointing northeast outside the girdle using the Astra-mantra,
he should place the enclosing sticks and the sacrificial seat upon them while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Kuśa grass, kāśa grass, uśīra, dūrvā grass, bamboo, barley,
viśvāmitra, and mauñjī— these are proclaimed as the eight types of darbha grass.

The *kuśa* grass that is native to the region, glossy, not having too many joints nor being overly long, with the color of a parrot, having the same appearance at the tip as at the root, and possessing seven leaves rather than growing from seven separate blades— [is recommended].

Those born in the seven [forbidden] regions should not be accepted as officiants for the three libations, nor for the spreading of grass, the seat, or the funeral cake, even when situated on the road, in an improper place, or in a cremation ground.
If the tip is thick, it is a woman; if the base is thick, it is a neuter;
and if the base and tip are equal, it is proclaimed as a *puṃdarbhā*.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The clay from the Śrī-liṅga is dark-green and highly auspicious for sacrificial rites;
that from the Pulliṅga is pale-yellow, slightly dark-green, and not neuter."
They should be employed in fierce rites, for they are censured in gentle rites.
(84a) Brahmā resides at the root of the *kuśa* grass, while Keśava resides in its middle.

Śaṅkara resides at the tip of the *kuśa* grass, and the *kuśas* are the presiding deities. With *darbha* grasses used for the reception of guests according to the principles, one should prepare a tuft (*kūrca*) eighteen finger-breadths long,
with a knot at its tip measuring two finger-breadths, which is the most excellent.
A broom with its bristles pointing downward is for the Madhyamaka;
one with bristles pointing upward is for nourishment (pauṣṭika); one with bristles pointing downward is for pacification (śāntika);
and a broom with bristles pointing inward should be made specifically for malevolent rites (abhicāra).
At the base of the *kūrca* is Savitṛ; at its center is Vaiṣṇavī;
and at its tip are all the sacred fords (*tīrthas*). These are the presiding deities (*adhidevatās*).

having formed the hands into a bud-like shape, one should place them at the region of the head.
The characteristic of the three-fold prostration consists in the number of its parts;
however, a single-limbed prostration is performed by bowing only with the head.
Then, having performed prostrations before Śiva with devotion according to the numbers three, five, three, seven, nine, and twelve, the man—
One obtains the supreme fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice even by those men devoid of devotion who, out of gluttony, have merely cast [food] into Śiva’s mouth.
Even a single act of salutation may become the remover of all sins;
therefore, that man who with devotion bows to the Liṅga even once [attains great merit].
One attains all desires and rejoices together with Śiva.
O best of suns, listen as I describe the sequence of circumambulation at Aṃśumatī.
(96a) It removes all sins and bestows the fruit of all gifts;
for the sake of destroying all diseases, one should then perform circumambulation.
The letter *pa* (pra) destroys all fear; the letter *da* grants the attainment of liberation.
From the letter *kṣi*, disease is destroyed; the letter *ṇa* bestows prosperity.
It is traditionally taught that it is called "pradakṣiṇa" because of its connection with the clockwise flow of the waters;
one should proceed from footstep to footstep, avoiding the movement of the hands.
Praise with the voice, meditation in the heart, and the fourfold circumambulation—
like a woman about to give birth carrying a jar filled with oil.
One should perform the circumambulation in such a way that [the river] flows slowly;
in the forenoon it destroys disease, and at midday it grants desired objects.
In the evening it destroys all sins; during the half-watch of night it grants liberation;
and on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight, as well as at the three junctions [of time], it bestows the same.
On the day of the Sun in the constellation Ārdrā, during the Karaṇa known as Viṣṭi,
at the solstices and equinoxes, and during the eclipses of the Moon and the Sun.
Having performed an ablution and circumambulation during a transit [of the sun] or a festival,
he who bows to Śiva with devotion shall attain all his desires.
One shall obtain a hundredfold merit; there is no doubt about this.
Thus, during these aforementioned times, one who is endowed with devotion and faith [attains this].
(96B) Beginning from sunrise until the setting of the sun,
by performing circumambulations during that time, one shall obtain all desires.
Furthermore, whatever man performs a circumambulation during these times, even for a single day and night, he enjoys infinite fruit.
Having traveled a long distance, even one who is devoid of hope for any reward,
should perform a circumambulation with devotion and bow down to the imperishable Śiva.
O Keśava, the path that arises there and the gait itself bestow upon men the fruit of circumambulation; of this there is no doubt.
A traveler who performs the circumambulation of a Śiva-liṅga and offers salutation shall obtain five times the fruit mentioned previously.
A person who performs a circumambulation during a festival or at the time of an offering obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every step.
The middle necklace is threefold; the boundary necklace is fourfold;
and the great boundary necklace, when made, is fivefold.
For men, that which is performed regarding a field or a grove externally becomes a hundredfold [in merit].
In the *Svāyambhuva*, it is stated:
"The twenty-first circumambulation is indeed the most excellent."
The middle [measure] should be the number of lunar days (fifteen), and the inferior [measure] by the number of sages (seven).
That which is performed by means of the number five is the lowest of the low;
that which is performed by means of the number of qualities is said to be the lowest of the low.

Therefore, it is declared in the *Svāyambhuva* that even a single circumambulation performed is most excellent: "A single prostration with one staff and even a single circumambulation [are meritorious]. (97a) p. 180)
A single prostration with one hand destroys previously accumulated merit.
For the sake of attaining one's desired success, one should perform circumambulations a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million, or even ten million times.
The fruit of circumambulating the human linga has been declared;
by means of a prostration, that fruit indeed becomes twofold, and it becomes half as much again [in the case of the ardhaliga].
The fruit at a divine linga is threefold;
that at a Ganeśvara linga is declared to be fourfold, and it becomes fivefold.
Likewise, through the gradual touching of the self-manifested *liṅga*,
according to the *Smṛtisaṅgraha*:
"One [touch] one should perform for Vināyaka, two for Sūrya, and three for Śaṅkara."
One should perform the circumambulation four times for the Goddess and seven times for Viṣṇu at the sacred fig tree (aśvattha).
In the *Brahmanārādīya*:
"By a single circumambulation, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
by a second, one attains eligibility [for higher offices]; and by a third, the prosperity of Indra."
Listen, O observer of noble vows, to the characteristics of the modes of circumambulation:
the clockwise (savya), the counter-clockwise (apasavya), and likewise the combined clockwise-and-counter-clockwise (savyāpasavyaka).
Moving to the left is called *apradakṣiṇa*, while moving to the right is *pradakṣiṇa*.
Moving both to the left and to the right is *savyāpasavya*; that which is performed by crossing the thread of Soma is so designated.
The width of the temple, its measurement,
and the *somasūtra* should be equal to half the size of the temple or equal to the full size of the temple.
One should join [the cord] at the side of the base of the *liṅga* in the northern direction;
it should extend thus as far as the end of the thread, avoiding the circumambulation.
One should perform the circumambulation of Śambhu without crossing the *somasūtra*;
however, in the case of a temple (*vimāna*), the circumambulation should be performed beneath its shadow.
When it becomes necessary to step over the shadow, how should one perform the circumambulation?
A wise person should leave a third part at the end and move through the [remaining] two parts at the beginning.
However, regarding the shadow of the *liṅga*, the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the temple (*prāsāda*), and likewise the image (*pratimā*);
during festivals, at the time of offerings (*bali*), as well as when attended by the Guru,
and at the time of performing circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*), no fault in the shadow exists.
Where there are two Soma threads, or in a temple of Viṣṇu, one should not perform the *apasavya* (leftward) rite; rather, O Lord, one should perform circumambulation clockwise.
Vṛṣa, Caṇḍa, and Vṛṣa; then Soma and Sūtra, and again Vṛṣa;
Caṇḍa and Soma and Sūtra; and again Caṇḍa and again Vṛṣa.
Thus, circumambulation here is said to be performed both to the left and to the right;
performing the circumambulation limb by limb, one should place one's own body upon the ground.
With his two arms joined together like a staff and having performed a single prostration with the body straight as a staff before Śiva, the man— (p. 182) —[should pray].
One should likewise perform circumambulations— one, three,
five, or even seven— for the cessation of all sins.
Having risen and performed prostrations again and again, one should conclude;
there should be a thousand circumambulations, with each circumambulation being performed individually.
In the *Svāyambhuva*:
"The left-hand path (savya) should be known as bestowing enjoyment (bhoga), while the right-hand path (apasavya) bestows liberation (mukti);
by the path of both left and right, it grants the fruits of peace (śānti) and enjoyment."
Wherever there is an enclosure, however, if the sacrificial altar or the bull is situated within it,
one should perform the circumambulation primarily around that [altar or bull].
Where there is circumambulation, whether around the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) or the Lord,
the wise practitioner should not pass between them within that particular enclosure.
Having bowed to and worshipped the two gatekeepers of the second enclosure, who are leaders of the Gaṇas, the devotee of Śiva, having offered praise in this manner, should enter within.
Having bowed again and again, he offered ten billion prostrations, encompassing one hundred, one thousand, and two hundred [prostrations] for each of the left and right sides of the human world.
There are seventy million [mantras] of Śiva;

one hundred thousand for the ancillaries (aṅga); one thousand in the Mahatī [courtyard]; and one hundred in the outer enclosure (prāṅkaṇa) according to the sequence of the enclosures (granthi-kakṣyā).
O faultless one, this sequence of circumambulation destroys sin at every step and bestows liberation.
Having performed five circumambulations of Śambhu,
Mekha performed ten million circumambulations on the earth consisting of the seven islands of the Siddhas.
May there be auspiciousness.
Salutations to the venerable gurus.
Now follows the procedure for eating.
Having performed the midday rites according to the rules, one should bring pure cooked food into a secluded, beautiful dining hall smeared with cow dung.
Then, having recited the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra seven times ending with *vauṣaṭ*, one should sprinkle him with drops of water contained within a bundle of *darbha* grass.
Having set aside the finest portion of all the cooked food, one should offer half to Śiva;
the other half, as the *chullikā*, one should prepare for the performance of the fire-oblation (*homa*).
The fire sacrifice and the portion for the Guru—this is the constant rule:
every day, the best of all cooked food should be offered to Śiva, the fire, the Guru, and the Brahmins.
The man who eats what he has offered to himself eats only sin;
as many times as there are offerings made to Śiva, the fire, and the guru that have been prepared.
For that many thousands of years, the donor shall dwell in the city of Śiva.
In the *Śivadharmottara* (99a):
"One should cook for the sake of the gods, the sacred fire, guests, and mendicants, and never for one's own sake.
He who cooks for his own sake out of delusion lives for the sake of hell."
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
Having washed his feet and sipped water for purification, he should first take his place together with devotees of Śiva who are of virtuous conduct, pure Śaivas whose wealth is their austerity.
The sage should eat with this person, seated in a single row together with those of his own caste, who are not intermingled with others and are not of low birth.
In vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or iron, well-prepared, the teacher, the practitioner, the son, and the initiate [sit] in due order.
Having first performed the circumambulation with a line of ashes around [the area], facing the four directions and observing silence, one should eat; otherwise, the mind is not [at peace].
Then, the ash should be placed in a pure bell-metal vessel or in a stainless vessel that has been purified seven times and consecrated with the Bahurūpa mantra.
With leaves of the palāśa, padminī, mango, and madhūka; with leaves of the rambhā, lotus, āmra, madhūka, and jackfruit.
With *kumbhī*, *campaka*, *puṇnāga*, *kuṭaja*, and *atimuktaka* in full bloom,
and with *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *arka*, *vātāri*, and *sajjapalla*, it becomes auspicious.
When [the recipient] has been excluded by these and other such reasons, one should not feed them.
[One should, however, feed them] upon a plantain leaf that has a handle and a tip, which has been purified from left to right.
One should eat from a vessel filled with clarified butter together with those of equal caste,
keeping the knees between the shoulders, observing silence, or remaining in the bound vīrāsana posture.
With his left hand placed on the vessel, having consecrated the rice as before,
he should kindle the fire with the "Weapon-Leaf" mantra.

One should eat pure food soaked in ghee mixed with broth; the consumption of food should be performed with the *praṇava* and other mantras, such as *prāṇāya*, beginning with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
Having offered five oblations ending with "svāhā," one whose abdominal fire is kindled [should meditate on] the five winds:
Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.
Svāhā to the secondary vital breaths!
In this manner, having offered the food-oblation (naivedya) to the Nāgas and others, one should drink water with the *puruṣa* mantra.
Having performed the offering of breath (*prāṇāhuti*) for the vital winds— prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna—
one should fill each portion with water using measured mouthfuls.
One should fill one-third of the stomach with the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa),
and likewise with the fruit of the Agastya, the Acyuta, and the Tvaṣṭṛ-āmālaka.
For one in whom these noble qualities prevail, Śiva is ever-present;
likewise, the Ālāmpu, the circular-shaped, the Prāntāka, and the Śvetaka [are present].
One should avoid the *upotakī* plant, which is vine-like, as well as the *raktiśiśra*. (100a) — [The following are also forbidden: the *śoka*, the *mahāśāka*, the *droṇaśāka*, and the *upotakī*.
Wild plantain tubers and ginger are recommended;
likewise, kadaka, madhuśigru, phalaṇḍa, garlic, and meat.
One should avoid food served from the hand and salt that has been touched by the hand;
[one obtains] the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice through fierce asceticism on a mountain peak.
One attains the fruit effortlessly by abstaining from honey and meat;
one should avoid liquor from afar, for it is the abode of all defects.
Where is liquor, and where is devotion to Śiva? Where is meat, and where is the worship of Śiva? For those established in wine and flesh, Śaṅkara remains far away.
Therefore, having abandoned what is forbidden, one should worship the devotees of Śiva.

Feeding one person at an ordinary meal yields a certain result; feeding ten learned Brahmins who know the specific [teachings] yields a hundredfold; and feeding a devotee of Maheśvara at the proper time yields a thousandfold that fruit.
Ten thousand for a son, a hundred thousand for a fellow practitioner, and ten million for the worship of the Guru—thus it is declared in the Śiva-āgamas; the donor enjoys the fruit thereof.
One should not drink water from another person, nor from one who has not washed their hands;
having discarded food that is defiled by flies, fingernails, hair, and the like, one should eat only a small amount.
Having touched ashes, one should eat pure food with a single-minded focus,
as well as curd, milk, ghee, oil, honey, and molasses.
Coconut fruit and plantain juice serve as side dishes;
however, that which is defiled by hair and the like, or that which has been licked by a cow, must not be consumed.
Having removed only that much, it becomes pure by the addition of ashes;
this applies likewise to black pepper, betel nut, grain, molasses, and turmeric.
In the case of curd, milk, and ghee, no defect of cooking exists;
however, a person should drink water with hands that have not been washed.
But here, for the sake of purification, one should wash the hands and feet on all sides with perfumes;
having performed the purification according to the rule by means of sixteen mouthfuls of water (gaṇḍūṣas).
One should sprinkle the water falling from the thumb onto the big toe of the foot;
thereafter, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, this is for the removal of defects in the food.
One should bind the mudrā called Paridhi from the navel to the tip of the nose;
thereafter, the recipient should apply and chew scents and betel-leaf.
As it has been said: "O King,
that man who chews betel-leaf at dawn, at the time of a meal, during sexual union with beautiful young women,
or in the midst of learned men— he is a beast."
Betel leaf is pungent, sweet, alkaline, and endowed with astringency;
it subdues wind, destroys worms, removes phlegm, and kindles the digestive fire like the fire of time.
It is an ornament for conversation with women, promotes relish in food, and cuts through grief.
These thirteen qualities described regarding betel-leaf are difficult to find even in heaven.
Betel nut that is unbroken, its leaf unwashed,
and its lime unpurified, destroys longevity, wife, and sons.
The man who eats betel nut without first placing a leaf in his mouth shall be poor for seven births; to pacify that [karmic effect], he should remember Śiva.
One should discard the tip of the leaf, the back of the leaf, the side, and the veins;
likewise, having discarded the tip and the back of the betel nut, one should take another that is well-cut.
One should consume betel leaf, and one will certainly obtain good health.
Thus ends the section on the rules for eating in the *Sakalāgamasārasaṅgraha*.
Hari Om.
May there be auspiciousness.
May the virtuous forgive the errors committed by the author.
Salutations to the illustrious Gurus! Salutations to the Lord of Ratnācala! This is the manuscript of Kāśicitta (or Kāśicitra), a scholar in the diversion of renouncing wealth.
Salutation to Ardhanārīśvara. Written by the hand of Sadāśivagurukkal himself.
The Great Resolve.

(102a) Oṃ! Of the glorious Lord of all, beginning with Dhyādi, who is immeasurable, who is being cherished by the seven, whose great tongue is blazing, in the midst of which is the supreme intellect, the singular bond of the cosmic eggs,
in this nectar of the sun, within the earth, water, fire, wind, and ether.

In the midst of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), resting upon the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), the Tortoise (kūrma), and the elephants of the eight directions, stands this world, encircled by the waters of the Lokaloka mountain and encompassed by the seven continents and seven oceans—
namely, the oceans of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water.

In the land of Bharata, within the subcontinent of Bhārata-varṣa—which is divided into nine sections by the refuge of the Nāgas, Saumyas, and Gandharvas; which is illuminated by the great Indra-lamp of Krauñca-uṣkara; and which possesses the essence of the Jambū-flower that outshines the Jambha—there lies Merudhā.

(192) At the junction of the Saumya and Anta regions, on the Jambū-madhyarekhā [central meridian], on the bank of the Tejottuṅga-Bhadrā river, at the Brahma-madhya-hasta [central cubit] point, there is much strife and great conflict; it is a place where thieves and robbers congregate, and it brings about the formation of the five great assemblies.

The loss of caste (*apātrīkaraṇa*) consists of: for a Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra, [the following acts]: wearing the clothes of a slave-girl or a prostitute; sexual intercourse with a bull or a female elephant; looking at the wives of others; eating the leavings of a cat;
approaching those who should not be approached; eating what should not be eaten; and consuming that which is forbidden to drink.

For the purpose of expiation regarding the descent into superior, inferior, or low-born [wombs], one should avoid the food of a Śūdra, food from a birth-impurity (sūtaka), food from a funeral meal (parihānna), food from delusion (samoha), the food of a king, the food of a thief, the food of a courtesan, the food of a *kuṇḍa* [bastard], and the food of a leper; and for the purpose of avoiding the faults of being without a protector, as well as the defects of the nine planets beginning with the Sun.

For the purpose of expiation— namely, for the sake of atonement for minor offenses (*anupātaka*), secondary sins (*yūpapātaka*), and major sins (*yuddhapātaka*); for deceiving Śūdras, selling a maiden, engaging in excessive cruelty toward the world, excessive cruelty toward children,
stealing the oil of a deity, reviling one's guru, committing a grave sin against one's guru, reviling a Brāhmaṇa, and [the sin of] Brahman-murder.

For the purpose of removing the defects of evil, such as going to a pond for removing sins, going to a sugarcane field or a tank, the coldness of trees, cutting [wood], from a thorny place, seeing a deity, the fault of residing in a village, bad vessels, the lap of a wicked woman, and ill-omened signs; may it be accomplished.
I shall perform bathing, giving, recitation, fire-oblation, and worship of the deity.
By means of this oblation, may all that has been, all that is to be, and every possession—everything here—is born for the sake of the seven elements. Om, salutation to Śiva;
Om, salutation to Śiva. May there be a great resolve.
Hariḥ oṃ.

It may have the form of a lotus, the shape of a chariot, or even the appearance of a rudrākṣa;
it may be clarified butter, honey, or fragrance, or it may have the form of a mountain from the netherworld.
At the rising of Taurus, in the fifteenth degree,
the nose is one-quarter less than four units; likewise,
from the neck downwards, the chin measures six units.
The throat of a bull, the tail of a goat, and ten drops of blood.
O Śaṅkara, having established the ten-fold womb-scheme with ten positions, one should establish Brahmā in the ninth;
the eighth is called Viṣṇu.
One should establish the seventh [deity], Ṣaṇmukha, and the sixth, Sarasvatī;
in the fourth part, Vināyaka.
Having established Bhairava as one-third [of the total], the location for the image (bera) is prescribed;
it is provided with a platform level with the base of the image,
along with a pedestal, a gopura, and a spacious, ancient city-like enclosure.
[One should avoid] those that are cramped in location, dilapidated, indistinct, beautiful, elevated, swift, or indistinct. (p. 195)
(103B) [The diagram] is surrounded internally by a hundred lotuses and externally by two paths, two yokes,
and eight lotuses for the quarters and intermediate directions;
it has six spokes, eight Śambhus, and is further encircled by a red path.
If it consists of thirty-three strings, it is the Śṛṅgāratilaka.
Thus ends the *Śṛṅgāratilaka*.
(Now) the Sarvatobhadra.
With twelve lines of elements and sixteen squares, there is a four-lotus design in the center;
in the corners, there is the play and dissolution of five-by-five [squares], with the crow's foot at the end of those squares;
in the center, there is a six-square pedestal lotus, and in the neck, two squares for the two Vedas.
In the fourfold lotus, bee, pedestal, and liṅga [arrangement], there is a lotus on both sides.
When divided into thirty-two parts, there is a lotus in the center; with sixty-four parts, there is a circle outside that; with three parts, there is a path; with one part, there is a path;
and with two parts, there are two doors for the sages on both sides, known as Gaurī and Līlā.
Outside of that, with three lines, there is a pedestal (pīṭha) consisting of variegated [ornaments] and the beloved of Umā (Śiva).
(B? thus it appears; however, [the reading] "vāgīśādyāḥ" appears as the side of the originator.
— [The region of Śambhu is entirely devoid of parts.]
Or else, it is the unstruck (anāhata) light-linga, beginning with the dissolution of Brahman.
Or else, it consists of a subtle drop on the forehead as the supreme syllable;
or it resides in the lotus of the heart in the form of a flame, higher than the highest.
Or, having meditated upon Sadāśiva in his gross form, the size of a thumb-joint,
and having remained thus until dawn, one should praise him with hymns and prostrate before him.
Having reflected upon auspicious deeds, one should remain composed in mind during the Kanyasa period.
Having risen and gone outside, holding a staff and a water-pot, [one should take] earth,
wood, cow-dung, flowers, sesame, and auspicious myrobalan fruit, as stated in the *Kālottara*:
"Earth, wood, cow-dung, flowers, sesame, and the auspicious myrobalan..."
Having taken kuśa grass, one should go to a river that flows to the ocean.
In the *Śivadharmottara*: "Having gone one hundred cubits from a village, [that distance] is fourfold from a city. In the *Sahasrantantra*:
It may be performed in any desired direction, excluding the northeast;
as stated in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Then, having covered his head and having spread grass beneath him, he should perform the cleansing."
Otherwise—
O deities, all sages, hosts, and likewise the nāgas,
arise from every side; I am preparing the ground outside.
I bow to that elephant-faced one, whom Vāgīśa and the other wise ones salute at the commencement of all undertakings, and by saluting whom they become fulfilled.
Salutations to Śiva and to Śakti, to the Bindu and to the Eternal One;
and to the Guru, to Gaṇeśa, and to the wise Kārttikeya.
Having always bowed to the feet of the illustrious Bhānu, who dwells in Kāñcīpura and is the sun for the lotus-hearts of his disciples, [this work on] the illumination of knowledge [is composed].
In the *Somaśambhu*:
"Having risen after sleeping at night and having meditated upon Śaṅkara in the morning,
one should perform every part of the ritual section (*kriyākāṇḍa*) daily, exactly as prescribed."

Now, for the benefit of practitioners belonging to the four stages of life, I shall fully explain the characteristics of purification and ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
In the *Suprabheda*:
"At the *brāhma-muhūrta*, the wise man, having meditated upon Śaṅkara in his mind,
[should perform this] at the end of the night, for three quarters of a *ghaṭikā* day after day."
The *muhūrta* is declared to be *brāhma*, and it is indeed said that he (Brahmā) awakens during it; according to the *Smṛti*:
"Four *ghaṭikās* of that duration are called *aruṇodaya* (the dawn)."
For ascetics, this is the time for bathing; the water is like the waters of the Ganges.
Otherwise— having divided the night into six parts and arisen during the final portion,
he gazes with his divine eye at whatever is divine as it occurs.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "One should meditate upon the supreme Guru, who is the supreme ether and tranquil;
remembering him as having the form of a beautiful lion, white, saffron-colored, and red."
In the corners, starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast,
one should worship Vimala, Sāra, Ārādhya, and Paramasukha in their proper sequence.
In its center is a red lotus, adorned with eight petals in the cardinal directions;
one should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Dīptā, upon the filaments.
From the east to the northeast, within the northeast, the nine Śaktis— shaped like the flame of a blazing lamp and facing in all directions— are to be meditated upon.
Holding lotuses and chowries in their hands, they are all red in color and adorned with ornaments on every limb; facing the sun, they are all decorated with every kind of jewelry.
Having meditated thus and performed worship, one should manifest Visphurā,
who resembles saffron in color and is adorned with all ornaments.
Having two eyes and a beautiful face, adorned with red garlands and unguents,
he is endowed with four arms, two of which are lotus-hands in the gesture of granting boons.
Endowed with the boon-granting gesture of fearlessness, adorned with a halo of light, and accompanied by [the aforementioned attributes].
Goddess Uṣā is on the right side, while Pratyuṣā is on the left;
she has two arms and—
