[He saw] the goddess with a lotus in her hand, of noble form, endowed with a reddish hue,
[and] the god who possesses the body of the sun.

If one desires liberation: [one should meditate on the deity] seated in the center of a circular mandala, possessing the luster of a white lotus and a pomegranate flower, and radiating the great brilliance of shimmering jewels.
One should meditate upon the Sun-god as having one face, two eyes, and red garments; his two hands hold a lotus with a stalk that is red, blossomed, and white.
Having performed the invocation and other rites with the appropriate mudrās,
one should worship the image for the sake of [the deity's] pleasure and display the bimba-mudrā.

Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa and established oneness, one should perform the oblation with the *avaṣolkin* mantra; then one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), water for the head (*śiro-arghya*), and worship the limbs.
Having worshipped the Sun with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the root mantra,
one should devotedly display to him the mudrās known as the lotus and the discus.
One should worship the Heart in the southeast, the Head in the northeast, the Crest-lock in the southwest, the Armor in the northwest, the Eye in the east, and the Weapon in the cardinal directions.
They are gentle, red in color, granting boons with lotuses in their hands, adorned, and possessing two arms.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Since these three are equal—the Guru, Śiva, and the Vidyā—just as Śiva is, so is the Vidyā; and just as the Vidyā is, so is the Guru."
The fruit of the worship of Śiva’s vidyā and of the gurus is equal;
then, having brought [the deity] near, one should worship the guru as before.
Having performed three circumambulations to the right, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground;
as he departs, one should follow behind him, and as he enters, one should enter after him.
One should not question his words, nor should one wake him from sleep;
eternal knowledge is obtained by prostrating at the feet of the guru.
If the Guru is present in the temple where the six-faced Lord resides,
one should first pay homage to the Guru and only afterwards worship the God.
There is atonement for the omission of Śiva, but there is no atonement for the omission of the Guru.
As stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"If the Guru’s son should consider another [disciple] unfit for the principles (tattvas), [he may act accordingly]."
His initiation is indeed fruitless, and he goes instead to the Great Kalpa.
In the *Cintyaviśva* (p.
202): Having obtained a teacher devoid of knowledge, how can liberation be attained?
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in one who has reached the further shore of knowledge.
Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to flower within the forest,
so too a disciple, craving knowledge, may go from one teacher to another teacher.
Having received [the teaching], even a disciple who releases it [without practice] certainly falls downward.
According to the *Ṣaṭsahasra*,
the Guru is to be worshipped like Śiva, and the Preceptor (Deśika) again like a father.
In the same way, practitioners always regard the spiritual son as they do their own mother.
Those who wish for auspiciousness should regard as friends those who abide by their commitments;
however, those who revile the guru among the initiates, spiritual sons, and others [must be avoided].

Therefore, one who, out of delusion, being most wicked, should utter a curse or a threat against his guru, must depart from that place immediately and go far away while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times.
Otherwise, another evil-minded person [who fails to do so] shall go to hell; both of them [the teacher and the disciple] would go to hell.
Having prostrated, one should diligently worship the guru with flowers at his feet.
Having obtained the fruit of a thousand cows by prostrating at the feet of the Guru,
one should pay homage to the Guru’s brothers and the Gaṇas for the sake of one's own excellence.
Furthermore, one should never cause another person who is pure and endowed with ascetic wealth to follow after him;
nor should the elder ever allow the younger to precede him in initiation or consecration.
One who excels in austerity and knowledge need not perform a salutation [to another]. (p.
203) Aṃśumatī said:
"The teacher is the father, the teacher is the mother, the teacher is the deity, and the teacher is the friend."
"There is nothing higher than the guru," thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śiva.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should then worship the Puṣpaka.
Paṅkajārka. (This leaf ends here. [p.
204] [blank page] [p. 205] (381ā) One should wear a twelve-faced rudrākṣa around the neck.
The twelve Ādityas, stationed in each and every mouth, blaze forth.
Whatever fruit belongs to the Gomedha sacrifice, the Aśvamedha sacrifice, and the Bahusvarṇa sacrifice—that fruit a mortal obtains; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Moreover, O child, he who wears a thirteen-faced Rudrākṣa shall have no fear of fire, nor shall disease afflict him.

It should be known as the granter of desires, the bestower of accomplishments, and the giver of all attainments; through it, the elixir, the rejuvenative, and the magical sandals are indeed perfected.
Having slain even his mother, father, or brother,
one is released from all sins, O Guha, by means of the thirteen-faced [mantra].
O child, if a fourteen-faced Rudrākṣa is obtained,
one should always wear it upon the head as the Śakti-bindu of Śiva.
One who wears Rudrākṣas is constantly worshipped by the gods and attains supreme merit: ten on the neck, twenty-two on the head,
six on each side of the throat, and twelve on each of the two hands.
He who wears one sacred thread on each arm at the digit of the moon, one on the topknot,
and one hundred and eight on the chest, is Rudra himself.
(B) A man who constantly wears a garland of one hundred and eight [beads] certainly obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every step.
By wearing it on the crest-lock, one gains ten million merits; on the ears, one hundred million;
on the neck, one thousand million; and by wearing it on the arms, the merit is incalculable.
If one dies after consuming a rudrākṣa at the time of departure [from this life], he attains the state of Rudra; there is no rebirth for him.
In the Kālottara:
"Even a dog that dies with a rudrākṣa placed around its neck attains the state of Rudra; how much more so, then, humans and others?"
One should never wear a rudrākṣa during a period of birth-impurity or death-impurity.
In the *Brahmakaivarta*:

"Some say that women are pure during childbirth, when discharging water or excrement, or when in fear; they are also pure while wearing a garland of a hundred thousand [flowers] for the sake of their own supervision."
Others said that it should always be worn on the arm or on the ears as a remover of evil; however, a great and precious garland should be worn on the neck with the protective mantra.
The Rudrākṣa is the root-Brahman; its stalk is said to be Viṣṇu;
its mouth is called Rudra; and the drop (*bindu*) therein is all the deities.
Having adorned them with worship and offerings, it bestows the fruit of a horse sacrifice;
ten thousand sacred threads and a hundred thousand bracelets for the hands.
A Rudrākṣa that is concealed is said to yield the fruit of *sārūpya*.
(This concludes this leaf. By means of this, one should not allow any remnant of impurity to remain.
For one who is devoid of purity and proper conduct, everything becomes fruitless.
Through right conduct one obtains knowledge; through right conduct one obtains wealth;
through right conduct one attains everything; and through right conduct one may attain liberation.

One should not collect roots from the bank of a river, in a temple, on an anthill, or at the site of a medicinal herb; nor should one take them if they are situated on a path, impure, or on the left side.
One should maintain ponds, wells, and tanks; from their water, one may take the mud, but one should not take earth from elsewhere.
Having brought [the water] and having purchased [the materials], one should divide them for bathing and purification;
thereafter, one should cleanse with water, taking sixteen mouthfuls (gaṇḍūṣa) in succession.
Purity has been specifically described; one should drink the incomparable water for sipping (ācamana). Having drunk either less or more than that, it becomes equal to the drinking of liquor.
Having sipped water according to the rule, one should perform the purification of the teeth with a twig that is of appropriate length, straight, clean, and without a knot.
The tooth-stick is praised when it is as wide as the little finger;
the *piribilva*, *karaṇḍa*, *śiṃśapā*, *khadira*, and *arjuna* trees are recommended for this purpose.

For those seeking liberation, it is said here that [the distance] should be eight finger-breadths; for those seeking worldly enjoyment, it should be made from the wood of the Jambu, Ambu, Kakubha, Aśoka, Kapittha, or Vakula trees.

For embodied beings, [the ash] produced from the Plakṣa, Udumbara, and Phullāṅghri; from the Jātī, Campaka, and Śaṅkha flowers; from the Atimuktaka and Kadamba; and from the Apāmārga [is recommended].
In the *Suprabheda*:
"One should indeed perform the cleansing of the teeth with *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, or *nimba* trees;
for the purpose [of purification], a twig from a thorny or milky tree should be twelve finger-breadths in length."
In the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī*:
"Alternatively, among the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of the lowest castes,
[the length] is prescribed as twelve finger-breadths, decreasing by one finger-breadth respectively."
The tooth-stick for women should be four finger-breadths in length;
[this applies] regarding the tooth-stick, being outside the village, and during purification, bathing, and recitation.
One should observe silence during the time of eating secret food, as well as during the eight [other occasions].
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī* (p. 209):
"For practitioners whose nature is that of Śiva, like the crest [of the flame], it is one finger-breadth of Hara;
for each of the four who possess the nature of the worlds, it is certainly one finger-breadth."
If the ascetic facing north is silent and has hands, and if he faces east,
the head should be worn with Īśāna and the throat with Tatpuruṣa;
it should be worn on the neck with Aghora and worn on the heart with Aghora.
O Sage, the sin committed over seven lifetimes will quickly perish;
for seven thousand lifetimes, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
[One should avoid wood] infested with worms, split or broken, or that which has come from a thorny tree;
likewise, [one should avoid] that which has been hollowed out by itself, or that which is coarse and has been held [in the hand].
One should likewise avoid a door whose opening is constructed in reverse;
furthermore, the chest from the throat down to the navel should be well-marked by beautiful garlands.
Austerity performed above the navel does not lead to long life, while that below the navel causes its destruction; therefore, one should make the rudrākṣa sacred thread level with the navel.
The necklace for the head is made from the navel; the necklace for the arms is equal to the arms;
the necklace for the hands is measured by the hands; and the necklace for the neck is equal to that.
In the Kālottara:
"A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and likewise a Śūdra—
these four castes should wear the Rudrākṣa, which bestows all perfections."
One should wear a rudrākṣa, conjoined with the purificatory rite of initiation for women;
whether pure or impure, one should always wear a rudrākṣa.
One should always wear [the mark] on the hand, the ear (or the neck), the crest-lock, or on the sacred threads;
together with ashes, one should apply it for the sake of pacifying all sins.
Beholding it pacifies sins, and touching it bestows all accomplishments;
one should always wear the meritorious Rudrākṣa according to the previously mentioned rite.
Whether it be talk of kings, talk of merchants, or especially talk of worldly affairs,
by the mere movement of a rudrākṣa, the fruit of extracting mantras shall be attained.
In the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa: "He who, firm in his vow, wears a thousand Rudrākṣas,
all the gods bow down to him just as they do to Rudra himself."
Briefly stated, each one of these should be known to yield the fruit of giving a cow;
even a Mleccha or a Cāṇḍāla [is freed] from the sins of his father.
One who is endowed with the wearing of rudrākṣas is Rudra himself; there is no doubt in this matter.
[Likewise, one adorned with] pearls, coral, crystal, silver, and lapis lazuli...
He who wears Rudrākṣas together with [other beads] becomes Śiva himself;
so too does that man in this world who wears even Rudrākṣas alone.
Sins do not touch him who, by virtue of his great merit, possesses even a single rudrākṣa on his body, just as darkness cannot touch the sun.
His birth would be as meaningless as being devoid of the *tripuṇḍra* mark;
for he who performs a head-bath while wearing a *rudrākṣa* on his head [commits a fault].
The fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā arises for him; there is no doubt in this matter. (p. 212) (371a) The drops of water that fell there became tears, which grew into great rudrākṣa trees.
Skanda: How many divisions are there, how many faces do they have, and what are their presiding deities? What is their quality like? Tell me according to the truth.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Ṣaṇmukha, I shall tell you all that in its true essence;
those Rudrākṣas are many, categorized by thirty-eight varieties.
Twelve Kapila [fires] are traditionally taught as having arisen from the Sun-eye;
sixteen Śveta [fires] have arisen from the Moon-eye, according to their sequence.
The black Rudrākṣa, born from the fire-eye, indeed has ten varieties;
however, the white-colored Rudrākṣa is said by its very nature to be Brāhma.
The Kṣatriya is red, the Vaiśya is a mixture of colors, and the Śūdra is black;
by meditating on Śiva as having one face, one directly removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The God of gods with two faces certainly destroys the sin of killing a cow;
the three-faced one is fire itself, who in an instant burns away the murder of a woman.
By assuming four faces, Brahmā removes the sin of killing a human being;
by assuming five faces himself, Rudra [removes] even the name of the Fire of Time (Kālāgni).
Through avoiding forbidden sexual intercourse and by not consuming what is unfit for food,
one is freed from sins through the wearing of the five-faced [liṅga].
Kārttikeya, however, should hold a six-faced [image] in his right hand;
by this, there is no doubt that sins such as the killing of a fetus are destroyed.
O Mahāsena, a man who possesses seven faces and is known by the name Ananta is liberated from the sins of stealing gold, killing cows, and other such transgressions.
O Mahāsena, the eight-faced one is the god Vināyaka himself;
likewise, he is the deception in measures, the deception in scales, and the deception in gold.
By the mere touch of the back, belly, or hand of another's wife,
such sins as these are destroyed through the wearing [of this amulet].
By wearing that nine-faced Bhairava on his left arm,
he is said to bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and shall become equal in strength to me.
Thousands of killings of embryos and hundreds of killings of Brahmins—
all that is quickly destroyed by wearing the nine-faced [mantra].
O dear child, the ten-faced one is indeed the Lord Janārdana himself;
so too are the planets, the piśācas, the vetālas, and the brahmarākṣasas.
By wearing it, serpents, Garuḍas, and all others perish;
thus, Rudra himself becomes the eleventh when an eleventh Rudrākṣa is worn on the mouth.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who constantly wears it upon the crest-lock:
it is equal to thousands of horse-sacrifices and tens of thousands of Vājapeya sacrifices.
The fruit that belongs to one who gives a hundred thousand cows, O gentle one,
that same fruit one obtains by wearing the eleven-faced [mantra].
Rudrā:
One should meditate upon the limbs of the Sun as being extremely fierce,
with terrifying fangs, and blazing with the brilliance of fire.
For instance, one should contemplate this weapon-mantra for the destruction of the host of obstacles:
the dhenumudrā for the heart and other limbs, and the two cow-horns for the eyes.
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"The mudrā of the weapon is for terrifying; that of the planets is salutation.
[One should visualize] Soma as having the luster of a white water-lily or a *kunda* flower, and Budha with the radiance of refined gold."
One should meditate on Jupiter as having the luster of yellow orpiment, Venus as resembling cow's milk,
Mars as red, and Saturn as resembling lapis lazuli.
They were black Rāhu with joined palms and Ketu resembling a smoky serpent;
all of them could assume any form at will and were adorned with divine ornaments.
With his left hand placed upon his thigh and his right hand granting fearlessness, he [worships] Soma, who holds a white lotus in his hand; while Rāhu and Ketu perform the añjali gesture.
With half their bodies visible and eyes looking upward,
they see Śani, who is formidable with fangs, and Rāhu, whose face is distorted.
Having worshipped in due order at the tips of the petals of the eastern and other directions— [p. 215] — [the remaining portion].

With devotion, one should offer water from the *arghya* vessel to Bhāskara;
having praised, prostrated, and fully worshipped him, one should present the offering.
Having withdrawn the aggregate of atoms with the *haṃ phaṭ* weapon-mantra, it was dissolved by the *saṃhārī* [power].
One should place Caṇḍa— whose mouth is red and terrifying, and whose two hands display the lotus and the gesture of fearlessness— within the Śiva-sun situated in the center of the heart-lotus.
With this, one should offer the remains of the sun's garland to Caṇḍeśa.
Thus ends the section on the performance of ritual purification and bathing and the worship of the Sun, within the *Sakalāgamasangraha*.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the worship of Śiva,
which removes all sins and brings happiness to all the worlds."
It yields the fruit of all forms of giving and bestows the fruit of all sacrifices;
it destroys the taints of such sins as the killing of a Brahmin and grants the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a seat for the worship of Śiva so meritorious, which bestows victory, confers prosperity, increases the kingdom, and destroys enemies.
In the Śivadharmottara:
"Having realized that there is no merit whatsoever greater than the worship of the Śiva-liṅga,
Sadāśiva should be worshipped with diligent effort."
(Regarding *smṛti*: Is it *smṛti*? *Smṛti* refers generally to the midday bath;
one should indeed perform worship there.
And with the nectar drawn up by inhalation (pūraka), which is the sacrificial oblation of the auspicious syllables (śivāṇu).
Having offered that according to the prescribed rite to the deity worshipped within, [one performs] the offering of the eight flowers and so forth; thereafter, the worship is fully described.
One should meditate upon Maheśvara, whose form is like the spotless autumnal moon,
with a white body, situated in the middle of the forehead.
O Ānandaceṭī, he sports independently and is delighted;
this is the truth, the absolute truth for those men who meditate constantly, O fair-faced one.
It becomes manifest quickly within his heart; of this there is no doubt.
And that which is produced by the mind appears like a reflection in a mirror.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always be established in meditation;
when the mind is firmly established in meditation, then one should abandon the external.
If, through delusion, he performs both [rites] in the wrong manner,
then that external rite must be performed, preceded by the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having thus requested the outer worship and received permission,
the sage should then perform the purification of the site according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
In the *Śivadharmottara*: "Seeing [the dust], one should sweep it away with a soft and fine broom;
by performing the sweeping slowly, the fruit of the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance shall be attained."
The merit of sweeping [the temple] a hundred times and anointing it a thousand times belongs to one who performs all his duties with water filtered through a cloth.
He is a sage, he is most excellent, he who— [filling the gaps]—
shall go to auspiciousness.
One should dispel obstacles with the *astra* mantra and by means of three claps of the hands (*tāla*).
One should perform the binding of the directions (*diśābandha*) with snapping fingers (*choṭikā*) and the construction of a protective wall (*prākāra*) with the *astra* mantra.
Then, having established the Kākavaca both externally and internally,
one should subsequently display the network of powers (śaktijāla) and the objects of perception by means of the Dhenu-mudrā.
The purification of the place has thus been declared; now hear about the [divine] power (*divyaddhi*).
In the *Śivadharmottara*: "One should prepare the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials."
A golden vessel is most excellent, while a silver one would be middling.
In the absence of a copper vessel, it should be made of clay;
that clay vessel should be prepared every day, and it is desired that it be new.
A vessel made of *pālāśa* or lotus leaves is equal to one made of copper.
In the *Tantrasāra*:
"On seven occasions, [one should offer] rice, ashes, earth, and water into a bell-metal vessel."
And one should purify copper in three ways with *dhara*, with *tintriṇī*, and with cow dung.

In one way, it consists of gold and silver; likewise, water [is perceived] in wood, ivory, cloth, and so forth. Thus, for vessels made of gold and other materials, the single water [of the weapon-mantra] is [manifested].
Having gazed at Ajitā (p. 219), one should not enclose her in the heart with the armor-mantra;
she is exceedingly full of spreading nectar, flowers, water, and unbroken rice.
In the heart (see page 220): one should place the mantra of the five Brahmans from the thumb to the little finger;
one should place them in rows like staffs, beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta.
One should collect the nine flowers between the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger;
and with the thumb and forefinger, one should discard the remains of the offering.

At the time of dismissal, one should place a flower upon the head [of the deity]. One should never, at that time, leave the Linga with its top exposed, as stated in the *Kiraṇa*: "One should never make the Linga have a vacant top."
One should place the worship, performed on that very day and not left overnight, in the northeast.
In the *Kāmika*:
"Having thoroughly purified the Śiva-liṅga together with its pedestal using the water of the weapon-mantra (*astra*),
one should thereafter perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the waters of the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*)."
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī* (p. 220):

"But at the conclusion of the daily worship, when the Lord of the Multitude of Mantras has been restrained and has entered there into the Linga and the pedestal in a peaceful form, [the ritual of] carving [should be performed] immediately."
Likewise, fierce obstructors who remain unattached create obstacles;
they destroy both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Therefore, one should subdue them beforehand.
Having bathed them again with the waters of the Heart-mantra, one should bathe the one situated on the pedestal with the Śiva-weapon mantra and that on the seat with the Pāśupata mantra.
Then the *liṅga* becomes pure, and the mantras will once again bestow their fruits.
Having purified the *liṅga* and then the pedestal (*pīṭhaka*) with the *kūrca* mantra many times, [one should proceed].
One should thoroughly wash it with the Astra-mantra, even many times;
then, having performed the purification of the measure, one should fashion the stalk on the left.
It may be made of gold, silver, or copper, or even fashioned from wood;
it should be square, elongated, or shaped like a shield (pheṭaka).

Alternatively, one should likewise place the *vṛtta* (circle) and the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*); then, having entered the inner sanctum, one should perform the opening according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship Bhīmarudra, who holds the embryo, who is accompanied by Rudra, who stands together with them,
who has four arms and three eyes, who is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
and who is attended by the parasol and the chowrie.
For the purpose of worshipping the Lord of Gods, the deity who is the end-maker of night-stalkers.
"O you who are the pure gateway, please be gracious to me as I enter;
having thus entreated Maheśvara, the God stationed in the midst of that [palace],"
Oṃ, salutations, O Lord of the gods of gods, sole leader of all the worlds!
Arise for the purpose of the ritual bath and for the sake of self-protection.
In the *Aṃśumatī*: "Having grasped the *liṅga* with both hands, one should bathe it and place it upon [the pedestal].
In the *Kāmika*:
Having performed worship with the Gāyatrī mantra upon the Liṅga’s head— worship prepared at the previous time— one should then offer the general arghya.
In the subtle [level],
having sprinkled [the deity] with water for the guest-offering (*arghyodaka*), one should perform the ritual placement of the faces (*vaktranyāsa*).
It is prescribed that immediately thereafter, the worship of the deity (*devapūjā*) must be performed.
Thus it is said in the *Yogayājñavalkya*:
"Having wrung out the bathing garment, having sipped water (ācamana), being self-restrained and pure,
one should perform the worship of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, free from envy."
Thus, there are pairs of deities:
Gaṇapati or Skanda; Sūrya or his consort; Sarasvatī or her consort; Śrī or Śrīpati; Gaurī or Gaurīpati. (p. 222)
Or perhaps something else is desired by you; these [options] are presented in their entirety according to your preference.
Manu says:
Devoted to the five great sacrifices, the Brāhmaṇa should worship the five: Āditya, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Gaṇanātha, and Maheśvara.
Thus it is said: some worship Gaṇapati, Āditya, Śakti, Acyuta, and Śiva in sequence; thus [they worship] Hari and Hara.
Regarding the transgression that occurs when this is not done for the proper reason, it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"He who, out of delusion, [does not give] water... [and so forth].
One who consumes a *dīnāraka* coin in this world is born as a worm.
Thus,
for the sake of avoiding transgression,
by all of them together— [the remainder of the sentence follows] — it must be performed.
It is established that one should act according to one's own inclination. Now, [one might ask: why is it that Śiva alone is to be worshipped?
To this we reply:
In this regard, there is equal status in terms of being worthy of worship and the fruit of worship.

Alternatively, if it is argued that there is a distinction, then— given this situation— it is understood from the force of the compound with the word "great" (*mahat*) that [the gods] possess merely the status of being worthy of worship.
According to the rule *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.61), the formation of a compound with the word *mahat*—
as in [the term for] Him who possesses infinite auspicious qualities such as unsurpassed knowledge, bliss, and supreme sovereignty— is appropriate.
Furthermore, the state of being the sustainer and the state of being entirely free from connection with all defects belong to Mahādeva alone;
this is determined by his being denoted by the word "Śiva.
For who else besides Mahādeva, the Lord of Umā, could possess these?
Is there an unconditioned denotability by the word "Īśvara"?
For in common usage, the word "Śiva" signifies, as an unconditioned term, the collective totality of the supreme human goal consisting of the nature and qualities of pure auspiciousness.
This is well known from the Veda;
for instance: "May your rites be auspicious, may your paths be auspicious, and may there be auspiciousness for the entire world."
Now, Śiva alone is recognized as superior to other deities; as it is stated in a certain part of the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Mahādeva is said to be the progenitor of the gods, beginning with Brahmā."
The Supreme Lord is the progenitor of heaven and earth, Indra and Agni, Viṣṇu, Dhātṛ, Yama, Varuṇa, and the Moon. In the Kūrma Purāṇa, these are the words of Īśvara addressed to Brahmā:
Satva was created as my first-born son for the sake of creation;
Puruṣottama was produced from my right limb, and [Rajas] from my left limb.
"From the region of the heart of that god Śambhu, this Atirudra with Ambā emerged; he is his supreme, other body. And in the Śivadharmottara:
Brahmā arose from your right side, Hari was born from your left side,

however, mantras consist of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), yet they are possessed of the impurity of sovereignty (*aiśvaryamala*).
Blazing with power, that [mantra] in the center bestows all desired objects;
this is declared to be the purification of the mantra, which one should perform at the time of worship.
O Aṃśumatī,
the wise one, having first gathered [the essence] from the *pheṭaka* of all the images,
should cover them with a cloth, remove that cloth, and sprinkle them with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*.
Having then discarded the floral remains (nirmālya), one should perform the mental bath (mānasa-snāna).
One should prepare a bathing altar using these six materials: gold, silver, copper, bell-metal (kaṃsa), tin, and lead; thus are the six substances declared.
The base-moulding, the lotus-ground, the fillet-neck, and the kampaka;
Having fashioned the *jagatī* for expansion like a horse, [the ritual proceeds]; [page 248 blank;

(104a) In the center of the house-like square, one should place the lotus-shaped moon and the Rohiṇī constellation of Kārtika; then, starting from the east, one should install the fivefold protective garlands and the mantras of the world-protectors,
which are the sprouts of all auspiciousness.

In the center of the field, which consists of mountain-lines and elemental squares, one should meditate on Keśava within a house; there, upon a lotus above a moon-disk, is the heavy intellect (dhī) at the twelfth door. One should contemplate the jar (kumbha) in its path, consisting of twenty-four squares, along with the arrows (five) and the row of skulls (four).
That which exists within the nature of speech is the moon-sprout together with its limbs.

In the twenty-five sections of the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*, one should worship the jewel, the lotus, the moon, and the two powers (*śakti*) in the center; then, having worshipped the eight-fold row surrounding that, [one worships] the seed-syllable of fire (*raṃ*) in the lunar square. In the sixteen squares of the earth, in the middle of the four Vedas, there is indeed the lotus above.
The moon, power, the two nooses, and the hook; (p.
250) that which is enclosed by them, within the enclosure of the two non-existent suns, is the sprout of Dharma, the youngest [son] who knows the Vedas and their branches.
The offering of the sprout is fourfold.
May there be auspiciousness.
Now follows the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
Of this Śrī Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (ṛṣis);

the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas are the meters (chandās); the deity is the power of life (prāṇa-śakti), the cause of the creation of the entire universe; "oṃ" (or "hrāṃ") and "hīṃ" are the seed-syllables (bīja); "svāhā" is the power (śakti); [it is employed] for my sake.
The application for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation is within that which consists of all mantras, yantras, and medicinal herbs.
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krāṃ aṃ ṅaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ khaṃ kaṃ aṃ, to the self of earth, water, fire, air, and ether; kroṃ hrīṃ āṃ īṃ, salutation to the heart.
Oṃ hrīṃ kroṃ īṃ ñaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ chaṃ caṃ | To the self of sound,
touch, taste, form, and smell: kroṃ hrīṃ laṃ hāṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the head.
HĀṂ HRĪṂ KROṂ AIṂ NAṂ SAṂ YAṂ DAṂ THAṂ TAṂ VAṂ,
to the self of skin, eyes, ears, tongue, and nose; KROṂ HRĪṂ ĀṂ AṂ, PHAṬ for the weapon—
thus is the binding of the directions with *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*.
May she who dwells upon a radiant, crimson lotus situated on a sea of red water, seated in meditative posture, holding in her lotus-like hands a noose,
a bow made of sugarcane, a goad, and five arrows— may that Jayaguṇā protect us.

[She] who bears [the remnants of] the great sacrificial oblation, the offering of water for the feet, the water for sipping, the respectful guest-offering, the perpetual festival, and the worship of the sandals; [she who is attended by] the mirror of ashes, the parasol, the fly-whisks, the hand-clappers, the multitude of songs, dances, and instrumental music. (The remainder of this verse is to be seen on page 254. (106a)
Beholding the *tāṇḍava* dance, the recitation of mantras, circumambulation, and the offering of water from cupped hands— these and others are the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the worship of Śiva.
Thus ends the daily worship in the glorious great tantra named Kāmika.
Oṃ!
I shall now describe the daily rite and the procedure for the daily rite, which destroys all defects.
The king, for the sake of attaining victory, [performed] that which is most auspicious for all living beings.

Oṃ. Having risen at dawn, having recollected Śiva, and having performed the necessary duties, [one should go] to a place on a path with abundant clay and water. With one portion of clay, there is cleansing of the anus;
with five portions for the left hand and ten for both hands, using clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit.
It is washed. Having thus performed the purification, sipping of water, and cleansing of the teeth, one proceeds with the ritual of bathing with mantras;
then the sipping of water for the feet, and the Vedic Śaiva *sandhyā* consisting of the Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Raudrī [mudrās].
Thus [are performed] the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), sun-worship (*sūryapūjā*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*),

ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), preparation of the general offering water (*sāmānyārghyakalpana*), and the worship of the door (*dvārapūjā*)— namely, Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, Nandin, Gaṅgā, Mahākāla, and Yamunā.
Vṛṣabha, Daṇḍin, Muṇḍin, Vijayin, Bhṛṅgin, Ananta, Vāsuki, and Madhu;
[this is] the worship of the doors (B), as well as the purification of the pedestal, the purification of the site, and the Liṅga-pīṭha-sumukha-bāhu.

p. 253) The arrangement of the feet and the back; the measurement of the lingas regarding their standing, sitting, and reclining postures; the measurement of the water for bathing; the purification of the linga with water; the substances for the bath and the water; the implements for worship; and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs, sub-limbs, minor limbs, and the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*).

The preparation of the five seats; the visualization of the body through the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the form and the *vidyā*; the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), making present (*sannidhāna*), firm fixation (*sannirodhana*), encircling with light (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*); the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and water for the face (*arghya*); the presentation of flowers; and at the time of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the extraction of the deity from the mantra-flowers.

At the time of consecration, there is the recitation of mantras according to the prescribed rite, the collection of materials for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) for the sprinkling, the worship,
and the binding with a sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) using a cloth from the time of the bath after the removal of impurities.

Having combined golden flowers with fragrant water, one should perform the consecration of the *liṅga* and its pedestal; then, having draped it with a cloth and wrapped it in a supporting garment, adorned it with the anointing of perfumes,
ornaments, and so forth, and having offered the covering, the mantra-food, the offering of water, and the mouth-freshener of betel.

The offering of oblations (*balipradāna*), the specific rites for the western gate, the perpetual fire offering (*nityāgnipradāna*), the quantity of materials for the *homa*, and at the conclusion of the *soma* sacrifice: purification; the fivefold enclosure of the sacred thread (*pavitra*);
worship with water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), and the waving of lights (*nīrājana*) (on folio 255).
The procedure for the daily rites (*nityakarman*) is completed.

O Goddess, are you the supreme power of life (*prāṇaśakti*), who is the color of the rising sun and the bestower of happiness?
*oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ* — *yaṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ* — *bhava sukhakarīṃ prāṇaśaktiḥ parāṃ vā?*
I am the swan. May the life-breath enter the womb; may there be all its limbs, all its sense organs—skin, mind, eye, ear, tongue, and nose. May it come; may it live happily;
may it remain, Svāhā!

Oṃ kroṃ hrīṃ āṃ oṃ oṃ. Homage to the self whose essence is arrival; homage to the self whose essence is the asura; laṃ, homage to the self whose essence is flesh; śaṃ, homage to the self whose essence is the elephant; ṇaṃ, homage to the self whose essence is marrow; saṃ, homage to the self whose essence is semen; kṣaṃ, homage to the self whose essence is the unmanifest. Oṃ.
The Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra is completed.
During the time of worship, as well as during fire-offerings, meditative absorption, and recitation in their proper sequence,
silence is prescribed for these six occasions, including at times when eating is mandatory.
(109ā) "Armed with weapons" refers to the fivefold enclosure worship (*pañcāvaraṇapūjā*), which consists of: wealth and abundance of grain;

water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), perfume (*gandha*), flowers (*puṣpa*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), food offerings (*naivedya*), drinking water (*pānīya*), the sacrificial oblation (*bali*), the fire sacrifice (*agnihotra*), the dismissal of the remains of the offering (*nirmālyavisarjana*), betel (*tāmbūla*), and mouth-fresheners (*mukhavāsa*).

The offering of water for the feet and other services, the presentation of incense and lamps, the *ārātrika* ceremony, the offering of sacred ash, the mirror, the umbrella, the fly-whisk, the fan, the daily festival, the performance of dance, the offering of the great oblation (*mahāhavis*),
the gift of sesame seeds, the gift of a cow, the gift of gold, the daily distribution of alms, the acceptance of gifts from Brahmins, and the performance of dance.

Having worshipped thus during the three junctions of the day with song, instrumental music, hymns, circumambulation, prostration, the request for the most secret of secrets, and the offering of water from cupped palms,
one should perform the propitiation of the Guru and the scripture, the honoring of guests, and the worship of Caṇḍeśvara at night.
Having performed the propitiation with half a *yāma* [of time] and the worship of the *kṣetrapāla*,
one should eat the *prāṇāgnihotra* food with a virtuous smile. Such is the daily procedure for the obligatory rites.
The daily ritual is completed.
May there be auspiciousness!

Village—(Peace)—Foundation.

Then, one should perform the collection of the clay.

one should cause the sound of all auspicious musical instruments to be proclaimed by those reciting benedictions.

At the root of a *bilva*, *aśvattha*, or *tulasī* tree— either to the east or near the north— or on a riverbank, a pond, the shore of the ocean, on a mountain peak, or in the southwest corner of a temple,
the preceptor, facing north, shall perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and the worship of Vighneśvara.

Having performed the ritual for the auspicious day through formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), one should meditate upon the Vāstu-puruṣa as residing in heaven, on earth, in the netherworld (*pātāla*), and so forth; then,
having visualized Ananta situated in the netherworld, Mahārākṣasa within him, Pannaga within him, Padma within him, and the Earth within him.
Having stood upon the entire *rākṣasa* [direction] between the earth and the intermediate space, having stood upon the *Vāstupati* in the midst of that *rākṣasa*,
and having stood upon the *viruti* at the head of that site (*vāstu*),
one places the foot of Īśāna in the south-south direction, and the right hand in the southeast corner (*agnikoṇa*).
The left hand [is placed] in the northwest corner; the meaning is that it lies upon the Vāstupuruṣa.
The months and asterisms: when the head is in the eastern direction, it is the month beginning with Bhādrapada;

and in the afternoon, as white-colored, facing west.

In the evening, he is yellow in color and faces the east; during the half-watch of the night, he is crystal-colored and faces downward—this is his constant form. place the golden vessel to the south, place the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) to the west, and place the Kundālī to the north; thus one should perform the invocation.
Having placed [the image] there facing downwards in meditation (dhyāna), endowed with two eyes,
four arms, matted hair on the crown of the head, and likewise a single face.
Having thus meditated upon her holding a water-pot and a rosary, and granting boons and fearlessness,
one should invoke the respective deities from Pātāla up to the end of the earth and the intermediate space (antarikṣa), starting with Pātāla:
Salutation to the one of infinite forms.
Within that [is contained] the *Śrīśivakavacastotra*.

Oṃ. Of this great mantra, the Śrī Śivakavaca-stotra, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi); Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda); Śrī Sadāśiva is the deity (devatā); Hrāṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hrīṃ is the power (śakti); Hūṃ is the pin (kīlaka). [It is recited] for the purpose of destroying all my sins.
The application (viniyoga) is for the sake of attaining the fourfold goals of human endeavor (puruṣārtha)— namely dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—

Hrām, salutation to both thumbs; Hrīṃ, salutation to both index fingers; Hūṃ, salutation to both middle fingers; Hraiṃ, salutation to both ring fingers; Hrauṃ, salutation to both little fingers; Hraḥ, salutation to both palms and backs of the hands. Oṃ.
