*Hrīṃ klīṃ*, svāhā to the head. (B) *Oṃ namo bhagavate śrīrudrarūpāya jvalajvalajvālāmāline oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*). *Oṃ namo bhagavate śrīrudrarūpāya jvalajvalajvālāmāline oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*.
Kavacāya hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ namo bhagavate śrīrudrarūpāya jvalajvalajvālāmāline oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ | Oṃ namo bhagavate śrīrudrarūpāya jvalajvalajvālāmāline oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ.
*Klīṃ astrāya phaṭ*. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ*—thus is the binding of the directions (*dikbandha*).
The meditation (*dhyāna*):
[One should meditate upon] Maheśvara, who has adamantine fangs, three eyes, and a dark-blue throat.
I constantly revere that fierce Sadāśiva, who possesses a thousand rays.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, who has the form of Śrī Rudra, who wears a garland of blazing, burning flames, who shatters the supreme mantras, supreme yantras, and supreme tantras of others,
who utterly destroys the mantras, yantras, and tantras of oneself, and who paralyzes the vidyās of adversaries.
For the establishment of the science of the Self and for the illumination of the knowledge of the Self (p.
268): Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ raṃ, obeisance to Rudra.
[The mantra] consists of three and five tridents and is likewise four-cornered.

They say that the Kṣīrodaka-yantra consists of Tārā (the letter *u*) accompanied by Hutabhū (the letter *ra*) on the outside, with Śaṅkara (the letter *ha*) in the middle for the sake of the essence (*vasārtha*), and surrounded [by the vowels].
Now, furthermore, [I shall speak of] that which is the secret of all Purāṇas,
the purifier that removes the entire flood of sins without exception,
the bestower of victory, and the liberator from all calamities.
I shall speak the Śaiva armor (kavaca), having performed the ritual procedure.
The sage said:
Having paid homage to Mahādeva, the all-pervading Maheśvara,
I shall proclaim the armor consisting of Śiva, which provides protection for all men.
Seated in a clean place upon a prepared seat, being wise,
with senses conquered and breath controlled, one should meditate upon the imperishable Śiva.
Seated within the lotus of the heart,
having pervaded the space of the body with its own radiance,
it is beyond the senses, subtle, infinite, and primordial.
One should meditate upon Maheśa, who consists of supreme bliss.
With all bonds of karma shaken off by meditation, his mind long immersed in the bliss of consciousness,
he was one whose self was composed through the placement of the six-syllable mantra.
One should perform protection with the Śaiva armor-mantra (kavaca).
(B) May the Lord, the soul of all deities, protect me who have fallen into the deep abyss of worldly existence;
may His divine name, the root of the jewel-like mantra, [protect me].
May he shake off all impurity dwelling within my heart.
May the one whose form is the universe, the self of consciousness consisting of a mass of light and bliss, subtler than the subtle and possessed of vast power, protect me everywhere.
May that God protect [us] from every fear.
May He protect us— He who sustains the universe in the form of the earth, who dwells upon the earth with His supreme form as the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva),
and who, in the form of water, brings about the welfare of men.
May he, the reviver, protect me from the snares of the Lord of Elephants.
May he who, at the end of the aeon, consumes all worlds with his manifold sports—
Kālarudra together with Kālāgni— protect me.
From the fear of whirlwinds and the like, and from the fall of that which is worshipped by all.

May He who, in the form of wind, attained mobility through the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth, protect me for the sake of firmness; may He who, in the form of space, provides all room— protect me.
He performs protection by means of the form of space.
He who is the maker of time and the witness of the fear of time, who by being the sun illuminates the three worlds for me,
and by being the moon is the lord of the forest herbs;
May he who possesses no horse protect you from the motionless one.
May He who is the enjoyer of the oblations in the sacrifice of the knowers, the witness of the senses in the form of the individual soul (jīva),
and the bestower of the fruits of virtuous deeds, protect me.
The embodiment of sacrifice who destroys the flood of sins.
Tatpuruṣa has three eyes and four faces; he possesses the luster of blazing lightning and gold, and holds in his hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a battle-axe.
May he protect me incessantly in the eastern direction.
Holding an axe, the Vedas, a goad, a noose, a trident, a drum, a rosary, and a mass of flames;
he has four faces, a blue luster, and three eyes.
In the southern direction, there is a white, very fierce jackal.
White as a jasmine flower, a conch shell, or crystal,
holding a rosary and a water-pot, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
he has three eyes, four faces, and great power.
May he who was born this very day protect me in the western direction.
Holding a rosary, a boon-granting gesture, and an axe in his hands, with a complexion like the filaments of a lotus,
three-eyed and possessing four beautiful faces— may he protect me.
May Vāmadeva protect [us] in the northern direction.
Holding a skull-topped staff,
a shield, a goad, and a noose in his hands, with a trident in his hand, he has two white tusks, five faces, and a coiled body.
Above Yishana is the supreme light.
May the moon-crested Lord protect my head; may the one with the eye in his forehead protect my brow;
may the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes protect my eyes.
May Viśvanātha protect them always.
May he whose fame is sung by the Vedas protect my hearing; may the Skull-bearer (Kapālin) always protect my skull;
and may the Five-faced One (Pañcavaktra) always protect my mouth.
May he whose tongue is the Veda always protect my tongue.
May the blue-throated Lord of the Mountains protect my neck;
may he who holds the Pināka bow in hand protect both my hands; and may he whose gait is like that of the bull upon whose shoulders he rests protect my shoulders. May he be served.
May Maheśa always protect my side.
May Dharmabāhu protect my root; may Dakṣamaravāntaka protect my chest;
may Girīndradhanvan protect my belly.
My waist is slender and it brings an end to the god of love.
May Cera protect my anus; may Pāyu protect my navel; may Ghaṭin protect me; may the Lord Dhūrjaṭi protect my private parts;
and may Hara protect my clothing. (130a)
May Jesus cover my back.
May the friend of Kubera protect my two thighs; may the Lord of the World protect my two knees;
may he whose banner is the bull protect the pair of my shanks.
May the feet of the one whose feet are like those of the celestial wish-fulfilling tree protect me.
May Maheśvara protect me during the first watch of the day; may Vāmadeva protect me during the middle watch;
may Tryambaka protect me during the third watch.
May the bull-bannered Lord protect me during the first watch of this auspicious day.
May the moon-crested Lord protect me at the beginning of the night; may the bearer of the Gaṅgā protect me at midnight;
may the husband of Gaurī protect me at the end of the night.
May Mṛtyuñjaya protect me at all times;
may Śaṅkara protect me dwelling within,
and may Sthāṇu always protect me standing outside.
In that interval, may the Lord of Beings, Sadāśiva, protect me on all sides;
may the sole Lord of the worlds protect me as I stand.
The Lord of the Pramathas [drank] the flowing beverage.
May the one who is to be known through the Vedānta protect me while I am standing;
may the imperishable Śikhin protect me while I am lying down;
and may Nīlarudra protect me on the path.
Śaila—among the mountains, the enemy of the cities (Purañjaya).
May the hunter of deer, possessed of noble power and great majesty from dwelling in the forest,
protect us— [he] whose fierce wrath is like that at the end of an aeon.
(130B) With his testicles shaken by a loud, manifest burst of laughter.
May Vīrabhadra, who is difficult to restrain even by the ocean-like army of Ghorāri and who is mounted upon a multitude of horses and elephants, protect us from great fear.
May his terrible axes and spears sever the hundred *akṣauhiṇīs* of advancing enemies— that army terrifying with thousands, lakhs, and crores of weapons.
May the flame of the trident of the Destroyer of Tripura, blazing like the fire of universal dissolution, slay the dasyus and the tigers,
lions, deer, and swans [that dwell] here.
The Pināka-bearer [Śiva] drew his bow completely taut.
[May there be protection from] bad dreams, ill omens, miserable rebirths,
wicked men, famine, calamities, unbearable misfortunes, and ill repute; [and from] portents, afflictions, the fear of poison, and the torment of malevolent planets.
May the Lord of the worlds destroy my diseases as well.
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Sadāśiva, who is the essence of all principles (*tattva*),
who is the destroyer of those who know all principles, the sole creator of the three worlds, the sole destroyer of the three worlds,
the sole sustainer of the three worlds, the sole teacher of the three worlds, and the sole witness of the three worlds.
To the one possessing all restrictive qualities, the bestower of boons upon all the worlds, the shatterer of all afflictions and misfortunes,
the sole benefactor of the entire world, the moon-crested one, the eternal, the self-abiding,
the supportless, the healthy, and the fearless.

Victory, victory to you, O Mahārudra, O Mahāraudra, who have descended as Bhadra! You who are free from attachment, devoid of qualities, and possessed of incomparable majesty; who are eternally pure, perfect, and the embodiment of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss; who are the two supreme sources of peace and light; whose form is splendor and who are composed of splendor.
O Mahābhairava, Bhairava, Kālabhairava, Kalpāntabhairava! You who wear a garland of skulls and hold a khaṭvāṅga, sword, shield, noose, goad, ḍamaruka drum, trident, axe, arrow,
spear, śakti, bhindipāla, tomara, mace, club, prāsa, parigha, and battle-axe.
O wielder of the *musala*, the *śataghnī*, and the discus; O you whose hands are terrifying; O subduer with a thousand faces;

O you who are formidable with tusks; O you whose loud, gaping laughter causes the entire circle of the universe to shatter; O you who wear earrings of lordly serpents, bracelets of lordly serpents, and a garment of lordly serpents; O conqueror of Death!

O Three-eyed One, Destroyer of Tripura, Bull-vehicled Lord of the Universe, Odd-eyed One, Face-on-all-sides, Adorned with Truth! Protect me, protect me from all sides! Blaze, blaze! Destroy, destroy the fear of great death! Drive away, drive away the fear of disease!

Destroy, destroy the fear of poison and serpents; destroy, destroy the thieves; drive away, drive away my enemies; rend, rend them with a trident; cleave, cleave them with an axe; cut asunder, cut asunder them with a sword!
Awaken, awaken with the khaṭvāṅga! Crush them with the mace! Strike them down, strike them down with the arrow!
Terrify the rākṣasas, terrify them! Put the bhūtas to sleep, put them to sleep! O kūśmāṇḍa, vetāla, and mārīca!

Scatter, scatter the hosts of brahma-rākṣasas! Grant me fearlessness, grant it! Comfort, comfort me who am terrified! Lift me up, lift me up from the fear of hell! Restore me to life, restore me to life from death! [Deliver me] from the utmost hunger and thirst!
O Amṛtakaṭākṣa, nourish me, nourish me with your glance! O Harivaha, gladden me, gladden me who am suffering! O Śivakavaca, shield me, shield me! Sadāśiva, salutations to you, salutations to you!
Thus, these supreme Śaiva armor-mantras of mine,
which pacify all afflictions, are a secret for all embodied beings.
For that wise man who always wears this supreme armor of Śiva,
no fear arises anywhere by the grace of Śambhu.
Whether one's life has reached its end and death is imminent, or one is afflicted by a great disease,
such a person attains immediate happiness and gains a long life.
It pacifies all poverty, increases auspiciousness,
and whoever wears this divine armor is honored even by their own gods.
One is liberated from the multitude of great sins (*mahāpātaka*) and from the minor sins (*upapātaka*);
at the end of the body, one attains liberation through the power of the Śiva-dharma.
You too, possessing faith and free from doubt, should wear this supreme armor proclaimed by me; indeed, you shall immediately attain the highest good.
Having spoken thus to that prince, the illustrious son of Ṛṣabha gave him an excellent conch of great sound and a supreme sword-bearer.
To whomsoever cow-dung has been given through the power of austerity and mantras,
show this sharp-edged sword clearly to him.
He dies instantly, even if he were Death himself manifest before his enemies,
upon merely touching the body of one who has received these great mantras that inspire fearlessness from serpents.
There shall be six thousand elephants for each of the two of great strength;
through the grace of the ashes, they attain power, sovereignty, fortitude, and mindfulness.
Accompanied by his young princes like the autumnal sky with its stars, he spoke to him with palms joined in reverence: "May that prince become a yogi."
This conch has been given by me through the power of my asceticism and mantras;
those enemies of yours who hear the blast of this conch [shall be overcome].
(133a) Those who have been consecrated embrace them, having cast aside their weapons; [they become] insentient.
The conch and the sword are great and divine, capable of routing the enemy host.
By increasing the heroism and splendor of his own army and those on his side,
and through the power of these two as well as the armor of Śiva;
And by the great power of twelve thousand nāgas,
you shall conquer the enemy army through the mastery of the one who wears ashes.
"Having attained the auspicious lion-throne, you shall protect this earth"—
thus [spoke he] to Bhadrāyus, who was thoroughly versed in other sciences.
Honored by those two, the yogi Śodhi departed with a steady gait.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Story Told by Śivaka," in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa.
May this be offered to Śrī Sāmbaśiva. May this be offered to Ardhanārīśvara. Om.
(134a) The Hymn to the Sun’s Armor.
May there be auspiciousness!

Oṃ. Of this great mantra, the *śrī-ādityastotra-kavaca*, the venerable Agastya is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chanda*), and Sūryanārāyaṇa is the deity (*devatā*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of recitation for the sake of pleasing Kṣīranārāyaṇa.
Oṃ, homage to Padmahasta with the two thumbs;
homage to Tejorāśi with the two index fingers; homage to Mārtāṇḍa with the two middle fingers;
homage to Āditya with the two ring fingers; homage to Sūrya with the two little fingers.
Homage! Homage to the Thousand-rayed One with both palms and backs of the hands. To the Lotus-handed One, the heart:
*huṃ*. To the Mass of Splendor, the head: *svāhā*. To Mārtāṇḍa, the crest-lock:
*vauṣaṭ*. To Āditya, the armor: *huṃ*. To Sūrya, the three eyes: *vauṣaṭ*.
*Sahasrakiraṇāyāstrāya phaṭ*. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ*—thus is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*).
Meditation:
[One should meditate on] the one mounted upon a lotus in the center of a circle with six spokes, situated within a square provided with eight petals.
I bow to that radiant god, the Maker of Light, who holds the great elephant,
the conch, and the lotus;
who is the embodiment of the Vedas, the triple-formed one, and composed of manifold qualities.
O King, one should constantly meditate upon the ancient Viśvarūpa, who has the form of the syllable *oṃ*, *hrāṃ*, and *hrīṃ*, and who is the supreme delight.
I bow down to the Sun, who resembles a *jaya* flower, the great son of Kaśyapa,
the giver, and the destroyer of all sins.
Now I shall fully proclaim this armor that grants all desires;
one who is free from fever should move about with this armor in mind.
May Ghrṇipāt protect my head always; may Bhāskara protect my forehead.
May Āditya protect my head, and may Divākara protect my ears.
May Bhānu protect my nose always; may Ravi protect my face and earrings;
may Jagannetra protect my tongue, and may Sulocanā protect my ears.
May Divyāyudha protect my shoulders; may Vibhākara protect my arms.
May Uṣṇakara protect my hands; may Bhānumān protect my heart.
May Saptāśva protect my belly; may Nabhomaṇi protect my navel.
May the twelve-fold one protect the waist, as well as Satvinī and Savitṛ.
May the best of gods, Sūrya, protect the thighs; likewise, may he protect the tops of the knees.
May Mārtaṇḍa protect the knees, and may Vibhāvasu protect the ankles.
May the Sun always protect my two feet, and may he protect my entire body;
this single [mantra] was created by Gaurī, which, when meditated upon, grants all desires.
By reciting this constantly after rising in the morning, one is liberated from disease.
Thus ends the Sūryakavaca in its entirety.
I bow to the Sun, the lowest-born among beautiful worlds, the nectar, the essence of the Vedanta,
knowledge, the embodiment of Brahman, the stainless Lord of the gods, the self-conscious mind of the world,
the sovereign of Indra, Aditya, and kings, the preceptor of the gods, and the crest-jewel of the three realms.
I ever revere the Sun, whose heart is the very nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
One should worship the rising sun as Brahman, the midday sun as Maheśvarī,
and the setting sun, measuring one cubit, as Viṣṇu himself— the Sun-god who is the embodiment of the three forms.
He is the self of time, the self of all beings, the self of the Vedas, and faces in every direction;
he is the destroyer of the fear of birth, death, old age, disease, and worldly existence.
Salutations again and again to the Supreme Lord, the supreme light who holds a lotus in his hand.
O Bhāskara, Jyotirmārtāṇḍa, Āditya, the light of lights, salutations to you!
(135B) O you of egg-birth, great witness; salutations again and again to Āditya! O you who possess the flowers of the lotus-mine and can assume any form at will; salutations again and again!
Salutations again and again to the Sun, the Lord of all, who possesses the deer-mark;
salutations again and again to the Eightfold Form (Aṣṭamūrti), consisting of the earth, water, fire, wind, ether, the sun, the moon, and lightning.
Salutations again and again to the supreme form, the highest goal, the destroyer of sin;
salutations again and again to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the teacher of all scriptures.
O mighty-armed one, [worship] the bridge and the five [faces]; salutations again and again to Tryambaka.
Salutations again and again to him who stands in the center of the solar orb, whose form is the Sun.
Salutations again and again to the one who possesses form, who is declared to be happiness, and who is the Savior;
salutations again and again to the stainless Sun, the peaceful one, and the partless.
Salutations again and again to the one who is both with parts and without parts, the eternal, the bliss of eternity;
salutations again and again to the Lord of the beautiful gods, who possesses all forms.
For the sake of protection, for the destruction of fear, and for the warding off of missiles and weapons.
It bestows good fortune, the attainment of wealth, and is the supreme increaser of longevity.
Caṇḍamāruta and Sarvābhya, when applied to the southern side, increase the growth of the earth;
they destroy epilepsy, consumption, leprosy, and their associated defects.
Within six months for all purposes, or by practicing for a year,
one succeeds in all undertakings and is glorified in the world of the Sun.
He is honored in the glorious world of the Sun.
Victory, victory to the Sun, the sole lamp of the seven worlds,
whose feet are accompanied by rays and who is the liberation from the suffering of the afflictions;
to the primordial form of Āditya, who traverses the dawn-red sky!
I bow to that Sun-god, who is both supreme and most distant.
Salutations to Savitṛ, the sole eye of the world,
the cause of the origin, maintenance, and destruction of the universe;
who consists of the three Vedas and assumes the nature of the three guṇas.
To the one whose self is Viriñci, Nārāyaṇa, and Śaṅkara.
The Sūryagāyatrī: Oṃ, let us know Bhāskara; let us meditate upon the maker of great light; may that Āditya inspire us.
Oṃ. We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he inspire our intellects.
Oṃ hrīṃ ghrīṇi sūrya ādityom | śrīṃ soham arkamahājyotir asomahom ||
Oṃ hrīṃ ghrīṇi sūrya ādityoṃ śrīṃ! I am Sohararka, the light, I am Śiva. I am the light of the Self, I am the pure one, I am the great luster of all lights. Oṃ hrīṃ ghrīṇi sūrya ādityoṃ śrīm!
Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Ravi, Sūrya, and Divākara— these six are indeed his eternal divine eye, consisting of ascetic power.
Salutations to the venerable gurus.
The Armor of Gaṇapati.

(136B) Oṃ. Of this great mantra of Śrī Gaṇapati, the Seer is Parabrahman; the metre is Anuṣṭubh; the deity is Śrī Mahāgaṇapati; the seed-syllable is *gaṃ*; the power is *ṇaṃ*; the pin is *paṃ*. [This is recited] for the sake of attaining the grace of Mahāgaṇapati and for the sake of accomplishing all desired objects.
The application (viniyoga) is for the sake of attaining enjoyment and liberation, and for the propitiation of Mahāgaṇapati.
Oṃ, salutation to Gajānana with both thumbs. Oṃ Gaṃ, salutation to Lambodara with both index fingers.
Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Śūrpakarṇa with the two middle fingers.
(p. 285) Oṃ raṃ, salutation to Mūṣikavāhana with the two ring fingers. Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇādhīśvara with the two little fingers.
Oṃ gaum, homage to Vighnarāja with the palms and backs of the hands;
oṃ, huṃ to the heart of Gajānana;
oṃ gaṃ, svāhā to the head of Lambodara.
Oṃ haṃ, to Śūrpakarṇa, for the tuft of hair, vauṣaṭ! Oṃ raṃ, to the one whose vehicle is a mouse, for the armor, hūṃ!
Oṃ śrīṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes of Gaṇādhīśvara.
Oṃ gauṃ, phaṭ to the weapon (astra) of Vighnarāja.
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ"—thus is the binding of the directions (dikbandha).
Meditation:
[I meditate upon] the Lord of the Universe, adored by all, of stainless fame, skillful among those who are skillful in all things,
whose noble intellect is manifest even in all calamities, the very breath of life of Pārvatī.

May he protect all the gods, including the excellent Indra, and the hosts of divine sages; may this son of the Siddhas, accomplished through compassion, remove obstacles within; I bow down to Vighnarāja, who certainly dispels impediments.
The syllable *kha* joined with *ta*, conjoined with *sa*, followed by *ya*, endowed with *māyā* (the vowel *ī*),
combined with the thirteenth day (the letter *ja*), and provided with the sixth vowel (*ū*).
O Prajāpati, this is declared to be the root mantra of Vighneśa:
Oṃ Gaṃ Haṃ Raṃ Śrīṃ Gauṃ Gaṇapataye Namaḥ.
The voice of Brahmā said:
O Nandikeśvara, omniscient one, bestower of grace upon devotees,
supreme granter of worldly enjoyment and liberation to men, and protector of all!
I desire to hear the armor-mantra (kavaca), which accomplishes all desired aims,
removes mental and physical ailments, is worthy of being heard, and is the cause of making one an abode for Lakṣmī.
O Nandikeśa, best among the gods, you should tell me how a mortal attains mastery over speech and the power to accomplish all desired objects.
Nandikeśvara said:
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall proclaim the supreme secret, more secret than the secret,
which was performed by the Moon-crested Lord for the benefit of all the worlds.
It is the destroyer of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and others, as well as brahmarākṣasas;
it wards off consumption, leprosy, skin diseases, and quartan fevers.
It pacifies great diseases, wards off the wrath of kings,
and [removes] diseases arising from wind and bile, as well as other truly terrible ailments.
p. 287) Thus, in all such cases when a time of fear has arrived, one should first recite the Armor of Vighneśa and then perform the hymn of praise.
Therefore, O Blessed One of great fame and four faces, listen:
having become pure and performed the ritual sipping of water three times, one should always recite this while drinking.
The wise one should especially recite [the mantra] during the *brahmamuhūrta*.
Oṃ macī-bhṛṅga-sabilva-badarī-durdhūraka-cāsura-apāmārga-bṛhatī-camī ca karavīra-śmāntara-skārjuna-kāntā-ḍāḍimī-devadāru-maruva.
Likewise, the sindhūra-leaf, the jātī, and the gaṇḍalī-patrikā, according to the proper rite,
constitute the sequence for the worship of Vighneśa.
May there be auspiciousness!
The Armor of the Auspicious Lord of Obstacles (Śrīvighneśvarakavaca).
Oṃ. Of this great mantra, the Śrī Vighneśvara-kavaca-stotra, the Seer is Ādipuruṣottama;
the Metre is Anuṣṭubh; the Deity is Śrī Vighneśvara; the Seed-syllable is Viṃ; the Power is Ghnaṃ; the Pin is Śaṃ. [It is recited] for the purpose of destroying all my sins.
The application [of this mantra] is for the sake of accomplishing the fourfold aims of human life—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;

for the sake of accomplishing all desired objects; for the sake of warding off all evils; for the sake of accomplishing cherished desires; and for the sake of pleasing Vighneśvara during the recitation.
Oṃ, to Gajānana, salutation to the two thumbs; Oṃ Gaṃ, to Lambodara, salutation to the two index fingers;
Oṃ Haṃ, to Śūrpakarṇa, salutation to the two middle fingers.
Oṃ raṃ, salutation to the one whose vehicle is a mouse, with the two ring fingers.
Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the Lord of the Gaṇas, with the two little fingers. Oṃ gauṃ, salutation to the King of Obstacles, with the palms and backs of the hands.
Oṃ, to the elephant-faced one, to the heart, hūṃ! Oṃ, to the large-bellied one, to the head, svāhā! Oṃ gaṃ, to the winnowing-basket-eared one, to the crest-lock, vauṣaṭ!
Oṃ raṃ, to the one whose vehicle is a mouse, for the armor: hūṃ! Oṃ śrīm, to the Lord of the Gaṇas, for the three eyes: vauṣaṭ!
Oṃ, to the King of Obstacles, for the weapon: phaṭ!
"Bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ" is the binding of the directions.
The meditation:
[I meditate upon] Vighneśa, who is worshipped by the universe, whose [splendor] is stainless—[he who is] all-capable and most skillful.

May he protect all—the excellent Indras, along with the hosts of gods and sages—who has manifested his noble intellect even amidst all calamities; who is the son of Parvatī’s very life-breath; whose elephantine face was attained through compassion; and who, by removing obstacles, certainly bestows success. I bow to Vighnarāja.
May Vighneśa protect [me] in the east, Gaṇādhyakṣa in the south,
Gajavaktra in the west, and Vighnanāśana in the north.
In the southeast is Citrabhānu; in the southwest, Skandapūrvaja;
in the northwest, Ākhuvāha; and in the northeast, Devapūjita.
May Sumukha protect from above, and Gajānana from the downward direction;
thus may Vikaṭa, the destroyer of evil, protect every quarter.
May Kapila protect [my] crest-lock; may he who assumes the form of the full moon protect [my] head;
may Kirīṭin protect our forehead; and may he who is established in glory protect the space between the eyebrows.
In the middle of the eyes is Triṇayana; in the ears is Gajakarṇaka;
on the cheeks is Madanabhi; at the roots of the ears is Madotkaṭa.

May he with beautiful teeth protect me between the teeth; may he who is the meter in speech and consists of two feet protect me; and may he who arises from the hand protect me at the chin and the nose.
May he whose upper lip is the universe protect me; may he who grants death when dead be on my lower lip;
may he with beautiful tusks protect my jaw, for he is the one who causes the cessation of the mind.
May the son of Pārvatī protect me— along with prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna— as well as glory, fame, and fortune.
May the Supreme Brahman protect the heart; may the Lord of the World, whose nature is the syllable *sva*, protect [it]; may Tutila protect the belly; and may the syllable *ga* protect the navel.

May the Great Yogi protect my penis; may he who has conquered his senses protect the testicles and the water [of that organ] from all demons; and may the elder brother of Guha protect my private parts.
May Śukra protect my white foot; may Sukhapradā protect my two thighs;
may Hrasvajaṅgha protect the region of the shanks; and may Jagadguru protect the middle of the knees.
May Rakṣākara protect the two ankles; may the beloved Nartana protect the feet;
and may Skanda, the crusher of the enemies of the gods, protect all the limbs.
May the God who is the soul of the universe, the giver of boons, and affectionate toward his devotees, protect [us], along with our wealth, grain, cattle, houses, and fields, without interruption.
But that place which is devoid of protection and lacking the armor—
there the Lord, who dwells on the path and has conquered his senses, protects it all.
Whether in the forest, on mountain peaks, or upon paths that bring both honor and dishonor;
whether in water or on land,
this divine armor, pure and wind-consuming, shall remove all deceptive illusions.
In times of calamity, death may occur when there is a warding off of fear.
It pacifies diseases of the abdomen, wards off spider-stings and boils,
and provides constant relief from diseases such as those caused by childhood spirits.
For one who recites and retains this, all accomplishments are within the palm of their hand;
wherever they may go, there they shall find the fulfillment of their aims.

O best of the twice-born, he who hears or recites this [text] which is worshipped by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, gods, and Siddhas, shall go with his sons, grandsons, and entire family to the immeasurable [state].
She destroys the impure beauty of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
The person who meditates upon that celibate one— who is inconceivable, manifold in form, impelled by the welfare of the three worlds, and the destroyer of calamities—
attains all perfections.
Having attained union with Vighneśa, one becomes free from doubt.
Thus ends the Vighneśvara-kavaca in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Brahmā and Nandikeśvara. (p. 292)
Salutations to the illustrious Lord of the Gaṇas.
(140a) The expiation for the Kṛttikā lamp.
O Six-faced One, I shall now describe the procedure for expiation regarding the lamp itself,
once this festival known as Mālā Kṛttikā has been observed.
Having performed the ablution fifty times, one should recite [the mantra] while giving a thousand as a sacrificial fee.
It is most excellent when conjoined with Kṛttikā, and middling when conjoined with Bharaṇī.
Rohiṇī joined with the lowest [degree], and Kṛttikā is remembered as being of three kinds;
likewise, are the betel nut, the coconut, the camphor, and the sandalwood.
Or a bamboo, or even an Arjuna tree, as well as a Tinduka or a Śiṃśapā.
It should be a ray of light, a *vakula* flower, or even a palm pillar;
it must be straight, free from cruelty, and devoid of worms or hollows.
A [wooden] post that is crooked, unstable, or defective brings about the increase of enemies;
if it has cracks, worm-holes, or bends, one should immediately perform a rite for pacification.
This is declared to be the lamp-post, made of either one or two types of heartwood;
having made that post eight parts, one part is for its foundation in the ground.
One should treat the tree according to its strength and its nourishment;
the lifespan of trees is proclaimed to be five hundred, one hundred, or eighty years.
(140B) Among children, the elderly, and the young, the young woman is considered superior;
for through her strength there may be the destruction of the village, while through the old woman there would be the loss of longevity.
Therefore, with every effort, one should have the *mūta* made from wood;
one should make those [implements] from trees and then perform the *śāntisūkta*.
Whether it be a fine leaf of coconut, or even a palm leaf, or likewise a date-palm leaf, a betel-nut leaf, or a plantain leaf— these are the [proper] leaves.
Alternatively, if a ketaki leaf is available,
the officiating priest should tie it to the lamp-stands and collect whatever [substances] are gathered by means of that dried [leaf].
If that leaf is dry and withered, there is no doubt it indicates eye disease;
it should be wrapped in a variegated cloth and adorned with waves.
If [the drum] lacks cloth, there is great agitation; if it lacks leaves, there is loss of strength.
Having recited the Aghora mantra one thousand times, [one should rectify] whatever is lacking.
One should perform the pacification rite with a mantra that is immediately effective, even if the army lacks a canopy;
however, one should commence the sowing of seeds during the night following the Kṛttikā constellation.
One should perform all the rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fire (*agnyādhāna*) as prescribed for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*).
Nine new vessels should be collected and filled with the ghee of a tawny cow (*kapilājya*).
(141a) Regarding the vessel, it is specifically proclaimed that the *ṣkala* is the best when made of camphor; however, if it is inferior, there is a loss of strength.
Then the wise one should cause it to be sown with fire, beginning with Īśa and the others in the cardinal directions;
at its conclusion, having tied the *kautuka* (protective thread), he should place the image upon the trident and the staff.
If the offering of the sprouts is omitted, there will be the destruction of the left-handed practitioners;
having recited the ten-syllable mantra a hundred times, one should perform a sprinkling with a *droṇa* measure of milk.
If the vessel is new but devoid of clarified butter, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra alone;
if it is devoid of camphor, one should recite the Vyomavyāpin mantra a hundred times.
One should install the Supreme Lord with twenty-five jars;
the lamps for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) emerge together with the Śiva-weapon mantra.
Accompanied by all musical instruments and hymns of praise uttered by those reciting auspicious words,
he should then proceed to the staff-pillar site and have the declaration of a "meritorious day" (puṇyāha) recited.
Having consecrated and worshipped the staff, one should begin with the binding of the protective thread;
for this [rite] would be deficient without the *kautuka*, one should sprinkle it with a *droṇa* measure of milk.
At its end, there should be the worship with palm-leaves; one should place it at its base.
However, the consecration lamp may be extinguished through negligence.
(141B) Having performed the immediate consecration (*adhivāsana*), the ritual bathing, and the *śānti*-oblation; this is called "consecration. Herein, the lamp is correctly described.
At the conclusion of the evening protection ritual, one should begin the offering of lamps;
however, one should omit half a *ghaṭikā* after the setting of the sun.
When the lamp is exhausted during the ritual, or likewise when it is time to collect the lamps,
one should offer a new lamp at an improper time and recite the root mantra one hundred times.
One should perform the sixteenfold ablution and carry out the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma). Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before Śiva, one should arrange the lamp-vessels.
Then, beginning with Vighneśa, one should cause the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
thereafter, one should worship [the deities] starting from Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta within five vessels.
In this way, the auspicious day (puṇyāha) would become deficient, and prosperity would perish;
therefore, one should bathe the Supreme Lords and consecrate them with a drona-measure of milk.
O Mahātāpana, there is no doubt that the worship of the vessel has not been performed;
having recited the root mantra one hundred times, one should bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having brought two vessels— one for the sake of the deity and one for the sake of Śivā—
and having placed a lamp in the center, he should establish it there in close proximity.
O Lord of Gods, although I am weak and possess few means, I perform worship at the conclusion [of the rite] with devotion; therefore, you should not consider me ignorant.
Having thus informed the Lord of the Gods,
and having especially adorned the god Umāskandeśvara together with the weapon-god, [he performed the rites].
(142a) Lamps and vessels joined together, accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments, provided with various lamps, and adorned by courtesans.
Having established the lamp-stand on level ground, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there;
then, having unified the lamps beginning with Sadyojāta and the others, one should worship them well.
If one joins it with the inverted [mantra], that illumination will be fruitless;
by reciting two hundred thousand [times] of the Aghora [mantra], that lamp shall be purified.
Taking a pair of lamps,
O Kuru, you should establish that lamp while gazing at the God of gods and recollecting the Jyotirliṅga.
Having bathed, become pure, and being intent on the supreme practice, one should,
while recollecting the seed-syllable of Śiva, take hold of a lamp with the hand.
Having quickly mounted it upon the staff, one should not join it to the tip of the banner;
the directions are traditionally assigned to Indra, Yama, Kubera, and Varuṇa.
The king, having mentally recited this lamp-verse for the increase of his kingdom, wealth, grain, and long life, fell prostrate upon the ground.
Recalling the great light from the tip down to the root,
one should maintain the excellent flame of the superior lamp for the duration of a *kāṣṭha* within a *ghaṭikā*.
If it is conjoined with *kāṣṭha*, one will perform the most base of base acts;
[yet] there will be victory, the prosperity of the kingdom, as well as increase in worship and strength,
the growth of villages, gold, and likewise disease, grief, and fear.
The fruit of the lamp itself is said to be from Umā onwards, up to Guhā.
If [the earth] should crack at the edges of the lamp-stands along with the staff, one should sprinkle it with water using a small axe;
if a fissure should appear, there will be the destruction of the village, so one should immediately perform a rite of pacification.
If one causes it to wander to the edge of the island or to a village, there is no doubt that a fault will arise in the inferior [deity].
One should consecrate the Supreme Lord with twenty-five water-pots.
At the time of mounting the vehicle, one should always perform proper wiping and sprinkling;
having applied the three roots and other substances, one should mark the ground at a distance of nine finger-breadths.
Alternatively, one should sprinkle even the Maṅgula tree with beautiful water;
because it was not sprinkled by him, the plague of fever spreads.
One should bathe the God of gods with twenty-five water-pots;
[the ground] should be free from depressions and elevations, moss, and thorns.
In the event of a quarrel, bleeding, or heavy rain accompanied by strong winds,
honey, sugar, and clarified butter should be used for the purpose of pacifying those afflictions.
The six products of the cow (ṣaḍgavya) are each proclaimed as a consecration;
they consist of three parts of water, one part of fruit, and one part of yellow pigment (rocanā).
O Supreme Lord, one should install [the image] which grants the attainment of desired fruits;
if a boar is seen in front, having killed it, one should perform a rite of pacification.
If the king fails to act, there will be a depletion of his mounts;
likewise, if he dwells surrounded by those who reside in the houses of the planets according to the great boundaries and injunctions.
When a person has died, there is great danger; therefore, one should perform worship at that very time.
If one performs worship out of delusion, there is no doubt that it will result in harm for the king.
The wise one should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed within the three dharmas;
at the time of departure, however, [he should offer] betel-leaf along with juice, fruits, and so forth.
One should offer [the offerings] to the Great Lords preceded by incense and lamps;
whoever, out of delusion, does not give them, for him there arises the production of obstacles through that delusion.
Then, having performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should cause the Lord to be bathed with sixteen vessels full of milk, adorned by courtesans.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with pearl jewelry,
she should perform the twilight dance extending from Indra to Īśāna.
However, for one devoid of the proper application of joints and intervals, one should either perform the ceremonial bathing or not at all;
furthermore, the *yāla*, *carma*, *sarañja*, *gāna*, and *kāṃsa* constitute the fivefold [classification].
When many [musicians] have arrived, one should cause them to sound at the time of departure;
however, if they are devoid of the five sounds, there will be a royal sacrifice involving blood.
(143B) One should recite the *pañcabrahma-śata* to pacify each respective defect;
having thus performed the circumambulation, one should enter the temple.
If it is devoid of the *nīrāñjana* rite, people will encounter suffering;
by reciting the ten-syllable mantra a hundred times as before, the *nīrāñjana* rite shall be accomplished.
The wise one should cause the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) to be performed according to the previously mentioned procedure;
likewise, he should perform the daily offering (*naivedya*), the perpetual fire-oblation (*nityahoma*), and the regular strength-offering (*balinirupta*).

At the conclusion of that, one should perform the pure dance (śuddhanṛtta), and at its conclusion, one should offer parched rice (pṛthuka). Thus, it is said, the rite becomes complete; one should immediately perform the rite for pacification (śānti).
Thirty, twenty, and ten are declared as the three highest;
having divided nine bhāras into three parts, they are declared as the three middling.
One *bhāra* consisting of four *droṇas* of rice-water is the lowest of the low;
the wise man should cause flattened rice (*pṛthuka*) mixed with sugar, ghee, and cumin to be given.
Having prepared coconut fruit combined with cardamom and cinnamon,
along with ten kinds of cakes, one should cause them to be offered to the God of gods.
At that time, she should immediately cause all the various items, including parched rice, to be given separately, and then she should cause betel-leaf to be offered.
When this is done for the king, it always brings victory;
if it is not done due to delusion, there is no doubt that his position will be lost.
For the purpose of pacifying those defects, one should perform an ablution with cow’s clarified butter (gavyājya) using one hundred,
fifty, or twenty-five [verses], applying these according to the excellence [of the recipient].
Indeed, thirty, twenty, and ten *prasthas* constitute the three intermediate measures;
likewise, seven, five, and three *pūsas* are proclaimed as the [three] lower measures.
(144a) One should perform the consecration with clarified butter according to the procedure previously described.
Thus ends the chapter on the expiation for the lamp in the Kīrtikā, within the great tantra known as the Vātula.
Homage to the Gurus.
The twelvefold ablution; the twenty-fivefold ablution.
One should place the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), the five products of the cow with kuśa-water,
as well as milk, curd, and ghee, on the side of the southwest corner.
One should place a ripe jackfruit, a coconut, a plantain,
and *kuśa* grass in the corners starting from the southeast, according to the prescribed rite.
One should place a ruby in the center, either accompanied by a golden lotus or not;
having placed it in a vessel of gold, one should set a golden blue lotus within it.
Having worshipped Śiva in the Śiva-kumbha and Manonmani in the Vardhanī vessel,
one should worship Vaikartana and the others outside according to their respective names.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter on the ritual bathing.
The twenty-fifth ablution.
The bath (snapana) and the twenty-fifth [rite] will be described by me;
having first performed the purification, the second is the anointing (anulepana).
The third is the arrangement of the thread, and the fourth shall be the mandala;
the fifth is the arrangement of the footprints, and the sixth is the arrangement of the *kūrca*.
The seventh is the placement of the mantra, the eighth is the placement of the deity;
the ninth is declared to be the ritual procedure, and the tenth is the examination of the cloth.
The eleventh is the offering of scents and flowers, the twelfth is incense and lamps,
the thirteenth is said to be the mudrā, and the fourteenth is the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
The fifteenth is the removal of the jar, and the sixteenth shall be the ceremonial bath.
One should purify the ground with the Astra-mantra and smear it with the Vāmadeva-mantra.
One should perform the laying out of the lines with the Aghora mantra and the sacrificial mound with the Puruṣa mantra;
one should place the jars with the Hṛdaya mantra, and [the placement] of the Īśāna mantra is not obtained [therein].
One should arrange the ritual substances with the root mantra, cause the deities to enter with the left [hand],
place the bowls with the principal seed-syllable, and the garments with the heart mantra.
One should offer the house and other items with the Īśāna mantra, the incense and so forth with the Kavaca mantra, present the mudrā with the Aghora mantra, and recite the Pavamāna hymn.
One should especially sprinkle [the vessel] with water for the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) as is appropriate;
one should lift up the jar with the *praṇava* and with the mantra beginning "mahāvyoma."
The eastern thread should be the eight-thread [line], and likewise the northern thread;
one should place the central nine-pitcher [array] while leaving aside six in each direction.
In the corners beginning with the southeast, the number of yugas is proclaimed;
[the offerings are] water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, the five products of the cow, and water with kuśa grass.
One should arrange milk, curd, and ghee as the lower covering;
likewise, sesame, bilva leaves, sandalwood,
and cloud [incense], as well as campaka, jackfruit, mustard, and nāgakesara.
That vessel is unstable, its interior is hollow, and it is indeed made of iron.
One should place cloves, leaf-fragrance, and camphor in their proper sequence.
One should worship Maheśvara and Mahādevī with the water from the jars in the center.
Furthermore, one should worship the Vidyeśvaras all around in the first enclosure.
In the second [mandala], one should worship the Lokapālas; and in the third, Bhava and the others.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, on the ritual bathing, in the great tantra known as the Vātula.
(303) The forty-eightfold ablution.
The ritual bathing (snapana) will now be correctly described for the eight, four, and six-faced [deities]. There should be a twelfth thread in the east, and likewise a thread in the north.
The central nine-square grid is to be grasped; it is proclaimed as having eight gates.
A wise person should abandon the specific corners corresponding to the number of planets in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
From Indra to Īśāna, one should place [the pitchers] at each point according to the number five;
however, in the center, one should place the Śiva-pitcher, and eight pitchers around it.
In this very manner, in this very sequence, the wise Guha should install [the image],
whether it be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
An earthen vessel, however, is auspicious when it is free from cracks;
one should know that a dark mark portends quarrels, while a crack forebodes the destruction of the family.
A hollow sound portends the destruction of the kingdom; for that reason, it brings about the ruin of the king.
A crackling sound causes a rupture, while a low, muffled sound gives rise to disease.
A burnt cloth brings about the destruction of one's children, while an old one brings about the destruction of one's wife;
therefore, one should avoid these defects with every effort.
The width should be three finger-breadths and the depth eleven finger-breadths;
the mouth should be known as four finger-breadths, and the length of the neck likewise ends at that.
The lip should be known to be one finger-breadth [in height] and half a finger-breadth in projection;
it is adorned with eight lines on the neck and resembles a ripe bimba fruit.
This is declared to be the Śivakumbha; now hear of another, which arises from the front, back, and mouth of the jars' own forms.

In the *tantras*, the blood-born [beings] are classified as male, female, and neuter, according to the distinctions of their birth. Furthermore, the final category is conceptualized as those born from eggs, moisture, and so forth.
Then one should fashion the Brahma, Daivika, Mānuṣya, and Paiśāca [forms],
with the final and intermediate syllables accompanied by the sound of a bell.
Thus endowed with these characteristics, accompanied by divine vessels, it may be white, red, or mixed; it may be cracked or possess the resonance of a bronze bell.
The Brahma-vases are joined with the word "pūrva" (east) and are endowed with the colors black,
red, white, and smoke-colored.
In every direction there were seven distinct human jars,
endowed with all colors yet adorned by a single color.
The *paiśāca* [language] is known to be associated with the word *mṛttikā* (clay) and the word *kalaśa* (jar);
for women, it is *bukodara*, while the masculine form is *vāk* and the neuter is *bṛhat*.
The root, the tip, and that which is even, as well as the colors, men, and jars—these they call "facing Bṛhaspati"; the end of the hair is called the mouth.

They say that one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpaka*) is the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and the feet; the elements (*bhūtasthā*) are said to be the back, and the flower garland (*puṣpamālā*) is the two arms.
(146a) Teeth, cloth, flowers, water, life itself, the elephant-treasure, veins, threads, and likewise that which is made of clay.
The jar for Śiva has been described; now hear about the jar for Śakti. The *vardhanī* for the Virāsana, however, has an extent of nine finger-breadths at its opening.
The height of that [face] should be four fingers; the chest should be one finger;
the lip should be two fingers; and on the sides, it should be joined with the nose.
One should fashion it in the shape of a blue lotus with a measurement of one and a half finger-breadths;
the neck is three half-finger-breadths, and its projection is one finger-breadth.
The characteristics of the *vardhanī* have been declared; now listen to those of the *kalaśas*.
Its width is eleven fingers (*rudrāṅgula*) and its height is seven fingers (*parvatāṅgula*).
The height of the neck is three and a half finger-breadths, while the chin is indeed equal [to that];
the width of the jaw is one finger-breadth, and the protrusion of the lips is a barley-corn.
They know it to be stainless, pure, and liquefied by the sound of *kaṃsa*;
it is completely filled with three *prasthas* of Veda, fire, and eyes, respectively.
Among the superior, middling, and inferior [vessels], one is suitable for the ritual bathing of the jar;
however, the Śiva-jar (śivakumbha) must be four times the size of all the other jars.
The *śaktikumbha* should be twice the size of the *kalaśa*.
It should be filled with conch shells, or with mother-of-pearl, or with the tips of cow horns;
it should be filled with conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and horn-tips according to their own respective proportions.
Sugar, sandalwood, iron, a granary, a water-jar, and flowers.
Patra, karpūra, nīvāra, danta, māṃsī, mura, and nṛṇa; śamī, dūrvā, śuklārka, bilva, ambaka, and śaṅkhinī.
Then [he should offer] apāmārga, viṣṇukrānti, and that which is known as dhūrta,
along with nandyāvarta and asitābja— forty-nine [offerings] in total.
O Six-faced One, having worshipped the deities according to the sequence of the array, listen:
having first sacrificed to the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), one should worship them with their respective names.
The wise practitioner should worship [the deities] from Indra to Īśāna in the central jar;
in the remaining jars, one should likewise worship with the Haṃsa mantra.
Out of affection for you, I shall declare this other [instruction]:
first there should be the east-west line (prāksūtra) and the north-south line (udaksūtra).
One should especially have seven Paritassat-sūtras made;
one should place four in the first enclosure and eight in the second.
In the third layer, Bhānu [is placed], and in the fourth, the twenty-four;
the wise one should cause the previously mentioned materials and deities to be arranged.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, the Bathing Rite, in the great tantra known as the Vātula.
The ritual procedure for the sixty-fourfold ablution.
The consecration bath shall consist of sixty-four [substances]; this will now be described.
One should lay out twelve lines toward the east and likewise twelve lines toward the north.
One should take the nine squares in the center and discard the sixteen surrounding them;
one should proceed by leaving a margin of three squares on all sides, starting from the cardinal directions.
In the first enclosure there are eight, and likewise twenty in the second;
thirty-six in the third, while sixty-four are proclaimed [for the fourth].
And red [flowers], the red mandāra, palāśa, as well as pāṭalī,
the red lotus, bṛhatī, aśoka, and piṇḍika.
Having placed [the deities] in the first enclosure, then in the second enclosure,
[one places] Cambaka, Karṇikāra, and likewise Aśvattha.
One should collect a black-colored basket and *viṣṇukrānti* [plant];
having placed them in the second enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), it is now described for the third.
Tulasī, Bilva, Badarī, Mācī, Bhṛṅga, Madhu, Dhūpa, Śamī, Karavīra, Sindhuvāra, and Gaṇḍīrī.
Aśmānta, apāmārga, and likewise ārjuna and ḍaḍimi;
kapittha for warding off [evil], and nīlā as well as śaṅkhinī.
Girikarṇī, the two types of Sahadevī, Tapasvinī, Haridrā, Arjuna, and Mayūra, as well as Śrīkṛṣṇatulasī.
The Nandyāvarta, the Śriyāvarta, the Mallikā, and likewise the Mādhavī;
the Jambū, the Cūta, and the Śamī, as well as the divine Amaruva.
And Damanā should gradually place these leaves upon Śiva and Gaurī, or else upon the two pitchers, following that same sequence.
And in the first enclosure, one should place the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyā-īśvaras), beginning with Vaikartana and Vivasvat; beyond that, all fears [are dispelled].
Mārtāṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi, and likewise Rudra;
and those named Pāśa and Ugra, as well as Lokabhāsa.
Lokasākṣin, Ananta, Mahān, Bhīma,
Trivikrama, Āditya, Sūrya, and Aṃśumān.
Likewise, one should place Divākara and Aiśāna in the second enclosure,
as well as Varada, Vīrabhadra, Vimala, and Viśvagocara.
The one who has reached the end of the Vedas, primordial bliss, the Supreme Lord, the great splendor,
the broad-chested one, the great goal, the pure abode of birth.
He has three eyes, is like the mind, holds a chisel in his hand, has arrived as the Great One,
holds a trident in his hand, possesses great energy, and has the form of Mahābhairava.
Hara, who has fangs and is invincible, who possesses a necklace and prosperity,
who wields the thunderbolt, who holds the staff, who is established upon the earth, and who wears a tiger skin.
The impurity of the anus, characterized by all [other] marks,
and likewise the three unbearable forms of gods and humans.
In the third enclosure, one should worship Gaṇeśa, Sureśa— who wears a serpent as a sacred thread— and Durgā, the protectress of the divine armies.
Thus ends the chapter on the sixty-four ablutions in the great tantra known as the Vātula.
p. 310) The twenty-sevenfold ablution.
Seventy-two jars;
indeed, seventy-two jars shall be described for the bathing of Guha.
[The pit] should be three cubits, five cubits, or likewise six, seven, eight, or nine cubits.
Then one should have a pavilion constructed that is eleven cubits, or thirteen cubits,
or fifteen cubits in size.
The *prāgupta* [mantra] consists of nine divisions, with the sages, the moon, and other deities;
it is joined with Agastya and endowed with the *jagatī* meter.
The triad of highest [metres] is said to be joined with Āditya;
that which is joined with Vasiṣṭha is called the Śaṅkarī metre.
The middle triad is said to be joined with Vighneśa;
it is joined with Vyāsa himself and endowed with the Anuṣṭubh meter.
The triad of the youngest [Vedas] is said to be joined with Skanda alone;
out of affection for you, the seers, the meters, and the deities have been revealed.
(148a) First, there should be the east-west line and likewise the north-south line;
the wise one should take the central nine-square area and place the auspicious water-pot (*śivakumbha*) therein.
Outside the sixteen [petals], one should arrange eight gates;
Indra and the others are proclaimed to be in the four directions, with a number equal to that of the planets.
One should install five water-jars in the corners according to the prescribed rite; all remaining squares should be discarded by means of cow-dung water.
Sprinkle the substances with water from two jars; now hear about the goddesses:
*tatkola*, *bhasmaniryāsa*, *harivera*, and *mañcari*.
The coconut, the wood-apple, the rose-apple, the kaccola, the pāṭali,
the punnāga, the śaṅkhapuṣpa, as well as the lakṣmī and the vyāghranakhī.
One should designate Siṃhī and the one known as Dhūdhūra as the sixteenth;
having assigned them in the four directions of the first enclosure, it is now further explained.
Dūrvā grass, mustard seeds, and Abhra; Nāraṅga and Panasa are considered [auspicious]; as well as Kadalī, Śatapatra, Dhātakī, and white Lobhṛva.
One should place the materials enumerated in the Gṛhya-sūtras in the eastern direction:
*yukṣusāra*, *lābjā*, *cambaka*, and scented oil.
One should place these nine substances— nīvāra rice, saffron, kuṣṭha, lāsī, and two types of mouth-flour— in the direction of Yama (the south).
Mudga beans, māṣa beans, and *cimba*; barley, bamboo, and *priyaṅgu*; mustard, rice, and *aḍaka*—these are [to be used] when they are fresh.
Having cast it in the western direction, it is said to be in the northern direction as well:
cardamom, cloves, kaccola, turdi, and likewise water-barley.
Kuṣṭha and saffron, [along with] guggulu, mārga, and uraṅgula—
these five substances should be placed as far as the boundary of the day.
One should place siṃhī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, apāmārga, dravallikā,
kṣudraparṇī, and tapasvinī in the northeastern direction.
One should place all these [mantras] in the cardinal directions starting from the east;
it is proclaimed that [the deity] has two arms, extends as far as the neck, and begins with the water for the feet (pādya) and ends with the final offerings.

One, two, three, or four *prasthas* of honey and the other ingredients are prescribed, as well as those named after the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth; likewise, it is taught that they may be one-quarter or even one-half [of the standard measure].
The quantity of clarified butter is proclaimed to be equal to that of oil; likewise, the desired measure for camphor, saffron, and other such substances has been proclaimed.
O Six-faced One, gems are praised when they are of their own standard measure;
however, iron measures are calculated by increasing [the base] tenfold and so forth.
There should be a standard measure for metals as well as for stones;
however, the measure for seeds begins with a fraction of a niṣka and increases up to the size of a fruit.
This should be the measure for rice and likewise for black sesame;
or according to the measure of fruits, one should honor the remainder with water.
The quantity of oil should be like that of the clarified butter, or it may be the full measure of the vessel;
or half of that, or even half of that again—this shall be the "flower-in-hand" portion.
An herb of equal potency has been declared; others are likewise desired.
In one devoid of honor, it brings poverty and destroys the power of the eyes.
Therefore, with every effort, one should employ the measure within the measure; for among all jewels, the diamond is considered supreme, and among metals, iron is so regarded.
Among all seeds and minerals, yellow orpiment is the best;
and in the absence of medicinal herbs, one should employ the *sahadevī*, the *śrīphala*, and the lotus.
To the one of golden luster, possessing great splendor, being bathed by the two elephants with their trunks—
Oṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī.
In the northeastern direction, having worshipped the seven gurus, one should worship Sadāśiva, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Ambikā; then,
while remembering the house, Kṛṣṇa, and Dhātṛ, one should worship the seven gurus.
The Lord, pure as a jasmine flower or the moon, whose body consists of the five Brahmans,
who possesses ten arms and a gracious countenance, is Sadāśiva with five faces. *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Guru Sadāśiva.*
The Lord should be meditated upon as having eight arms, four faces, and three eyes, with the luster of crystal,
wearing a serpent as his sacred thread, and holding the goddess Vighnī.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the infinite Guru.
Five-faced, fifteen-eyed, ten-armed, and terrifying;
though mounted upon a bull, he wears the sacred thread, and Rudra is as radiant as a jasmine flower or the moon.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Guru Śrīkaṇṭha.
Red in color, adorned with a blazing white garment,
and endowed with all ornaments; [he beholds her] whose thighs and hips are full—
Oṃ hām, salutation to the Guru of Ambikā.
Abounding in three eyes and fragrant flowers, adorned with locks of hair,
the goddess holds a lotus and a water-lily, her hands granting boons and fearlessness.
Oṃ hām, homage to the Guru Ambikā.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Skandaguru.
Six-faced and twelve-eared, he is encircled by six crowns;
he has a reddish luster, twelve eyes, and is endowed with twelve hands.
In his right hands, he holds a sword with its scabbard, a discus, a noose, a goad,
a banner, a shield, a bow, and a vajra.
Holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, adorned with red garlands and unguents;
Oṃ, salutation to Skandaguru.
One should meditate upon the Lord Hari, who is dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments, bearing the conch and the discus,
accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, and adorned with all ornaments.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Guru Viṣṇu.
The god with four faces and four arms, holding a water-pot and a sacred thread,
accompanied by Sāvitrī and adorned with all ornaments.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Guru who is Brahmā.
One should worship the gurus, who set all knowledge in motion, like Śiva;
then, having received permission, the practitioner of mantra should perform sacrifice as prescribed in the scriptures of Śiva.
Having offered the *arghya*, [he says]:
"Homage be to the Guru-Nātha for the sake of favoring the worlds;
O Lord, grant me permission for the performance of the worship of Śiva."
Having adorned her with garments, perfumes, ornaments, and so forth, one should then [place her] on the northern part of the pedestal—
[thereby visualizing her] seated upon the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā), with a body as white as the ocean of milk,
bearing the form of a sprout from a seed upon her head, and bestowing boons and fearlessness.
To the Śakti Kriyā, who holds a noose and a goad, and whose form is the Foundation (Ādhāra):
Oṃ hām, salutation to Ādhāraśakti.
Therefore, one should worship [the deity] seated upon the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā), mounted on the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā), whose mind is blissful Śiva;
who is the bulbous root of the earth (pṛthvīkanda), whose single stalk extends to the end of the creative power (kalā), and whose thorns are the contemplative beings (bhāvaka).
The agitated Māyā, possessing great progeny and joined with many parts,
pervaded the white Lord and went toward that region in its midst.
With their manes appearing variegated and looking at one another from behind,
they serve as the sandals for Śiva’s seat in the forms of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages.
Dharma-knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty follow in due order;
therein, Dharma has the form of a bull, and knowledge has the nature of a lion.
Detachment should be worshipped as the father, and sovereignty as the white elephant;
one should worship camphor, saffron, gold, and substances with the luster of collyrium.
Oṃ hām, homage to Ananta.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Takṣaka!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Cā(vā)suki!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kārkoṭaka!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Padma.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahāpadma.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Śaṅkha.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gulikā.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the one seated upon the Kṛtayuga. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the one seated upon the Tretāyuga.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the one seated on the throne of the Dvāpara Yuga! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the one seated on the throne of the Kali Yuga!
(150B) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dharma!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Knowledge. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dispassion.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to [Power].
Those on his limbs were like crystal, possessing three eyes and lion-heads;
their arms, heads, and necks were stiff, and their heads were fixed upon their sandals.
[One should worship] those in human form with their upper bodies, feet, weapons, and heads [as follows]:
Oṃ hām, obeisance to Adharma;
Oṃ hām, obeisance to Ajñāna.
Oṃ hām, homage to non-detachment (avairāgya).
Oṃ hām, homage to lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya). In the southwest—to the one who contains Akṣubdha and Māyāntaka within himself.
Oṃ hām, homage to the lower sandalwood tree. In the northeast: homage to the upper sandalwood tree, which contains within it the essence of pure ignorance.
One should worship a white eight-petaled lotus, which is itself an infinite lotus; then, above the row of lions, one should display the lotus mudrā.
The bulb is like a ruby, the stalk has a luster equal to sapphire,
the thorn has the hue of coral, and the petal indeed has the brilliance of silver.
Having worshipped the petals as the eight forms of the Vidyeśvaras,
one should contemplate the filaments as having the luster of gold and adorned at their tips with strings of pearls.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the bulb (kanda).
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the stalk (nāla).
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the seed (bīja).
Oṃ hām, homage to the sprout.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the buds.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the petals.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the filaments! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the pericarp!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the great lotus!
From the east to the northeast—
(151a)— all [the goddesses] are equal to ten million suns, adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon;
they have four arms and three eyes, and hold chowries in their hands.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, their lotus-hands resting upon Śiva—
having thus visualized them in the filaments from the east to the northeast—
the presiding deities of the Vidyeśvaras, beginning with Vāmā and Jyeṣṭhā, are to be worshipped in sequence.
One should worship the eight Śaktis and display the mudrā of salutation (namas).
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāmā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jyeṣṭhā.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Raudrī.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kālī.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Balavikaraṇī.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Balapramadanyā! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sarvabhūtadamanyā!
Having thus worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ," [one should worship] in the northeast petal... o.
She has the luster of the rising sun, possesses three eyes and four arms,
is adorned with a crown of matted hair and a crescent moon, and holds a chowrie.

One should meditate upon Manonmanī at the pericarp, who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in her lotus-hands, whose lotus-hand is joined with that of Śiva, and who is as white as cow’s milk.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Manonmanī.
On the circle at the tip of the third petal, outside the enclosure: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the solar orb (sūryamaṇḍala).

Brahmā has four faces and is yellow; he is adorned with four staff-like arms, equipped with a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), a staff, and *akṣa*-berries and *kuśa* grass, and he stands in the center of a solar disc.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc.
On the circle at the tips of the filaments: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc.
Viṣṇu has four arms, wears a crown, and holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus;
he has the luster of a blue lotus stalk and stands in the midst of the lunar orb.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar maṇḍala.
On the circumference at the tip of the pericarp: *oṃ hām agnimaṇḍalāya namaḥ*.
(p. 319) [One should meditate on] Rudra, who is situated in the center of the fire, blue-throated and three-eyed.
He whose fire is the mudrā of exposition, who possesses the knowledge of the trident, and has four arms.
Adorned with all ornaments and wearing a sacred thread made of mountain-silk,
obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the circle of fire.
In the center of the pericarp—
seated upon the mandala of Śakti, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
with the moon as his crest-jewel, three-eyed, and pure like clear crystal.
The god holds a sword, a trident, an arrow, and a rosary in his hands, while displaying the gesture of fearlessness; he carries a water-pot and bears an excellent lotus.
[He is] adorned with a lion and elephant skin, according to the sequence of the lords of the [eight] directions. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Īśvara, the sovereign of the Śakti-maṇḍala.
In the middle of that:
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva (śivāsana).
(152a) For the Linga: Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva.
Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to the head of Yōśāna; thus on the head.
Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to the face of Tatpuruṣa; thus on the face. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the heart of Aghora; thus on the heart.
Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to the secret Vāmadeva; thus at the secret place. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Sadyojāta; thus at the foot.
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the heart, the body of knowledge; thus at the heart.
Having performed the placement of the eyes with "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the eyes," one should recite:
"Oṃ aṃ, obeisance; Oṃ āṃ, obeisance."
Oṃ iṃ namaḥ | Oṃ īṃ namaḥ | Oṃ uṃ namaḥ |
Oṃ ūṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ṛṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ṝṃ namaḥ |
Oṃ ḷn namaḥ | Oṃ ḹn namaḥ | Oṃ eṃ namaḥ |
Oṃ aiṃ namaḥ | Oṃ oṃ namaḥ | Oṃ auṃ namaḥ |
Oṃ aṃ namaḥ | Oṃ aḥ namaḥ | Oṃ kaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ khaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ gaṃ namaḥ |
Oṃ ghaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ṅaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ caṃ namaḥ | Oṃ chaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ jaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ jhaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ñaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ṭaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ṭhaṃ namaḥ |
Oṃ ḍaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ḍhaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ṇaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ taṃ namaḥ | Oṃ thaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ daṃ namaḥ | Oṃ dhaṃ namaḥ | (Oṃ naṃ namaḥ) | Oṃ paṃ namaḥ |
Oṃ phaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ baṃ namaḥ | Oṃ bhaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ maṃ namaḥ | Oṃ yaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ raṃ namaḥ | Oṃ laṃ namaḥ | Oṃ vaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ śaṃ namaḥ |
(152B) Oṃ ṣaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ saṃ namaḥ | Oṃ haṃ namaḥ | Oṃ laṃ namaḥ | Oṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ hoṃ, homage to Īśāna, the lord of all vidyās, to Śaśinī!
(As stated on p.
321: "Oṃ Hoṃ, the Lord of all beings—salutation to Aṅgadā. Thus, [one should worship] on the eastern head.
Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Brahmādhipati, the lord of Brahmā, who is presided over by Brahmā;
thus on the right head.
Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Marīci, may there be auspiciousness.
Thus, on the eastern head:
*oṃ hoṃ sadāśivoṃ jvālinyai namaḥ*.
Thus, on the western head.
Thus is the pentad of the kalās of Īśāna.
Oṃ heṃ, we know that Tatpuruṣa; salutation to Śānti. At the eastern face.
Oṃ heṃ, we meditate upon Mahādeva; salutation to Vidyā. At the southern face.
Oṃ hoṃ, may Rudra be established for us; salutation to Pratiṣṭhā. At the northern face.
Oṃ heṃ pracodayāt, obeisance to Nivṛtti; [this is] on the western face.
Thus are the four kalās of Puruṣa.
Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Aghorā and Tamā; at the heart. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Aghorā and Mohā; at the throat. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Aghora-rakṣā; on the right shoulder.
(153a) Oṃ hūṃ, homage to the most non-terrible and to the ultimate state; on the left shoulder. Oṃ hūṃ, homage to all-encompassing death; at the navel.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to all and to illusion; in the belly.
Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to you, O Rudrabhayā; obeisance! [To her] on the back. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the forms, O Jarā; [obeisance! on the chest.
Thus is the eightfold group of the many-formed arts (bahurūpakalāṣṭaka).
Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva, obeisance to Rajā; at the secret place (guhya).
Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā, obeisance to Rakṣā; at the two testicles (vṛṣaṇa). Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Rudra, obeisance to Rati; on the right thigh.
Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Kāla, salutation to Pālinī; *vama* on the thighs.
Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Kalakāmā; on the right knee. Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Vikaraṇa, salutation to Saṃyāminī; on the left knee.
Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Balakriyā; on the right shank.
Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Vikaraṇa, salutation to Buddhi; on the left shank. Oṃ, salutation to Balakārī; on the right buttock.
Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Pramathana, obeisance to Dhātrī—at the left hip.
Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Sarvabhūtadamana, obeisance to Brahmaṇī—at the waist. Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to Manomohinī—at the right side.
Oṃ hīṃ nonmanyai [name of deity]... on the left side.
(153B) Thus are the thirteen kalās of Vāmadeva.
Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation to Siddhi. On the right side.
Sadyojātāya vai namaḥ; salutation to Ṛddhi. On the left foot. Oṃ hāṃ, to Bhava and Utpatti; salutation. In the belly.
Oṃ hāṃ abhave lakṣmyai namaḥ | At the left ear. Oṃ hāṃ anādibhave medhāyai namaḥ | At the nostril. Oṃ hāṃ bhajasva māṃ kāntyai namaḥ | On the head.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhavasvadhā; on the right arm. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Udbhava and Dhṛti; on the left arm.
Thus ends the eightfold division of Sadyojāta.
Meditation:
[One should meditate on Him] seated upon a lotus posture, five-faced, with three eyes in each face,
large-eyed, possessing both the powers of action and grace, and endowed with the digit of the moon of knowledge.
The face of the Lord of Dhavala is white;
the Tatpuruṣa face is yellow; it is endowed with the black Aghora face, and its northern face has a reddish luster.
The one facing west is proclaimed as Sadyojāta, who is very white,
wears a serpent as a sacred thread, is peaceful, and is adorned with matted locks and a crescent moon.
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial garlands;
his lotus-like hands were busily occupied with a spear, a sword, a trident, and a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga).
(154a) You two are on my right or left, bestowing all desires.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Aghora!
The left [face] has the luster of red and deep red, and wears a garland, garments, and a sacred thread.
With a prominent nose and a red turban, holding a sword and a shield in his hands.
Oṃ heṃ, homage to the secret Vāmadeva.
Richly adorned with white garlands, perfumes, and ornaments, wearing a cool turban and white garments, he is gentle, crowned by the moon upon his head, youthful in form, and possesses three eyes.
Sadyojāta has one white face and displays the gestures of granting boons, holding a lotus, and appearing awe-inspiring.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta.
One should display the cow, the path, the trident, the sword known as *kasṛgakā*, and the *sṛva* mudrā for Īśāna and the other [deities].
One should contemplate the eye of the All-pervading Lord as being ruddy in hue, consisting of the powers of sight and action.
The form of Trita is a forest-circle (vanya-maṇḍala) surrounded by three [circles],
with the faces of the limbs beginning with the heart protruding, and joined with the hand-held implements and so forth.
Or, according to the teaching of Śiva, one may have a single face, with a trident and a serpent in hand;
his heart is like the moon, and his head has the luster of gold.
(325) His crest is rich with the color of vermilion; his armor shines like a bumblebee;
his eye resembles lightning; his weapon is fire...
[seated upon his own seat]... wearing a crown of matted hair marked by the crescent moon.
[He visualizes] three-eyed [deities] with four arms, adorned with all ornaments, facing Śiva, and holding a spear, a trident, and the gesture of fearlessness in their hands.
(154B) Having meditated thus: "In the hand [is] a weapon with a brilliance equal to fire," one should say:
"Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the eyes, on the northern part of Īśāna."
In the southeast, to the heart: *namaḥ*; in the northeast, *oṃ hīṃ*, to the head: *namaḥ*.
In the southwest (Nairṛti): Oṃ hūṃ [vajra]phaṭ namaḥ.
Oṃ haiṃ kavacāya namaḥ.
In the northern part of the northeast (Īśāna): Oṃ hauṃ netrebhyo namaḥ.

Having worshipped in the four directions with "Oṃ haḥ, obeisance to the Weapon (astra)," one should display the gesture of salutation (*namaskāramudrā*) for the limbs. (Having worshipped the power (*śakti*) of the heart and the other limbs in their respective locations: "Oṃ hām, obeisance to Ambikā."
Oṃ hām, obeisance to Gaṇāmbikā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaurī. Oṃ hām, obeisance to Umā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāminī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Cakrāṅgī. This is the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa).
Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. Oṃ hom, obeisance to Ambikā.
Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa. Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Gaṇāmbikā.
Oṃ hūm, obeisance to Aghora. Oṃ hūṃ (haṃ), obeisance to Gaṅgā.
Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva. Oṃ hīṃ (hiṃ), salutation to Gaurī.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta. Oṃ hām, salutation to Umā.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Heart. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāmā.
Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to the head. Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to Nīlī.
