Oṃ haiṃ, salutation to the armor (kavaca). Oṃ haiṃ, salutation to Pāśāṅgī.
Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the eyes. Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Khaṭvāṅgī.
Oṃ haḥ, salutation to the weapon (astra). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaulikā.
In the second enclosure, to the east is Ananta, resembling gold in color.
I salute that subtle [form] residing within the portion of fire, which possesses a radiance equal to fire.
I salute Śivottama, who resembles the tamāla tree, located in the southern quarter; and in the southwest, I salute Ekanetra, who dwells together with Śrī and appears like a bee.
In the western quarter, one should resort to a form that is white like a jasmine flower or the moon and has a single face;
in the northern quarter, one should take refuge in a form resembling frost, which possesses three bodies.
I take refuge in Śrīkaṇṭha, who stands like one of red color in the northern direction;
and in the northeast, I take refuge in Rudra, who has a pale-white form, and in the east, Śikhaṇḍin.
I bow to the Lord who resides in the four cardinal directions beginning with the East, as well as in the intermediate directions, appearing like the syllables of his own name.
Or rather, I praise the Lord who is the source of all, resembling the syllables of his own name.
With his right hands, he holds a sword, an arrow, a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a lotus; with his left hands,
a shield, a bow, and so forth...
Those Vidyeśvaras who were supported by the Lord from the four-faced one, facing him, endowed with three eyes, seated upon beautiful thrones,
and holding [the world]— [they were seen].
(155B) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhūmidevī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Svāhādevī.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Svadhādevī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kāntidevī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Prabhādevī.
Oṃ hām, obeisance to Ananta. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sūkṣma.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sūkṣma; obeisance to Śivottama. Oṃ hām, obeisance to Ekarudra.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Trimūrti. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śikhaṇḍin. [In] the third enclosure.
Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgī, Gaṇapati, Vṛṣabha, Kārttikeya, Pārvatī, and Caṇḍanāyaka.
Nandīśa has four arms and three eyes, is dark-complexioned,
endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, and is fierce, bearing a staff and a trident.
Oṃ hāṃ, [homage] to Nandin. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhadrā.
Mahākāla has three eyes, is black in color, and possesses four arms; he is endowed with two gestures of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*) and holds a trident and a lance (*tomara*).
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahākāla. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Devayoni.
[He visualizes] Bhṛṅgīśa, who has four arms and three eyes, with a tawny complexion;
in his right hands he holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and a battle-axe (ṭaṅka), while in his left hands he holds the boon-granting gesture (varada) and a trident (śūla).
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhṛṅgin. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kuntī.
[One should meditate on] Gajānana, who has three eyes, the luster of saffron, and four arms;
he holds a noose and a tusk in his right hands, while in his left hands he holds a goad and a *laḍḍuka* sweetmeat.
(156a) [He sees] Gaṇādhipa, who has a serpent as his sacred thread and protruding lips.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gaṇapati! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kālī!
— Previously, all were red and dead.
The eye consists of white and black, and the two horns are red in color.
The two ears have a reddish hue and are adorned with a yellowish-green [garland];
there is a broken garland with a golden luster, either placed or worn.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vṛṣabha. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mantriṇī.
[Mahāsena] is clad in red garments, has two eyes and four arms;
in his right hands he holds the gesture of fearlessness and the vajra, while in his left hands he holds the boon-granting gesture and the goad.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Skanda. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mālinī. (p. 329) ... O Cāriṇī!
[The vital winds] Prāṇa, Apāna, as well as Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna.
One should likewise protect the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as Nārāyaṇī;
O Vārāhī, protect my life, and may Yoginī protect my dharma.
May Vaiṣṇavī protect my fame, renown, and fortune;
may Indrāṇī protect my lineage, and may Caṇḍikā protect me in the highest way.
O Mahālakṣmī, protect my sons; O Vaiṣṇavī, protect my wife;
may Kṣetrakarī protect me on the road, and may the ever-auspicious Vijayā protect me at all times.
Whatever place is devoid of protection and lacking the armor,
O Goddess Jayantī, destroyer of sins, protect all of that for me.
Having donned this armor fashioned by Brahmā for the Goddess,
a man shall not take even a single step further if he desires to attain perfection.
Wherever one who is constantly protected by the armor goes,
there he shall obtain wealth and victory at all times.
Whatever desirable object one contemplates, that very thing one obtains with ease;
a person attains incomparable, supreme sovereignty upon this earth.
The mortal becomes fearless and remains unconquered in battles;
he shall live for a hundred excellent years, his merit increased and his untimely death destroyed.
All diseases— scorpions, boils, and the like— as well as poison, whether of stationary origin, mobile origin, or artificial, are destroyed.

(330) All the *kumbhīra* [demons], as well as all the mantras and *yantras* on the surface of the earth— whether they move on the ground or in the sky, those born of the *kula*, or even the *ādeśika*— [are subdued].
(B) Yaśasvinī is in the middle of the eyebrows;
Citrakhaṇḍā is in the eyes; and Śaṅkhinī is in the palate.
Śaṅhinī protects the space between the eyes; Vindhyavāsī protects the two ears; Kāmākṣī protects the chin; and Sarvamaṅgalā protects speech.
May Bhadrakālī protect my neck, and Dhanurdharā my back;
may Nīlagrīvā protect the exterior of my throat, and Nalakūbarā my nose.
May Khaḍgadhāriṇī protect both my arms, Vaṃtridhāriṇī my three [limbs],
Daṇḍinī my hands, and Guhyeśvarī likewise my private parts.
May Durgā protect my anus, and likewise Bhagatī my hips;
may Medhā, the leader of devotees and the bearer of the ram, protect my thighs.
Mahābalā is said to be on the two knees, Vināyaka on the two shanks,
Nārasiṃhī on the two ankles, and Dvitaunasa on the back of the feet.
Śrīrakṣā dwells on the toes of the feet, while Pādakṛtsthala-vāsinī dwells on the soles of the feet; Daṃṣṭrākarālā dwells on the nails, and Muktakeśinī dwells on the body hair.
Vāṇī [took] the body hairs; Kauberī the skin; Vāgīśvarī the blood, marrow, and flesh; and Pārvatī the bones and fat.
Antrāṇī and Kālarātrī, Meḍhra and Makuleśvarī,
Padmāvatī and Padmakeśī, as well as Kumbha and Cūḍāmaṇi.
Likewise, Jvālāmukhī and Jvālāmabhedā at all the joints;
O Brahmāṇī, protect me—white in color—and likewise Chāyā and Chatreśvarī.

"I protect my ego, mind, and intellect; may Bhairava protect me even when dead. One should first cause the offering of the eight Bhairavas to be given, as well as the destruction [of obstacles], the *vāstu-bali*, and the movement of the *bali* offerings.
One should perform the offering of bali at the western gate and at the liṅga in the western quarter.
Having circumambulated the boundary offering (antabali), the preceptor should cause it to be offered according to the prescribed rite;
having placed the offering for the deity of the southern gate, the preceptor [proceeds].
One should offer the *bali* at the doors starting from the south and ending with the fire (southeast);
one should perform the *bali* for the northern door and the *liṅga* with the northern (Saumya) direction.
From the east of the temple, one should perform [the rites] for Indra and the others up to Īśāna.
To the west of the Ālaya is the village; beginning with Vāruṇī, it extends toward the southwest.
To the south, he should cause the temple to be given, and to the north, the village itself;
from Soma to Vāyu, he should cause these to be bestowed according to the prescribed ritual.
In the north is the Ālaya, and in the south the village;
from the south up to the southeast, the bali offering is performed according to the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama).
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the offering at the four gates within the causal [mandala].
The Octad of Bhairavas.
I meditate upon Kālabhairava, who is accompanied by spirits and vetālas playing cymbals, who wears matted hair, and who is eternally great. || 1 ||
I meditate upon Kālabhairava, who wears a garland of skulls, whose eyes are like the fire that consumes the world,
and who is formidable with a skull in his hand.
I meditate upon Kālabhairava, who is described as having a hooded serpent as his staff, adorned with a girdle of tinkling bells, wearing earrings, and holding a skull-bowl and a trident.
I meditate upon Kālabhairava, whose lotus-feet rest upon jeweled pedestals, whose lotus-hands hold the great trident, and who has transferred the essence of sacred stories into his ears. 4.
I meditate upon Kālabhairava, who is sky-clad, the color of a hibiscus flower, free from old age and death, and adorned with a beautiful crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
I meditate upon Kālabhairava, who possesses the radiance of the sun and its light, whose locks of hair are dark and soft, and who is adorned with shimmering staffs and skull-bowls.
I meditate upon Kālabhairava, who is like a forest fire to the enemies of the gods, yet as cooling as a white water-lily to the gods; he is the unity of Śiva and Keśava.
I salute Kālabhairava, by whose command the entire world— both the stationary and the moving—
perpetually exists free from fear.
Whoever always recites this *Kālanādhāṣṭaka* with devotion shall indeed attain Kāśī, as well as Prayāga and Gayā.
Let there be a journey to Kāśī and a vision of Viśveśvara;
thereafter, let there be a return to one’s own country and the sight of kinsmen once more.
He bestows desired food at the proper time;
he holds a skull-bowl in his hand, wears earrings, carries a staff,
is dark blue like a fresh rain-cloud, and has a serpent as his sacred thread.
May Gharakanātha, who removes obstacles and breaks through impediments for those who have mastered the ritual conventions, be victorious through his accomplishment for the sake of the practitioners.
With locks of hair as soft as sapphire and a complexion as red as liquid lac,
his lotus-face possesses a smile that captivates the mind;
he bears a beautiful mass of matted locks adorned with auspicious *daṇḍaka* grass.
I pay homage to Mahāvaṭukanātha, the bestower of desired accomplishments.
Thus ends the Bhairava-stotra in its entirety.
(p. 335) Now follows the procedure for the removal of faded flower offerings (nirmālya-vidhi).
May there be auspiciousness!
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual for the *nirmālya*; listen.
*Caṇḍadravya* and *nirmālya* are thus proclaimed to be of six kinds.
He [should avoid] houses and other such things, as well as the property of the gods and so forth,
clothing, ornaments, scented oil, and flowers.
Sandalwood, pure food, and the remains of offerings are proclaimed [as appropriate];
now the worship of the Linga with the marks of the learned is specifically described.
The *nirmālya* offered to Him is superior even to food for the devotees of Śiva;
it bestows auspiciousness, brings about the withdrawal of the mind, increases longevity, and promotes strength.
The self, the *liṅga*, and the *nirmālya* are indeed described;
if the *liṅga* is human, it is undoubtedly the *nirmālya*.
The offering (nirmālya) is stainless, pure, and food for those of pure self;
however, it is not consumed by those whose bodies are bound by impurity.
Therefore, the food offering to Śiva is remembered as pure substance;
one who has been initiated by Śiva is called a Śiva-brāhmaṇa.
For the nature of Śiva is pure and beyond the reach of speech, mind, and other senses;
therefore, the twice-born Brāhmaṇa who [realizes] Śiva is called a pure Brāhmaṇa.
The remains of Śiva’s offerings are suitable for [the practitioner], but not at all suitable for others.
Having placed them in the custody of others, one should perform the duties pertaining to one's caste.
Upon touching [impure objects], however, one should wash the hands and feet, perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with water,
wash the hands used for touching, and perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
Having eaten out of negligence, one goes to hell for as long as the moon and sun endure; this applies whether eating in water, in the presence of a Pāśupata, on the ground, or even upon ashes.
Then, one should feed everyone after having offered the food-oblation to Vināyaka and the food-oblation to Goddess Umā.
The food offering and meal of Subrahmaṇya bring victory and prosperity;
however, the food offering of Bhāskara results in the destruction of sins and diseases.
Then, one should offer the food-offering (naivedya) along with its attendants and cause all to partake of it. Thus ends the procedure for the remains of the offering (nirmālya-vidhi).
At the end, heaven and liberation [are attained]; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Salutation to the illustrious Goddess.
The Armor of the Goddess.
"O Father, tell me that which is the supreme secret in the world, which provides protection for all men, and which has never been told to anyone."
Brahmā said:
O Brahmin, O high-minded one, listen to this most secret and meritorious armor (kavaca) of the Goddess, which brings benefit to all living beings.
This should be given to a devotee, and never to one who is not a devotee,
nor to an atheist, nor to the wicked, nor to the miser, O great sage.
The seer of the armor-mantra is proclaimed to be Brahmā; the meter is Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is Śrī Mahālakṣmī, the bestower of the fulfillment of all desired aims.
Being burned by fire, or situated in the midst of enemies in battle,
or even when trapped or in an impassable place, those terrified by fear have come for refuge.
Nothing inauspicious shall arise for them in the perils of battle;
nor do I perceive even the slightest trace of sorrow, suffering, or fear in them.
For those by whom she is constantly praised with devotion, prosperity arises;
for Cāmuṇḍī, Vārāhī, and Mahiṣāsanā abide among the spirits of the departed.
Māheśvarī is mounted upon a bull; Kaumārī has the peacock as her vehicle;
Aindrī is seated upon an elephant; and Vaiṣṇavī has Garuḍa as her seat. (O Goddess, [this is] the wrathful [form].)
Brahmā is mounted upon a swan, adorned with all ornaments,
enriched by the splendor of various jewels, and decorated with diverse gems.
(120B) O Goddess, they are seen mounted upon chariots, composed in their wrath,
bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, the spear, the trident, and the club as weapons.
The shield, the javelin, the axe, and the noose—
these were for the destruction of the bodies of the Daityas and for the granting of fearlessness to his devotees.
Having carried and brought [the jewel] through battle for the benefit of the gods,
it was adorned with sapphires and great sapphires of supreme luster.
And with auspicious, divine pearls, necklaces, anklets, and earrings— Oṃ,
salutations to you of great form and most terrible prowess!
O you of great strength, of great heroism, who utterly destroys great fear!
Protect me, O Goddess, from the evil gaze of enemies, O increaser of worldly existence!
May Mahendra protect me in the east, and the deity Agni in the southeast.
May Rakṣavārāhī protect in the south; Khaṭgadhāriṇī in the southwest;
Vāruṇī protect in the west; and Mṛgadhāriṇī in the northwest.
"Protect me in the north, O Kauberī; in the northeast, O Śūladhāriṇī! Protect me above, O Brahmāṇī, and likewise below, O Vaiṣṇavī!
Thus may Cāmuṇḍā, who carries a corpse, protect the ten directions."
May Jayā protect me from the front, and Vijayā protect me from behind; may Ajitā protect my left side and Aparājitā my right;
may Udyotakarī protect my topknot, and Umā, stationed upon my head.
One who wears a garland on the forehead shall obtain [the fruit]— (this concludes this leaf)— p. 340 (124a).
O Skanda, truth shall become a source of long life and devotion shall arise.
One should protect the crest, Kumāra, and likewise the head of Kārttikeya;
Viśākha the forehead of Pārvatī’s son, and likewise the pair of eyebrows.
Krauñcabhedinī is at the two eyes, Śikhivāhana is at the nose,
Śaktiyuktā is likewise at the two ears, and Ṣaḍānana is at the roots of the ears.
May the General protect both lips, may Tārakāpahā protect the tongue,
may Guha always protect the teeth, and likewise may Gāṅgeya protect the chin.
May Bhavodbhava protect the throat; may Śambhunandana protect the speech;
may Pārvatīnandana protect the neck, and likewise Agnibhū protect the outer throat.
May Bāhuleya protect the nose, and likewise Skanda, the son of the six mothers, the shoulders;
may Viśākha protect the pair of arms, and Vaṇik the hands.
May the younger brother of Vināyaka protect [my] fingers, he who is adorned with beautiful nails;
may Subrahmaṇya always protect my armpits, and may the slayer of the enemies of the gods protect my belly.
The Lord of the World should likewise know Vaigaṇḍa and protect his body;
he is a hero in battle at heart, yet his mind is restrained by compassion.
My belly is the vessel for the mind-wandering [deity], who is devoted solely to his devotees; he is the supreme wonder within the navel, the bestower who has chosen the womb.
May the Moon-bearer protect the private parts; may the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow protect the buttocks; may the Son of the Wind protect the thighs; and may those dear to Agni protect the knees.
May the Lord of Wealth protect my shanks; may the one of great strength protect my ankles and feet;
may the destroyer of sin protect my feet; and may he whose banner is a cock protect all my limbs.
May the crest-jewel of the gods protect the crown within the range of his lotus-eyes— [the crown] which is pure like well-offered marrow, fat, blood, skin, and brain.
May Mahāparākrama protect us; may Kapardin, the son of Śambhu, protect us;
may Śivānanda, the abode of treasures, who is served by sages such as Buddhi and others, protect us.
May the omniscient one with six faces always protect the vital breaths beginning with prāṇa up to the anus;
likewise may the Lord protect our fortune, fame, virtues, lineage, wife, and sons.
May she whose abode is the dissolution of ignorance protect [us], she who bestows fearlessness upon all the gods;
wherever there is a place that is empty for even a moment, it is devoid of armor.
They both constantly protected all that was within the sphere of youth;
by the recollection of this armor, there shall always be the attainment of desired objects.
It brings victory in battle and is the cause of triumph for all;
it destroys ghosts, spirits, and demons, as well as desolate places and evil deeds.
In the midst of all directions beginning with the east, the beloved of Śakti protects;
by reciting [the mantra] from "ā" through "śūnya" and so forth, one shall obtain the fruit of rites such as *abhicāra*.
Thus, whoever should constantly recite or even hear this armor of Skandaka,
having attained all fortunes, shall reach union with Śiva.
Thus ends the Skanda-kavaca in the Skanda Purāṇa.
To him whose pair of lotus-feet are worshipped by Vajra, Viriñca, Jaleśa, and others who precede them;
who is beneficial to the entire world, yet both one and many.
I praise Skandakumāra, the son of Umā. || 1 ||
I praise him whose crown is equal to a thousand suns, who possesses a mass of earrings as red as clusters of stars,
whose rows of eyes are like lotuses, and who has twelve arms and six faces.

I praise Skanda Kumāra, the son of Umā, whose teeth shine with a most radiant smile that surpasses the luster of the bimba-fruit lips; who utters the cry of a peacock, and whose neck is adorned with a beautiful, shimmering conch-shell ornament.
I praise Skanda Kumāra, the son of Umā, who bears a banner of peacock feathers with a row of creeper-like arms, who holds a mass of asura soldiers, and who possesses a powerful spear.

I praise the lord of the hosts of gods, the first-born, the worshipful one of most beautiful form, the son of Īśa, who rides upon a peacock with variegated plumage, who has twelve arms and six faces. (5)

I praise Skanda Kumāra, the son of Umā, who is the pacifier of Tāraka, whose nature is to destroy the demonic hosts by means of the Discus, Varuṇa, Kubera, and the Maruts, and who possesses the sharp edge of his spear.

The supreme swan (paramahaṃsa), who reads this hexad of Skanda-kumārakas with focused attention and unwearied diligence, attains the highest state of Śiva, in which all enemies are destroyed and all desires are fulfilled.
Salutations to Śrī Subrahmaṇya.
May there be auspiciousness!
Oṃ, to the one born in the forest of reeds, who holds a spear in his hand, whose banner is a cock, to Kumāra,
the twelve-syllabled one, the destroyer of all enemies, the performer of all protection— Oṃ, homage to Kumāra!
The Devī-kavaca (The Armor of the Goddess).

(122B) Oṃ. Of this great mantra, the *Śrī Devī Kavaca Stotra*, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chanda*), the illustrious Ambikā Mahālakṣmī is the deity (*devatā*), *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*),
*śrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), *hrauṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of liberation.
O Mahiṣimardini, salutation to the two thumbs;
O Cāmuṇḍi, salutation to the two index fingers;
O Vārāhi, salutation to the two middle fingers.
To Māheśvarī, salutation with both ring fingers;
to Indrāṇī, salutation with both little fingers;
to Dharmacāriṇī, salutation with both palms and backs of the hands.
Mahiṣimardini—hṛdayāya hūṃ!
Cāmuṇḍī—śirase svāhā!
Vārāhī—śikhāyai vauṣaṭ!
Māheśvarī—hūṃ, for the armor. Indrāṇī—vauṣaṭ, for the three eyes. Dharmavāriṇī—phaṭ, for the weapon.
*Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar om*—thus is the binding of the directions.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
O slayer of Mahiṣa, O Great Illusion, O Cāmuṇḍā, O wearer of a garland of severed heads!

O Brahmacāriṇī, grant, grant to me that which is desired and contemplated; O Mother, who exerted yourself in the effort of taking the life of Madhu, Kaiṭabha, and Mahiṣa; O you who effortlessly accomplished the slaying of Dhūmralocana; O destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa!
O Durgā, who has utterly destroyed the seed of the blood-drinking demons, who eternally slays Niṣumbha and destroys Sumbha—O Ambikā, salutations to you; destroy my evil deeds!
O crusher of the buffalo-demon,
you who possess the conch and discus and wield the arrow and trident; having saluted you,
the divine Yoginī, who is innate with the fire of primordial consciousness.
I always take refuge in Durgā.
(125) The Subrahmaṇyaka Armor.
Oṃ. Of this glorious Subrahmaṇya Mahāmantra, the Seer (ṛṣi) is Parabrahman; the Metre (chandas) is Devī Gāyatrī;
the Deity (devatā) is Śrī Subrahmaṇya; the Seed-syllable (bīja) is Sauṃ; the Power (śakti) is Śrīṃ; the Pin (kīlaka) is Klīṃ.
[This is employed] for the sake of attaining the grace of Subrahmaṇya and for the sake of one's desired objects.
The application (viniyoga) is for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, and for the propitiation of Śrī Subrahmaṇya during the recitation (japa):
Oṃ śrīṃ, to Skanda, born in the forest of reeds—salutation to the two thumbs. Oṃ klīṃ, to Sanatkumāra, born of the union of Rahu and Bha—salutation to the two index fingers.
Oṃ hrīṃ haṇabhavaśara ṣaṇmukhāya—to the middle fingers, *namaḥ*. Oṃ aiṃ sauṃ ṇabhavaśaraha senādhipataye—to the ring fingers, *namaḥ*.
Oṃ raṃ bhavaśarahaṇa subrahmaṇyāya—to the little fingers, *namaḥ*.
Oṃ naṃ laṃ vaśarahaṇabha śaktihastāya—salutation to the palms and backs of the hands.
Thus is the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ om"—thus is the binding of the directions (*dikbandha*).
Meditation (dhyāna):
[One should meditate upon the deity] red as vermilion, with a face as lovely as the moon, the body adorned with divine ornaments such as armlets and necklaces, and the bestower of heavenly bliss.
We worship Subrahmaṇya, who holds a lotus, a shield, a spear, and a cock; whose limbs are red and who blazes with a crimson luster; we bow down to him who is ever intent on destroying fear.
The instruction on *dhvani*: Oṃ Oṃ Aṃ Kṣaṃ Aṃ Kṣaṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Śaṃ Śāṃ Śiṃ Śīṃ Śuṃ Śūṃ Śeṃ.

To the hundred [deities] beginning with Pāpa, who share in the sacrificial post; to the hundred [deities] beginning with Pāva; to the hundred [deities] beginning with Skandha; to the Subrahmaṇyā; to the Rahas; homage to Kumāra! To you, O Lord Guha-hā, Svāhā!
The root mantra is:
Oṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ sauṃ raṃ naṃ laṃ śarahaṇa bhava ṣaṇmukhāya namaḥ.
May it be for you a source of great merit, bringing affection to all living beings;
by mere recitation, it destroys sin and bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
O Lord, this divine hymn of the lords of sages wards off all afflictions;
like the armor of Skanda, it destroys disease through its recitation.
It pacifies the affliction of fire, destroys the calamities caused by thieves,
and brings divine peace through mere remembrance of the Piśācas, Bhūtas, and diseases. This Skanda-kavaca, as it has been proclaimed, should be worn upon the heart by people.
For them, the misfortune of poverty shall never occur.
On earth, having attained imperial sovereignty, he shall finally obtain the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*)—
(from here onwards, on page 124a, it should be considered whether the word *māpnuyāt* [he shall obtain] that begins there is connected with this).

(bā) lā (pa) ñcagam (351 puṭe sthitasya śeṣo'yam) (108B) sakala hrīṃ mahātripurasundariṃ vai bhava svāhā || The remainder [of the mantra] residing on folio 351 is: (bā) lā (pa) ñcagam. (108B) [The mantra is: *sakala hrīṃ mahātripurasundariṃ vai bhava svāhā*.
Salutations to the glorious gurus.
O Lord of Ratnācala, whose hair is curly, who possesses the splendor of a forest fire, O Master, grant me your assistance!

O Āyī! O Ānandavallī! O you who hold the nectar in the palm of your hand! O Supreme Power (Parā Śakti)! O Māyī! O you whose very nature is Māyā! O you who are composed of crystal gems! O Māmataṅgī! O you who possess the six limbs (Ṣaḍaṅgī)! O Knower!
O you whose form is the meaning of knowledge! O you who possess the fragrance of the lotus! O you whose form is the syllable 𑆙 (Aṃ)!
O Yoginī, established in the yogic posture, the subduer of the worlds, the beautiful one; salutations to you, O Saum! || 1 ||

She who wears a garland of mantras, whose side-glances are my heart’s companion, who is fierce with the state of intoxication, who possesses a sacrificial thread of lightning, whose matted locks rest upon formidable peaks, who is the power of heroes and full of grace;
she who is youthful, whose crown is the young moon, who is consecrated by the trunks of intoxicated elephants, and who is independent.
O Kālī, whose form is a skeleton, who subdues the lord of birds (Garuḍa), the enemy of Ruruṇī; *klīṃ*, salutations to you! || 2 ||
The Great-Souled One residing in the Mūlādhāra, the friend of fire, the three-eyed one possessing the root-mantra, adorned with necklaces and armlets, the Mother who encompasses the entire universe,
the consort of Śiva; she who is the altar, the resonance of Vedānta, the shore of manifold wealth, the Vīra-tantrī, Bhavānī.
O Sārī, you who are the very form of saṃsāra, who consist of all virtues, O beautiful one, salutations to you! || 3 ||

Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauṃ! O Goddess of all, remover of every fear, you who bestow grace through the tradition; Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ! O foremost of seed-syllables, Himaki... (the remainder of this is on page 352, folio 108a): Aḥ! Kuṭilā, Māyā, Śākinī, and likewise Ḍākinī.
The mare moving through the intermediate space is the Dākinī and the Great Kalā.
Planets, spirits, and piśācas; yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas; brahmarākṣasas, vetālas, kūśmāṇḍas, bhairavas, and so forth.
They perish at the mere sight of him when this armor is established in his heart;
it produces loftiness of mind, serves as clarified butter for sacrifice, and is the supreme increaser of splendor.
Furthermore, the scholar on this earth increases in fame and renown;
indeed, a man protected by this armor shall be worthy of worship throughout the three worlds.
This divine armor, however, is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
he who, being self-restrained, should daily recite it at the three junctions of the day, shall be endowed with prosperity.
The Goddess shall become his power, and he shall be unconquered throughout the three worlds;
one should recite the *Saptaśatī* of Caṇḍī, having first performed the *kavaca*.
The accomplishment arising from the recitation of Caṇḍī shall be attained without obstacle,
having meditated upon the entire circle of the earth together with its mountains, forests, and groves.
For that long the lineage of the practitioner of recitation remains upon the earth;
and at the end of the body, he attains the supreme state which is difficult even for the gods to reach.
One attains that state until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus ends the complete Devī-kavaca.
Salutation to the Lord of Śrī Ratnācala.
The glorious root mantra of fifteen syllables.

Regarding the four gates:
(107a) in the east is Bhṛṅgin, and likewise in the southeast is Yoginī.
In the south is Bhṛṅgiṇī, and likewise Jambhinī in the southwest;
in the west is Śaṅkhinī, and likewise Mohinī in the northwest.
In the north is Siṃhamukhī, and likewise in the northeast is Ḍambinī;
these are the presiding deities of the great seats (mahāpīṭha) and the sacrificial seats (balipīṭha).
One should offer the bali-oblation accompanied by that mantra;
then, having entered the inner sanctum, one should purify the hand.
Afterwards, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) and present betel leaf (tāmbūla).
One should perform worship at the eastern gate, extending from Indra to Īśāna.

One should perform the *bali* offering for the *liṅga* at the western gate and for Varuṇa; having circumambulated and offered the *bali* up to the south-western corner according to the prescribed rite,
the preceptor should then place the *bali* for the deity of the southern gate.
One should offer the bali-oblation at the doors starting from the south and ending with the fire-altar (Agni).
One should offer the bali-oblation with the Saumya [mantra] to the liṅga at the northern gate.
Furthermore, one should cause the bali to be given from Soma up to Vāyu;
indeed, the bali should consist of sacrificial food (haviṣya), as well as for the spirits (bhūta) and diseases.
(349) Herein is the worship of the Fivefold Youth residing in the belly.

(B) He whose form is the light of the river of sound, who is gracious, *hrāṃ kṣīṃ maṃ*, the essence of the power of mantras, the *praṇava* (Oṃ), whose nature is the limited *bindu* and the end of *nāda*: *sāṃ kṣāṃ kṣūṃ*.
O you who grant fearlessness and destroy desire, salutations to you, Kālakālī! || 4 ||
She whose form is both meditation and non-meditation, who causes fear to the asuras, who is the singular light of the river of the Self,
who is directly perceptible, who dwells upon the sacred seats (pīṭhas), who causes fear to the three worlds, and whose nature is that of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
she is the pure Self, the embodiment of purity, self-acting without instruments, and the follower of the pure mind.
O Goddess who is the form of the creation and maintenance of the universe, who causes fear to the Triple City, salutations to you, the Goddess of all serpents! || 5 ||
Thus ends the Bālāpañcaka.

I bow to her who is seated upon the throne of the syllable *aiṃ*, whose fire is internalized, who bears the digit *khāṃ sauṃ klīṃ*, who wears golden garments, who possesses supreme nectar, who is endowed with a white upper cloth,
and whose uplifted hands shine with a book, a noose, a goad, and a rosary.

From the recitation of that Bālā Tripurī, whose body consists of three steps and who moves through the six cakras— from the recitation of the mantra perfected by recitation— perfection shall be attained here.
[This is] the *Bālātripurasundarī Stotra*.
To the venerable Lord Ratnācaleśvara, together with the venerable Arālakeśī as his companion.

(105) Seated comfortably upon the tortoise-throne, he is the one who opened the door-panels, whose pure arms are like serpents, who is the causeless destroyer of the bird [the sun], the pacifier of the cloth [the wind], and who worships with the Vāstu-Brahma-Gāyatrī.

Facing north, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the hands for purification, the conjunction with the self, burning, drying, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), immersion in nectar, the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), the placement of the hands (karanyāsa), the placement of the syllables (akṣaranyāsa), and the placement of the digits (kalānyāsa); then, one should cast off the natural state of contemplation.

I am Śiva; [this is] the meditation, the purification of the site for the internal sacrifice, the purification of the substances, the purification of the pedestal, the purification of the ground, and the dismissal of the floral offerings.

p. 354) Caṇḍeśvara, the Pūjā-liṅga, the Pīṭha, the Pāśupata-weapon, the Kūrma-stone, Ādhāraśakti, Andavāsukhī, Takṣa, Kātkoṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, Vāla, Gulikā, and others—beginning with Brahmā and the rest; [these belong to] the Dvāpara and Tretā ages created by Dāsa.

The qualities of the Kali Yuga are knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and so forth. Then there are the downward-facing and upward-facing [lotuses], the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*), the stainless throne (*vimalāsana*), and the lotus-throne (*padmāsana*).
At the tips of the buds, stalks, petals, and filaments of the lotus are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, and Balavikaraṇī.

The subduer of the powerful, the tamer of all beings, the one who transcends the mind; she whose seat is the presiding lord of the *ātmatattva*, the *vidyātattva*, and the *śivatattva*; she who is the *saṃhitā-mūrti* (the unified form), the embodiment of knowledge (*vidyā-deha*), and the creative power (*kalana*) of the respective presiding lords of the solar orb, the lunar orb, the fire orb, and the power orb.

[Perform] invocation (āvāhana), installation (sthāpana), presence (sannidhāna), firm fixation (sannirodhana), piercing (avakuṇḍana), the rite of nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa), the display of splendor (prarocana), the offering of water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the presentation of the respectful offering (arghya); then, following the purification by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), [perform] the consecratory bath (abhiṣeka), and [apply] the fragrant paste of flour (piṣṭa), turmeric (udvartana), and the powder of emblic myrobalan (āmalaka-rajas).
The offering of water scented with fragrance, water mixed with gold, and water with *kuśa* grass for washing the feet (*pādya*) and so forth;
the anointing with fragrant unguents such as sandalwood; ornaments such as golden bands and jewels;
and the decoration with garlands of lotuses, blue lilies, and other flowers, along with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Then, following that, the first enclosure consists of the imperishable *trapradāna*, as well as Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta, Hṛdaya, Śiras, Śikhā, Kavaca, Netra, and Astra.
Ānandeśa, Sūkṣma, Ekanetraka as spoken by Śiva,
Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin.
Thus ends the second enclosure.
Nandīkāla, Bhṛṅgin, Vighneśa, Vṛṣa, Ṣaṇmukha, and Caṇḍa— O Goddess, these are to be known as the deities intended for the third enclosure.
One should worship Dakṣiṇāmūrti in the south and Pitāmaha in the north;
Viṣṇu is to be worshipped in the west, and one should sacrifice to Vṛṣabha in the east.
But Gaurī is to be worshipped in the north; this is considered the fourth enclosure.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, as well as the noose and the goad; likewise, the trident, the wheel, and the lotus—this is [the sequence]. [Then] the drum and the citron.
Holding a snake, a rosary, and a blue lotus with five hands,
he bears multitudes of weapons in his five hands.
Having intentionally dissolved the mere manifestation of power above the form by means of the suppression of the shape of the *liṅga*, one should abandon the state of being a *liṅgin*.
Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being;
freed from sorrow, he beholds through the grace of the Creator that Lord, whose majesty is fashioned from darkness.

Oṃ ha, salutation to the one whose body is knowledge (vidyādeha). Having invoked [the deity] with the Prāsāda mantra and placed a flower upon the crown of the liṅga, one should display the mudrās for invocation and so forth using the Sadyojāta and other mantras.
Having displayed the Dhenu-mudrā with the root mantra, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) with the root mantra from beginning to end.

Having offered [the oblation] in two ways upon the five heads in the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Svāhā using the root mantra, having offered the rinsing water (ācamana) with the root mantra ending in Svadhā, and having offered flowers with the root mantra ending in Vauṣaṭ, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa.
Having first performed the anointing and other rites, one should visualize the consecration (abhiṣeka) as Maṇḍaleśvarī;
then, having offered garments, golden sacrificial threads, crowns, earrings, and other ornaments, and having seated her, [one should recite]:
"Oṃ hāṃ haum, obeisance to the Lord of the Ātma-tattva."
(157) Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śivāsana, the Lord of the Vidyātattva.
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the Śivatattva.
Having offered perfume, flowers, garlands, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, incense, and lamps.
Having struck the bell with the Astra-mantra and displayed the Manoratha-mudrā,

one should worship the limbs of dissolution (layāṅga), perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the deities beginning with Īśāna and ending with Astra at the locations starting from the head and ending at the feet,
and then worship the five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇa).
[I bow] to the Lord, who has the luster of crystal, the cause of the universe, three-eyed,
with the moon upon his crest, gentle, [and] holding a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands.
Oṃ hām, homage to Īśāna!
He is a man clad in yellow garments and a sacred thread, resembling gold,
holding a citron and a rosary, and bearing the moon upon his crest.

Oṃ Heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa. Then [one should meditate on him] as three-eyed, wearing a moon upon his crown, gentle, adorned with earrings, with tawny hair on his head, possessing fangs, and having a formidable face.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, decorated with snakes and scorpions,
[he holds] a khaṭvāṅga, a rosary for recitation, a shield, and a noose.
In his four left hands he holds a quadrangular shield, and in his four right hands he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, and a staff that crushes enemies.
Thus, the nine clouds shine;
[the mantra of the state beyond]— *oṃ vyomavyāpine vyomāya vyomarūpāya sarvavyāpine śivāya anantāya*.

Obeisance to Śiva, who is without support, without dependence, eternal, established upon the seat of Yoga, the eternally united one, the one who carries meditation; obeisance to Śiva, the source of all,
whose head is Īśāna, whose face is Tatpuruṣa, whose heart is Aghora, and whose private parts are Vāmadeva.
Obeisance again and again to the one whose form is that of the newly born;

to the protector of the most secret among secrets; to the one who is deathless; to the sovereign lord of all yoga; to the one whose nature is light; to the Supreme Lord; to the supreme; to the conscious and the unconscious; O sky, O sky! O pervader, O pervader! O formless one!

Formless, first among the first, heat, heat, light, light, without fire, without ash, beginningless, manifold, manifold, dhū dhū dhū dhū. Oṃ bhūḥ. Oṃ bhuvaḥ. Oṃ suvaḥ. Without end, O end, arising from the end, auspicious, auspicious, all, all, Supreme Self, Maheśvara.
O Mahādeva, Lord of the six states of existence, Sovereign of the yoga of great splendor, release me, release me! O Primordial One, Primordial One,
All-pervading One, All-pervading One, Source of Existence, Source of Existence, Arisen from Existence, Bestower of happiness upon all beings,
Maker of the presence of all, Supreme Brahman, Viṣṇu, and Rudra!
Unhonored, honored; unstudied, studied; previously situated, previously situated; witness, witness! Act, act! O bird, bird; tawny, tawny; knowledge, knowledge; sound, sound; subtle!
Subtle Śiva, Śiva, Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva, Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva, Oṃ, obeisance, obeisance!
May there be auspiciousness!
One should perform the rite for the Śiva-liṅga in the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), while for a mere Brāhmaṇa,
it should be performed in half of the pavilion (ardhamaṇḍapa).
The consecrated ascetics were attended by the bathing pavilion,
while the king, the Vaiśyas, and the Śūdras were attended by the great pavilion.
Otherwise, for all [deities], starting from the gate of the city-gate (gopura),
if the sequence of service is inverted, there is loss of position and destruction of the lineage.
[This concludes] the meditation on Annapūrṇā.
In her left hand, she holds a ruby vessel filled with honey; her lotus-hand shines, adorned with clusters of radiant gems;
her body is crimson, a pearl necklace glitters upon the slope of her breasts, and she possesses three eyes.
I bow to Ambikā Annapūrṇā, whose face blossoms like the full moon.
Vināyaka:
— (Ā) One should there meditate upon the Guru Brahmā, endowed with red-colored matted locks; [the mantra is:
"Oṃ, homage to Mahābrahmaguru."
I shall describe the vow of Vināyaka; listen, O best of men, for it destroys obstacles in the world and bestows the fruit of all desired objects.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśvara for the sake of destroying all calamities,
one should then worship the Lord of Gods at the beginning of the night of that day.
One should worship Vighnanāyaka with the nectar of the five products of the cow;
the wise one should tie a protective thread (kautuka) and wrap [the image] in a new cloth.
One should cause Gaṇeśvara to be offered unprecedented milk-rice accompanied by side dishes, as well as betel-leaf for fragrance.
Having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings, perform whatever hymn you desire;
then, having gratified [the deity] with dances and songs, pass the remainder of the night.
Then, at the time of dawn, one should perform the daily ritual;
one should surround the colored powder design with incense, perfumes, lamps, and the weapon-mantra.
Having purified the vessel with various substances according to the prescribed rites and having it accompanied by Vighneśvara,
one should inform the Lord of Devas of the vow, using the nectar of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should bathe Gaṇeśvara with other substances for bathing as well,
having adorned him especially with perfumes, flowers, garlands, and so forth.
One should offer edible foods such as cakes and the like, served with incense, lamps, and other offerings;
having worshipped them thoroughly with the root mantras, the wise practitioner should pray for their desired object.
Thus, at the time of dawn, one should worship Vighnanāyaka. [The meditation:
One should meditate upon the Lord who is as pure as a jasmine flower or the moon, five-faced, and of massive form.
One should remember that Guru who has ten arms and a serene countenance.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutations to the Gurus who are Sadāśiva. I take refuge in the Guru Ananta, who is red in color, possesses three eyes, is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and is equipped with the *ḍamaru* drum and the trident.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the infinite gurus. || 2 ||

I take refuge in the Guru Śrīkaṇṭha, who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a deer, and a trident in his hands; who has a bull as his vehicle; and whose radiance is white as camphor.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Gurus beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha. (3)
The goddess stands upon a lion, holding a trident and a blue lotus in her two hands;
she is adorned with a jeweled casket crown and decorated with strings of pearls.
Having meditated thus in the mind, one should take refuge in the Guru of Ambikā:
Oṃ hām, obeisance to the Gurus of Ambikā. || 4 ||
He has one face, a serene expression, and is red in color with three eyes;
he holds a spear and a trident in his hands, and is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should remember Guha, the teacher of the gods, whether he is seated or standing; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the teachers who are Skanda. || 5 ||
One should meditate there upon the Guru Viṣṇu, the god who holds the conch and the discus, Hari, clad in dark blue and yellow garments, together with Śrī and Bhūmi at his two sides.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu and the Gurus.
Four-faced and four-armed, holding a staff, a rosary, and a water-pot,
adorned with [the aforementioned] ornaments.
Mounted upon a vehicle drawn by jackals, with lions, tigers, and other beasts as her mounts;
she who is fond of human blood, the embodiment of illusion (māyā), and who partakes of offerings of honey and meat.
The man who would constantly hear this, or whoever would recite it,
[attains] the removal of ten million battles and the destruction of disease and poverty.
One always attains all accomplishments and achieves every desire by [worshipping] the Goddess,
who brings bliss to her devotees and whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.
[I worship] Tripura, the presiding deity, who is the mistress of desired objects, the perfection consisting of all powers, and who resides in the eighteen sacred seats.
I bow to the Goddess Viśveśvarī, who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
likewise, this meditation on the Saptashatī is the granter of all protection.
The means for attaining cyclic existence shall be accomplished through the perfection of the pill and gold;
likewise, the pair of sandals shall be perfected, as well as the sword and the power of the hand.
It bestows the accomplishment of Sarasvatī, prosperity, and likewise brings about the perfection of mantras;
it removes afflictions of the home and so forth, as well as destroying all calamities.
Honor from the king of beauty, the increase of sons and grandsons,
sovereignty, the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi), and the state of a yogin who can assume any form at will.
A man who constantly remembers my deity Caṇḍikā, who is ever-present prosperity, with diligent effort, shall attain her within six months.
By removing great fear and likewise destroying enemies,
one attains unshakable prosperity through the goddess Padmarāgaprabhā, who is as red as the rays of the rising sun.
The goddess has ten feet, bestows gifts, and is filled with ten mandalas;
she has ten faces, three eyes, and uplifted breasts.
One should thus meditate upon the Great Radiant One, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura, who is clothed in red perfumes and garments, and adorned with red garlands and unguents.
She is adorned with all ornaments, seated upon the vehicle of the Great Lion,
standing in the midst of the eight Mothers, and worshipped by the eight Bhairavas.
[She is] Cintāmaṇi Mahādurgā, the destroyer of all enemies,
the eradicator of all poverty, and the warder-off of all suffering.
In the midst of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), [I meditate upon] the Goddess who has a great mouth and terrifying hands, whose tongue is food,
who possesses ten thousand arms, and who wields various weapons and missiles.
The Goddess, who is intent on the slaughter of Raktabīja, is prepared for various battles, possesses a universal body, is of the nature of Śiva, and is the destroyer of the Dānavas.
Caṇḍī, who wears red garments, is terrifying and exceedingly formidable;
she is Lakṣmī in the full bloom of youth, Kālikā, seated upon a lotus.
She who destroyed Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura,
the severer of the heads of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, and the one who brings joy to all the gods.
She who destroys Raktabīja, who devours the hosts of Asuras,
who possesses a twofold vigor against Sumbha, and who is infinitely terrifying.
The body adorned with a garland of great cosmic eggs— (B) obeisance.

Purification through the three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*), the placement of syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*), the severing of the knots characterized by [the emergence of] the [divine] forms, the union with the Self, burning, flooding, and the flooding with nectar.
The ritual placement of the self and the non-self (*ātman-anātmaka-nyāsa*), the thirty-eight-fold placement of the *kalās*, the placement of the *mātṛkās*, the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*),

the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), the contemplation "I am Śiva" (*śivo'ham-bhāvanā*), the consecration with water from the weapon-mantra (*astrāmbu-sthāpana*), the preparation of the general offering (*sāmānyārghya-sādhana*), the purification of the self, the purification of the materials, the purification of the mantras, and the worship of Ṛṣabha.
The sprinkling of the doorway, the worship of the door-keepers,
the worship of the eternal garments on the right and left pillars of the door,
the meditation upon Bhuvaṅga and Pataṅga, and the worship of Nandi and Gaṅgā on the right side of the door.

One should worship Mahākāla and Yamunā to the left of the door; above the door, one should worship Gaṇapati on the right, Sarasvatī in the middle, and Mahālakṣmī on the left. On the two door-panels, one should worship Vimala and [the others], and on the lintel (paṭṭikā), one should worship Skanda and the ritual peg (kīla).

Having worshipped Vighneśa and Guha, and having deposited the nine powers (*navashakti*) into the cavity, one should worship Śiva; then, having expelled the obstacles of the ground and the atmosphere from the door— specifically those guarding the right and left doors— one should perform the installation.

Having worshipped the Pāśupata weapon at the entrance to the inner chamber, having honored the Great [Liṅga] and the Guṇa, having performed the worship of the guardians of the internal door and the Lord of the Site (Vāstvadhipati), and having completed the dismissal of the remains of the offering (nirmālya-visarjana) and the purification of the self-originated (Svāyambhuva) and other liṅgas, as well as the purification of the site and the pedestal of the liṅga...
(120a) Then, at the time of evening, one should bathe [the image] with fragrant waters;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should offer incense, lamps, and the like.
One should cause Gaṇeśvara to be offered cakes, flattened grains, parched rice, gu----, pieces of sugar-cane, jackfruit, amṛgadalī, and other such foods.
The preceptor should perform sacrifices with sixteen types of oblations and pray for his desired goal;
thereafter, he should conduct a festival according to his financial means.
Having offered abundant oblations, one should give edible foods such as cakes and the like;
there, one should worship the preceptor with garments, gold, and finger-rings.
Thus, the mortal who performs this shall attain the supreme state.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for the Vināyaka vow in the Aṃśumat Tantra. 15.
May there be auspiciousness!
Regarding the daily worship (nityapūjā): [p. 336]

Oṃ. Having risen at dawn, [one should perform] the remembrance of Śiva, purification, sipping water, cleansing the teeth, purification of the nose, bathing according to the prescribed rules, the bath with earth, the bath with water,
the ash-bath, the Mahendra-bath, the Brahma-bath, the Varuṇa-bath, the mental bath, and the mantra-bath.
The stringing of the weapon, the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), the twilight worship of Śiva, the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra,

[the invocation of] the gods, sages, and humans— [then] the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), the offering of water to the Sun, the entry into the temple, the washing of the feet, and sitting upon the tortoise-seat (*kūrmāsana*), the yoga-seat (*yugāsana*), and the beautiful seat (*rucirāsana*), followed by the purification of the hands and the ten [fingers].
